title: Lemma 9.3.12
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Lemma 9.3.12 . D245F9712FB1 Let $M$ be a complex manifold, let $(v,w)$, $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ k)$ with $k\geq 0$, be holomorphic coordinates on an open set $U\subset M$, and let $N=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} \subset U$. Then for every $y\in U$ the ideal $I_{N,y}$ of germs vanishing on $(N,y)$ is generated by the germs of $w_1,\ldots ,w_ k$; it is the unit ideal if $y\notin N$. Moreover, for $y\in N$ the germ $(N,y)$ is irreducible, and its dimension is $\dim _ yM-k$, the dimension of $N$ at $y$. Proof. If $y\in U\setminus N$, then some $w_ l$ does not vanish at $y$, so it is a unit, and $(N,y)$ is empty because $N$ is closed in $U$; both ideals are the unit ideal. Let $y\in N$, and let $g$ be holomorphic on a polydisc centered at $y$ in the coordinates $(v,w)$, vanishing on $N$. Then $g(v,0)=0$, and \[  g(v,w)=\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}g(v,tw)\, \mathrm dt=\sum _ lw_ l\int _0^1\partial _{w_ l}g(v,tw)\, \mathrm dt,  \] where the integrals are holomorphic by differentiation under the integral sign. Hence the germ of $g$ lies in the ideal generated by $w_1,\ldots ,w_ k$; conversely, the $w_ l$ vanish on $N$. Consequently, the map $g\mapsto g(v,0)$ identifies the quotient of $\mathcal O_{M,y}$ by this ideal with the ring of germs of holomorphic functions of $v$ at $v(y)$, which is an integral domain (section 9.2 ); so $I_{N,y}$ is prime. Since $y\in N$, the germ $(N,y)$ is nonempty, and it is irreducible by proposition 9.3.1 . All points of $N$ near $y$ are regular points of $N$ of dimension $\dim _ yM-k$, so this is the dimension of $(N,y)$, by proposition 9.3.9 . $\square$

title: Corollary 9.3.13
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Corollary 9.3.13 . F1291FB3DBB9 Let $A$ be an analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$. The singular locus $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is an analytic subset, and at every point of $A$ the intersection of $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ with each irreducible branch of $A$ has smaller dimension than that branch. More precisely, if $x\in A$ and $A_1,\ldots ,A_ p$ are sufficiently small representatives of the branches of $(A,x)$, then near $x$ \[  A_{\mathrm{sing}}=\bigcup _ i(A_ i)_{\mathrm{sing}}\cup \bigcup _{i<j}(A_ i\cap A_ j);  \] thus a point near $x$ is a regular point of $A$ if and only if it lies on exactly one $A_ i$ and is a regular point of $A_ i$. Let $A$ have dimension at most $d$ at every point, and define $A^{(0)}=A$ and $A^{(j+1)}=(A^{(j)})_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Then $A^{(d+1)}=\varnothing $, and $A$ is the union of the sets $A^{(j)}_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $0\leq j\leq d$, where $A^{(j)}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a complex submanifold of dimension at most $d-j$ of the open set $M\setminus A^{(j+1)}$. With $d$ as in (2), the set $A$ is locally a countable union of real submanifolds of dimensions at most $2d$, and also of images of compact cubes in $\mathbb R^ r$, $r\leq 2d$, under Lipschitz maps. The image of a compact cube in $\mathbb R^ r$ under a Lipschitz map is $\mathcal H^ s$-null, in the sense of section 5.11 , for every $s>r$. In particular, in every chart $A$ is locally $\mathcal H^ s$-null for every $s>2d$. Proof. (1) Let $A$ first be a small representative of an irreducible germ of dimension $e$ in $\mathbb C^ n$, pure-dimensional by proposition 9.3.9 , and choose generators $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ of $\mathcal I_ A$ on a neighborhood, by theorem 9.3.10 . At a regular point, these generate the ideal of the manifold $A$, which is generated by $n-e$ normal coordinates (lemma 9.3.12 ); differentiating, we see that the matrix of differentials of the $g_ j$ has rank $n-e$ there. Every minor of size $n-e+1$ therefore vanishes on the dense covering locus, hence on $A$, so the rank is at most $n-e$ everywhere on $A$. Conversely, if it equals $n-e$ at $y\in A$, choose $n-e$ of the $g_ j$ with independent differentials at $y$. Together with $e$ suitable coordinate functions they form holomorphic coordinates near $y$, by the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 5.2.4 (2)), so their common zero set is an $e$-dimensional submanifold $N$ near $y$, and it contains $A$. Every branch of $(A,y)$ has dimension $e$ and is contained in the germ $(N,y)$, which is irreducible of dimension $e$ by lemma 9.3.12 , so it equals $(N,y)$ by proposition 9.3.9 ; hence $A$ is a manifold near $y$. Thus $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is the subset of $A$ where all minors of size $n-e$ of this matrix vanish, an analytic subset. For a general analytic set $A$ near a point $x$, let $A_1,\ldots ,A_ p$ be small representatives of the branches of $(A,x)$. A point $y$ near $x$ lying on only one $A_ i$ is regular for $A$ if and only if it is regular for $A_ i$. A point $y\in A_ i\cap A_ j$, $i\neq j$, is singular. Indeed, otherwise $(A,y)$ would be irreducible, hence equal to some $(A_ k,y)$, and we may assume $k\neq i$; then $(A_ i,y)\subset (A_ i\cap A_ k,y)$. But $\dim (A_ i\cap A_ k,x)<\dim A_ i$ by proposition 9.3.9 , so $\dim (A_ i\cap A_ k,y)<\dim A_ i=\dim (A_ i,y)$ by upper semicontinuity and purity, contradicting monotonicity. This proves the formula for $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ near $x$, which is therefore analytic by the irreducible case. Finally, let $y\in A$ and let $B$ be a branch of $(A,y)$. By corollary 9.3.6 , $B$ contains points of the covering locus of a parametrization of $B$ outside the other branches of $(A,y)$, arbitrarily close to $y$, and these are regular points of $A$. Hence the germ of $A_{\mathrm{sing}}\cap B$ at $y$ differs from $B$, and it has smaller dimension than $B$, by proposition 9.3.9 . (2) By (1), each $A^{(j)}$ is analytic, and $\dim (A^{(j+1)},x)<\dim (A^{(j)},x)$ at each point $x$ of $A^{(j+1)}$, because every branch of $(A^{(j+1)},x)$ lies in a branch of $(A^{(j)},x)$ and in the singular locus. Hence $A^{(j)}$ has dimension at most $d-j$ at each of its points, and $A^{(d+1)}=\varnothing $, a set of dimension $-1$ being empty. Each $A^{(j)}_{\mathrm{reg}}=A^{(j)}\setminus A^{(j+1)}$ is a complex submanifold of $M\setminus A^{(j+1)}$ of dimension at most $d-j$, and $A$ is the union of these sets. (3) Each of the submanifolds in (2) is locally a countable union of coordinate charts, so $A$ is locally a countable union of real submanifolds of dimensions at most $2d$. Each such chart is a countable union of images of compact cubes in $\mathbb R^ r$, $r\leq 2d$, under Lipschitz maps, because the image of the chart in $\mathbb R^ r$ is a countable union of compact cubes, on each of which the smooth inverse of the chart is Lipschitz, by the mean value inequality. Such an image is $\mathcal H^ s$-null for $s>r$: covering the cube by $O(\delta ^{-r})$ cubes of side $\delta $, whose images have diameter $O(\delta )$, we cover the image by $O(\delta ^{-r})$ balls of radii $O(\delta )$, and the sum of the $s$th powers of these radii is $O(\delta ^{s-r})$, which tends to zero with $\delta $. A countable union of $\mathcal H^ s$-null sets is $\mathcal H^ s$-null, which completes the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.3.14 (Constant rank theorem)
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Lemma 9.3.14 (Constant rank theorem) . F802E1301C0F Let $F$ be a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$ to $\mathbb C^ K$ whose differential has constant rank $r$ near a point $p$. Then, after a permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb C^ K$, there are a biholomorphic map $\phi $ from a neighborhood of $p$ onto a polydisc $Q'\times Q''\subset \mathbb C^ r\times \mathbb C^{m-r}$ and a biholomorphic map $\psi $ of $Q'\times \mathbb C^{K-r}$ onto itself such that \[  F\circ \phi ^{-1}(y',y'')=\psi (y',0)\qquad \text{for }(y',y'')\in Q'\times Q''.  \] In particular, the fibers of $F$ near $p$ are complex submanifolds of dimension $m-r$, and $F$ maps a neighborhood of $p$ onto a closed complex submanifold of dimension $r$ of a neighborhood of $F(p)$. Proof. After permuting the coordinates of the source and of the target, we may assume that the matrix $(\partial F_ i/\partial x_ j(p))_{i,j\leq r}$ is invertible. The map $\phi (x)=(F_1(x),\ldots ,F_ r(x),x_{r+1},\ldots ,x_ m)$ has invertible derivative at $p$, so by the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 5.2.4 (1)) it maps a neighborhood of $p$ biholomorphically onto a polydisc $Q'\times Q''$ centered at $\phi (p)$, on which the rank of $G=F\circ \phi ^{-1}$ is $r$. This map has the form $G(y)=(y',G''(y))$ with $y'=(y_1,\ldots ,y_ r)$ and $G''=(G_{r+1},\ldots ,G_ K)$. For $i,j>r$, the minor of the Jacobian matrix of $G$ formed by the rows $1,\ldots ,r,i$ and the columns $1,\ldots ,r,j$ equals $\partial G_ i/\partial y_ j$, because the first $r$ rows are $(I,0)$; since the rank is $r$, these derivatives vanish. As $Q''$ is convex, $G''(y',y'')=G''(y',c'')$, where $c''$ is the center of $Q''$. The map $\psi (w',w'')=(w',w''+G''(w',c''))$ is a biholomorphism of $Q'\times \mathbb C^{K-r}$ onto itself, with inverse $(w',w'')\mapsto (w',w''-G''(w',c''))$, and $G(y',y'')=\psi (y',0)$. The fibers of $G$ are the slices $\{ y'\} \times Q''$, and its image is $\psi (Q'\times \{ 0\} )$, a closed submanifold of $Q'\times \mathbb C^{K-r}$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.3.15
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Lemma 9.3.15 . A814C831E915 Let $N$ be a complex manifold with a countable basis. If $F\colon N\to \mathbb C^ K$ is a holomorphic map whose differential has rank at most $k$ at every point, then $F(N)$ is $\mathcal H^ s$-null for every $s>2k$. If an analytic subset $Y$ of an open subset of $\mathbb C^ K$ is $\mathcal H^{2k+2}$-null, then $\dim (Y,y)\leq k$ for every $y\in Y$. Let $A\subset N$ be an analytic subset with $\dim (A,x)\leq d$ for all $x\in A$, and let $F\colon N\to M$ be a holomorphic map to a complex manifold such that $F(A)$ is an analytic subset of an open subset of $M$. Then $\dim (F(A),w)\leq d$ for every $w\in F(A)$. Proof. We use the properties of $\mathcal H^ s$-null sets recalled in section 5.11 : subsets and countable unions of such sets, and their images under Lipschitz maps, are again $\mathcal H^ s$-null, and an $\mathcal H^ s$-null subset of $\mathbb R^ b$ with $s\leq b$ is Lebesgue null. Moreover, the image of a compact cube in $\mathbb R^ r$ under a Lipschitz map is $\mathcal H^ s$-null for $s>r$, by corollary 9.3.13 (3), and a $C^1$ map is Lipschitz on every compact convex subset of its domain, by the mean value inequality. (1) We argue by induction on the dimension of $N$. Since $N$ has at most countably many connected components, each of them open with a countable basis, we may assume that $N$ is connected, of dimension $n$. If $n=0$, then $F(N)$ is a point. Let $n\geq 1$, and let $r\leq k$ be the maximal rank of $\mathrm dF$ on $N$. The set $N_1$ of points where the rank is less than $r$ is the common zero set of the minors of size $r$ of the Jacobian matrix in local coordinates, so it is an analytic subset of $N$ different from $N$. Hence it is nowhere dense, and its germs, being proper subgerms of the irreducible manifold germs of dimension $n$ (lemma 9.3.12 ), have dimension at most $n-1$ by proposition 9.3.9 . On the open set $N\setminus N_1$ the rank is constantly $r$. Let $p\in N\setminus N_1$, and choose $\phi $, $\psi $ and $Q'\times Q''$ as in lemma 9.3.14 , in a chart around $p$. Let $C'\subset Q'$ be a compact cube, a product of closed squares, containing the first $r$ coordinates of $\phi (p)$ in its interior, and let $V=\phi ^{-1}(\operatorname{Int}C'\times Q'')$. Then $F(V)\subset \psi (C'\times \{ 0\} )$, the image of a compact cube in $\mathbb R^{2r}$ under the restriction of $\psi $, which is Lipschitz there because $C'\times \{ 0\} $ is a compact convex subset of the convex domain of $\psi $. Hence $F(V)$ is $\mathcal H^ s$-null for $s>2r$, in particular for $s>2k$. Countably many such sets $V$ cover $N\setminus N_1$, because $N$ has a countable basis. By corollary 9.3.13 (2), $N_1$ is the union of finitely many complex submanifolds of open subsets of $N$, of dimensions at most $n-1$; they have countable bases, and the restriction of $F$ to each of them has rank at most $k$. By the induction hypothesis their images are $\mathcal H^ s$-null for $s>2k$, and therefore so is $F(N)$. (2) Suppose that $\dim (Y,y)\geq k+1$ for some $y\in Y$, and let $Y_1$ be a branch of $(Y,y)$ of dimension $e\geq k+1$. By corollary 9.3.6 , $Y_1$ contains points of the covering locus of a parametrization of $Y_1$ outside the other branches of $(Y,y)$; near such a point $p$, the set $Y$ is a complex submanifold of dimension $e$, so it contains a complex submanifold $P$ of dimension $k+1$ through $p$, for instance a coordinate slice. The orthogonal projection $\Pi $ of $\mathbb C^ K$ onto the tangent space $T_ pP$, a complex subspace of dimension $k+1$, is $1$-Lipschitz, and its restriction to $P$ has invertible derivative at $p$. By the inverse function theorem, $\Pi (P)$ contains a nonempty open subset of $T_ pP\cong \mathbb R^{2k+2}$. On the other hand, $\Pi (P)\subset \Pi (Y)$ is $\mathcal H^{2k+2}$-null and hence Lebesgue null. This contradiction proves (2). (3) By corollary 9.3.13 (2), $A$ is the union of finitely many complex submanifolds $A_ l$ of open subsets of $N$, of dimensions at most $d$. Let $(V,\chi )$ be a holomorphic chart of $M$ around a point of $F(A)$, with values in $\mathbb C^ K$. The restriction of $\chi \circ F$ to the open subset $A_ l\cap F^{-1}(V)$ of $A_ l$ has rank at most $\dim A_ l\leq d$, so by (1) the set $\chi (F(A)\cap V)=\bigcup _ l\chi \circ F(A_ l\cap F^{-1}(V))$ is $\mathcal H^{2d+2}$-null. Near each of its points it is an analytic subset of an open subset of $\mathbb C^ K$, so (2) shows that $\dim (F(A),w)\leq d$ for $w\in F(A)\cap V$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.3.16
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text:
Corollary 9.3.16 . 725857B32C0E Let $A$ be an analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$. The regular locus $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is dense in $A$. The closures of the connected components of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ are irreducible analytic subsets of $A$, called the irreducible components of $A$; they form a locally finite family with union $A$, and none of them is contained in the union of the others. Every locally finite family of irreducible analytic subsets with union $A$, none of which is contained in another, consists of these components. If $M$ has a countable basis, there are at most countably many irreducible components. The regular locus of an irreducible component $Z$ is connected, and a holomorphic function defined near $Z$ that vanishes on a nonempty relatively open subset of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ vanishes on $Z$. Proof. Fix $x\in A$, let $A_1,\ldots ,A_ p$ be representatives of the branches of $(A,x)$, and for each $i$ choose a parametrization polydisc $P_ i$ of $(A_ i,x)$ so small that $A\cap P_ i= igcup _ j A_ j\cap P_ i$. By corollary 9.3.13 (1), $A_{\mathrm{sing}}\cap A_ i$ is an analytic subset of $A_ i$ whose germ at $x$ differs from $(A_ i,x)$. Hence $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ meets the connected covering locus of $A_ i$ in a proper analytic subset, and by lemma 9.2.9 and corollary 9.3.6 , the covering locus minus $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is connected and dense in $A_ i\cap P_ i$. The set $R_ i=A_ i\cap P_ i\cap A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ lies between this connected set and its closure, so it is connected and dense in $A_ i\cap P_ i$. In particular $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is dense in $A$. Let $\{ S_\alpha \} $ be the connected components of the manifold $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and $Z_\alpha =\overline{S_\alpha }$. Each $R_ i$ above is connected, so it lies in a single component $S_{\alpha (i)}$. Let $U= igcap _ iP_ i$. Then $S_\alpha \cap U$ is contained in the union of the $A_ i$ with $\alpha (i)=\alpha $, because points of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap A_ i\cap U$ lie in $R_ i$; conversely $A_ i\cap U\subset \overline{R_ i}\subset Z_{\alpha (i)}$. Hence \[  Z_\alpha \cap U= igcup _{i:\, \alpha (i)=\alpha }A_ i\cap U.  \] Thus each $Z_\alpha $ is analytic, only finitely many of them meet $U$, and their union is $A$. Since $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is open in $A$ and its connected components are open in it, $S_\alpha $ is open in $A$. So every point of $S_\alpha $ has a neighborhood that meets no other $S_ eta $, and therefore does not lie in $Z_ eta =\overline{S_ eta }$ for $ eta 
eq \alpha $. Thus $S_\alpha \cap Z_ eta =\varnothing $ for $ eta 
eq \alpha $, and no $Z_\alpha $ is contained in the union of the others. The same remark shows that $S_\alpha \subset (Z_\alpha )_{\mathrm{reg}}$: near a point of $S_\alpha $, the set $Z_\alpha $ coincides with the manifold $A$. Hence $(Z_\alpha )_{\mathrm{reg}}$ lies between the connected set $S_\alpha $ and its closure, and is connected. If $Z_\alpha $ were the union of two analytic subsets $Z'$, $Z''$ different from it, then $S_\alpha \cap Z'$ and $S_\alpha \cap Z''$ would be analytic subsets of the connected manifold $S_\alpha $ different from $S_\alpha $, since otherwise their closure would be $Z_\alpha $. As proper analytic subsets of a connected manifold, they would be closed and nowhere dense in $S_\alpha $ (lemma 9.2.8 ), and so would their union, which is $S_\alpha $. This contradiction shows that $Z_\alpha $ is irreducible. If $M$ has a countable basis, so does $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$; each $S_\alpha $ is open in $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and contains a basic open set, and disjoint components contain different ones, so there are at most countably many components. Finally, a holomorphic function vanishing on a nonempty open subset of the connected manifold $(Z_\alpha )_{\mathrm{reg}}$ vanishes on all of it by the identity theorem, and hence on its closure $Z_\alpha $. It remains to prove uniqueness. Let $A= igcup _ eta Y_ eta $ be a locally finite decomposition into irreducible analytic subsets, none contained in another. A connected manifold is not a locally finite union of closed nowhere dense subsets, since such a union is closed and nowhere dense. Since proper analytic subsets of the connected manifold $S_\alpha $ are nowhere dense (lemma 9.2.8 ), each $S_\alpha $ lies in some $Y_ eta $, and then $Z_\alpha \subset Y_ eta $. Conversely, fix $ eta $. By what we have proved, applied to the analytic set $Y_ eta $, the set $Y_ eta $ is the union of its irreducible components, and it has only one, for otherwise it would be the union of one of them and of the union of the others, two analytic subsets different from $Y_ eta $. Hence $(Y_ eta )_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $Y_ eta $ and covered by the locally finite family of closed analytic subsets $(Y_ eta )_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap Z_\alpha $; as before, $Y_ eta \subset Z_\alpha $ for some $\alpha $. Choosing $ eta '$ with $Z_\alpha \subset Y_{ eta '}$, we get $Y_ eta \subset Y_{ eta '}$, so $ eta '= eta $ and $Y_ eta =Z_\alpha $. Thus every $Y_ eta $ is an irreducible component of $A$; and every component $Z_\alpha $, being contained in some $Y_ eta =Z_{\alpha '}$, equals it, because $S_\alpha \cap Z_{\alpha '}=\varnothing $ for $\alpha '
eq \alpha $. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.3.17
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Corollary 9.3.17 . 27E8771DE67A Let $Z$ be an irreducible analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$. Then $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $Z$, and: all branches of all germs $(Z,x)$, $x\in Z$, have the dimension of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$; in particular, $Z$ is pure-dimensional; every analytic subset $Y\subset Z$ different from $Z$ is nowhere dense in $Z$, and $\dim (Y,x)<\dim Z$ for every $x\in Y$; if $Z'\supset Z$ is an irreducible analytic subset of $M$ with $\dim Z'=\dim Z$, then $Z'=Z$; if $Z$ is contained in the union of a locally finite family of analytic subsets of $M$, then it is contained in one of them. Proof. By the uniqueness in corollary 9.3.16 , applied to the family consisting of $Z$ alone, $Z$ is its own only irreducible component; so $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected and dense in $Z$, and its dimension is constant. (1) Let $B$ be a branch of $(Z,x)$. By corollary 9.3.6 , $B$ contains points of the covering locus of a parametrization of $B$ outside the other branches of $(Z,x)$. Near such a point, $Z$ coincides with $B$ and is a manifold of dimension $\dim B$, so the point lies in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and $\dim B=\dim Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. (2) The analytic subset $Y\cap Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of the connected manifold $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has empty interior in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$: otherwise it would be all of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, by lemma 9.2.8 , and the closed set $Y$ would contain the closure $Z$ of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Since $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is open and dense in $Z$, it follows that the closed set $Y$ has empty interior in $Z$. Now let $x\in Y$. Every branch $Y_1$ of $(Y,x)$ is contained in a branch $B$ of $(Z,x)$, and it differs from $B$: otherwise $Y$ would contain the points of $B$ near $x$ outside the other branches of $(Z,x)$, which form a nonempty open subset of $Z$ by corollary 9.3.6 . By proposition 9.3.9 and (1), $\dim Y_1<\dim B=\dim Z$. (3) Let $e=\dim Z=\dim Z'$. By corollary 9.3.13 (1) and by (1), $Z'_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension less than $e$ at each of its points, so by (2), applied to $Z'_{\mathrm{sing}}\cap Z\subset Z$, there is a point $p\in Z_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus Z'_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Near $p$, the set $Z$ is a submanifold of dimension $e$ of the manifold $Z'$ of dimension $e$; since the germ of a manifold is irreducible (lemma 9.3.12 ) and proper subgerms of irreducible germs have smaller dimension (proposition 9.3.9 ), $Z$ and $Z'$ coincide near $p$. Thus the analytic subset $Z$ of $Z'$ has interior points in $Z'$, and $Z=Z'$ by (2). (4) Let $Z\subset \bigcup _\beta Y_\beta $ with $(Y_\beta )$ locally finite. The sets $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap Y_\beta $ are closed analytic subsets of the connected manifold $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ with union $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. A locally finite union of closed nowhere dense sets is closed and nowhere dense, so one of them has interior points and is therefore all of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Then $Z\subset Y_\beta $, because $Y_\beta $ is closed and $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is dense in $Z$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.3.18
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Corollary 9.3.18 . 6DDD0384D260 Let $A$ be an analytic subset of codimension at least two of a complex manifold $M$. Then every plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $M\setminus A$ is locally bounded above near $A$ and extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $M$, whose value at $a\in A$ is $\varlimsup _{M\setminus A\ni y\to a}u(y)$. Proof. The assertion is local, and extensions defined on overlapping charts agree, since their values on $A$ are given by the same formula. Near a point where $M$ has dimension at most one, the codimension condition forces $A=\varnothing $. Otherwise, let $\Omega $ be a connected coordinate chart of dimension $n\geq 2$. Then $\dim A\leq n-2$, and corollary 9.3.13 (3) shows that $A\cap \Omega $ is locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since $2n-3>2(n-2)$. By theorem 5.11.3 , $u$ extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ with the stated values on $A$; being upper semicontinuous, the extension is locally bounded above. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.3.19
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text:
Lemma 9.3.19 . 113991711A43 Let $D$ be an irreducible analytic subset of codimension one of a complex manifold $M$ of dimension $n$. Every point $x\in D$ has an open neighborhood $V$ with a holomorphic function $f$ on $V$, a local equation of $D$, such that $D\cap V=f^{-1}(0)$, the germ of $f$ generates $\mathcal I_{D,y}$ for every $y\in V$, and $f$ vanishes to order one along $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap V$: near each point of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap V$ it is a unit times a holomorphic coordinate $	au $ with $D=\{ 	au =0\} $. On $V$ we have $[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$. In particular, $[D]$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $M$ with measure coefficients. Proof. By corollary 9.3.17 , $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $D$, and all branches of $D$ at all points have the dimension $n-1$ of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Let $x\in D$ and let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ k$ be representatives of the branches of $(D,x)$. We construct a generator $f_ i$ of the ideal of each $D_ i$ near $x$, and show that $f=f_1\cdots f_ k$ has the required properties. Step 1: an equation of one branch. Fix $i$, and take a parametrization of $(D_ i,x)$ as in theorem 9.3.4 , in coordinates centered at $x$. Its base dimension is $d=n-1$, by proposition 9.3.9 , so $z''=z_ n$ is a single coordinate. For $z'\in \Delta '\setminus \{ \delta =0\} $, the $q$ points of $D_ i$ over $z'$ are distinct, and therefore so are their coordinates $z_ n$; put $P(z',T)=\prod _{z\in \pi ^{-1}(z')}(T-z_ n)$. The coefficients of $P$ are, up to sign, the elementary symmetric functions of these coordinates; they are holomorphic, because the sheets are graphs of holomorphic maps, and bounded, because $\Delta ''$ is bounded, so they extend holomorphically to $\Delta '$ by lemma 9.2.9 . As $z'	o 0$, the points of $D_ i$ over $z'$ tend to $0$, because $\pi $ is proper and $\pi ^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $; hence the extended coefficients vanish at $0$, and $P$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $q$ in $z_ n$. The function $P(z',z_ n)$ vanishes on the covering locus, hence on $D_ i\cap (\Delta '	imes \Delta '')$, by density and continuity. The germ of $P(z',z_ n)$ generates the prime ideal $I_{D_ i,x}$. Indeed, let $g\in I_{D_ i,x}$, and let $R$ be the remainder of the division of $g$ by $P$ (proposition 9.2.2 ), a polynomial in $z_ n$ of degree less than $q$ with coefficients holomorphic near $0$ in $\mathbb C^{n-1}$; it vanishes on $D_ i$ near $0$, since $g$ and $P(z',z_ n)$ do. For $z'$ near $0$ with $\delta (z')
eq 0$, the $q$ points of $D_ i$ over $z'$ are close to $0$, so $R(z',\cdot )$ vanishes at their $q$ distinct coordinates $z_ n$ and is zero. The coefficients of $R$ thus vanish on a dense subset of a neighborhood of $0$, and $R=0$. Let $f_ i$ be a holomorphic function near $x$ with the germ of $P(z',z_ n)$. The sheaf $\mathcal I_{D_ i}$ has finitely many generators near $x$ by theorem 9.3.10 , and each of them is a multiple of $f_ i$ at $x$, hence on a neighborhood; so $f_ i$ generates $\mathcal I_{D_ i,y}$ for $y$ near $x$. In particular, at every point near $x$ outside $D_ i$ the ideal of $D_ i$ is the unit ideal, so $f_ i$ does not vanish there, and $f_ i^{-1}(0)=D_ i$ near $x$. Step 2: the product $f=f_1\cdots f_ k$. Let $y\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be close to $x$. By corollary 9.3.13 (1), $y$ lies on only one $D_ i$, and $D=D_ i=\{ 	au =0\} $ near $y$ for a local coordinate $	au $; then $f_ i$ is a unit times $	au $, since both generate $\mathcal I_{D_ i,y}$ (lemma 9.3.12 ), and $f_ j(y)
eq 0$ for $j
eq i$, by Step 1. Thus $f$ vanishes to order one along $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near $x$, and $f^{-1}(0)=D$ near $x$. Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ on which all this holds and on which, in addition, $D_ i\setminus  igcup _{j
eq i}D_ j$ is dense in $D_ i$ for every $i$; this is possible by corollary 9.3.6 , since the branches are irredundant. Let $y\in V$ and $g\in \mathcal I_{D,y}$; we show by induction on $l$ that $g\in (f_1\cdots f_ l)_ y$. For $l=0$ there is nothing to prove. If $g=f_1\cdots f_ lh$ with $l<k$, then $h$ vanishes near $y$ on $D_{l+1}\setminus (D_1\cup \cdots \cup D_ l)$, where the $f_ i$, $i\leq l$, have no zeros; this set is dense in $D_{l+1}$, so $h$ vanishes on $D_{l+1}$ near $y$, and $h\in (f_{l+1})_ y$. Hence $f$ generates $\mathcal I_{D,y}$. Finally, in the notation of section 5.5 , the regular part of the zero set of $f$ is $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap V$, with multiplicity one. By theorem 5.5.6 , $[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$ on $V$; hence $[D]$ is closed and positive, with measure coefficients of locally finite mass. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.3.20
section: 9.3 Analytic sets and their local branches
text: Theorem 9.3.20 . D73EBFFE10D2 Let $A$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$, and let $R$ be a closed real $(1,1)$-current on $M$ with measure coefficients and support in $A$. Then \[  R=\sum _ D c_ D[D],  \] where $D$ ranges over the irreducible components of $A$ of codimension one, the real coefficients $c_ D$ are uniquely determined, and the sum is locally finite. If $R$ is positive, then every $c_ D\geq 0$. In particular $R=0$ if $A$ has codimension at least two. Proof. Working on each connected component of $M$ separately, we may assume that $M$ is connected, of dimension $n$. Step 1: supports of high codimension. Suppose first that, near a point, the support of $R$ lies in a real submanifold $\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $ with independent differentials $\mathrm dg_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dg_ k$, $k\geq 3$. Since $R$ has measure coefficients and $g_ j$ vanishes on its support, $g_ jR=0$; since $R$ is closed, $\mathrm dg_ j\wedge R=\mathrm d(g_ jR)=0$. Take real coordinates $x$ whose first three are $g_1,g_2,g_3$. For $l\leq 3$ and $l\notin \{ a,b\} $, the coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dx_ a\wedge \mathrm dx_ b$ in $\mathrm dx_ l\wedge R$ is, up to sign, the coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ a\wedge \mathrm dx_ b$ in $R$, so this coefficient vanishes. Since no pair $\{ a,b\} $ contains all three indices $1,2,3$, every coefficient of $R$ vanishes, and $R=0$ near the point. Now let $A$ have codimension at least two. Near a point of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the set $A$ is a complex submanifold of real codimension at least four, so $R$ vanishes there, and the support of $R$ lies in $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$. This is analytic of smaller dimension near each point by corollary 9.3.13 (1), and again of codimension at least two; repeating the argument, we find after finitely many steps near each point that $R=0$. This proves the last assertion. Step 2: regular points of codimension one. Let $y\in A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be a point where $A$ is a complex hypersurface. Choose holomorphic coordinates $(\zeta ,w)$ near $y$ with $A=\{ \zeta =0\} $, write $\zeta =\xi +\mathrm i\eta $, and let $t\in \mathbb R^{2n-2}$ be the real coordinates of $w$. The identities $\mathrm d\xi \wedge R=\mathrm d\eta \wedge R=0$ of Step 1 force $R=\mu \, \mathrm d\xi \wedge \mathrm d\eta $ for a real measure $\mu $ supported on $\{ \xi =\eta =0\} $, so $\mu =\delta _0(\xi ,\eta )\otimes \sigma (t)$ for a real measure $\sigma $. Since $R$ is closed, $\mathrm dR=\sum _ l(\partial \mu /\partial t_ l)\, \mathrm dt_ l\wedge \mathrm d\xi \wedge \mathrm d\eta $ vanishes, the derivatives in $\xi $ and $\eta $ disappearing after the exterior product with $\mathrm d\xi \wedge \mathrm d\eta $; so $\partial \mu /\partial t_ l=0$ as distributions. Testing this against functions $\chi (\xi ,\eta )\psi (t)$ with $\chi =1$ near $0$, we find that all distributional derivatives $\partial \sigma /\partial t_ l$ vanish. On a smaller ball in the $t$-variables, the convolutions of $\sigma $ with a smoothing kernel therefore have zero gradient and are constant; integrating them against a fixed test function of integral one, we see that these constants converge as the kernel shrinks, and that $\sigma $ is a constant multiple $c$ of Lebesgue measure. Hence $R=c[\{ \zeta =0\} ]$ near $y$, with $c$ real. (If $n=1$, $\sigma $ is a measure on a point and the same conclusion holds.) Step 3: conclusion. Let $D=Z_\alpha $ be an irreducible component of codimension one, the closure of the connected component $S_\alpha $ of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By Step 2, near each point of $S_\alpha $ we have $R=c[D]$ for a real constant $c$, and this constant is locally constant on the connected manifold $S_\alpha $; we call it $c_ D$. By corollary 9.3.16 the sum $\sum _ Dc_ D[D]$ is locally finite, and by lemma 9.3.19 it is a closed real current with measure coefficients. The difference $R'=R-\sum _ Dc_ D[D]$ vanishes near every point of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$: near a point of $S_\alpha $ with $Z_\alpha $ of codimension one by Step 2, since the other components do not meet $S_\alpha $; and near a point of $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ where $A$ has codimension at least two by Step 1, since no component of codimension one passes through such a point. Thus the support of $R'$ lies in $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$. We show that $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has codimension at least two; then $R'=0$ by Step 1. A branch of $A$ of dimension $n$ at a point $y$ would be a subgerm of the germ $(M,y)$, which is irreducible of dimension $n$ by lemma 9.3.12 , hence equal to it by proposition 9.3.9 ; then $A$ would contain a neighborhood of $y$, which is impossible because $A$ is nowhere dense. So the branches of $A$ have dimension at most $n-1$, and $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$, which has smaller dimension than each branch (corollary 9.3.13 (1)), has codimension at least two. The coefficients are unique, because near a point of $S_\alpha $ the current $R$ determines $c_ D$; and if $R\geq 0$, then $c_ D\geq 0$, because $[D]$ is positive and nonzero near such a point. $\square$

title: 9.4 Reduced spaces and normalization
text:
The main result of this section is the existence and uniqueness of the normalization of a reduced complex space (theorem 9.4.6 ), which we construct locally from weakly holomorphic functions. A reduced complex space is a Hausdorff topological space $X$ with a sheaf $\mathcal O_ X$ of continuous complex-valued functions, its structure sheaf, such that every point has an open neighborhood $U$ and a homeomorphism $\phi $ of $U$ onto an analytic subset $A$ of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$ with the following property: a function $g$ on an open set $V\subset U$ belongs to $\mathcal O_ X(V)$ if and only if $g\circ \phi ^{-1}$ is, near each point of $\phi (V)$, the restriction of a holomorphic function on an open subset of $\Omega $. In other words, $\phi $ identifies $\mathcal O_ X|_ U$ with $\mathcal O_ A=(\mathcal O_\Omega /\mathcal I_ A)|_ A$. We call $(U,\phi )$ a local model , or local embedding, of $X$; holomorphic functions on $X$ extend locally to the ambient domains. As stated in the Conventions, all complex spaces are reduced, paracompact and Hausdorff; in this appendix we also assume that they have a countable basis of open sets. A compact space with such local models has a countable basis automatically, since finitely many local models cover it. A continuous map $F\colon Y	o X$ of complex spaces is holomorphic if $g\circ F\in \mathcal O_ Y$ for every local section $g$ of $\mathcal O_ X$, that is, if in local models of $X$ the components of $F$ belong to $\mathcal O_ Y$. By the definition of $\mathcal O_ Y$, these components extend near each point of $Y$ to holomorphic functions on an open subset of the ambient space of a local model of $Y$; consequently, compositions of holomorphic maps are holomorphic. An isomorphism is a holomorphic bijection whose inverse is holomorphic. Two local models at the same point differ by an isomorphism of analytic sets which, together with its inverse, is locally the restriction of holomorphic maps between the ambient domains. Such an isomorphism maps analytic subsets to analytic subsets, and it maps submanifolds to submanifolds, because a holomorphic map defined on a manifold that has a holomorphic left inverse is an injective immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image, so that its image is a submanifold by lemma 9.3.14 . Hence regular and singular points, local branches and dimension are well defined on $X$, independently of the local model. An analytic subset of $X$ is a closed subset that is analytic in every local model; with the restricted structure sheaf it is again a complex space. The structure sheaf is coherent as a module over itself. Indeed, in a local model let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ q$ be sections of $\mathcal O_ X$ with holomorphic lifts $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$, and let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ generate $\mathcal I_ A$ near a point, by theorem 9.3.10 ; the relations of the $f_ i$ over $\mathcal O_ X$ are the images of the projections to the first $q$ coordinates of the relations of $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q,g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ over $\mathcal O_\Omega $, which are locally finitely generated by theorem 9.2.7 . Thus lemma 9.2.6 applies to $\mathcal O_ X$-modules. Each local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a quotient of $\mathcal O_ N$, hence Noetherian. The zero set $V(\mathfrak a)$ of a coherent ideal sheaf $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ X$ is an analytic subset; conversely, the ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_ Y\subset \mathcal O_ X$ of functions vanishing on an analytic subset $Y\subset X$ is locally generated by the images of generators of the ideal sheaf of $Y$ in an ambient domain, so it is coherent by theorem 9.3.10 , lemma 9.2.6 . A holomorphic map $F\colon Y	o X$ is proper if inverse images of compact sets are compact, and finite if it is proper with finite fibers. It is bimeromorphic if there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $E\subset X$ such that $F^{-1}(E)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ and $F$ restricts to an isomorphism $Y\setminus F^{-1}(E)	o X\setminus E$. A proper map is closed: if $C\subset Y$ is closed and $F(y_ j)	o x$ with $y_ j\in C$, the points $y_ j$ eventually lie in the compact inverse image of a compact neighborhood of $x$, so a subsequence converges to some $y\in C$, and $F(y)=x$. Lemma 9.4.1 . F56FCBEF9522 Let $F\colon Y	o X$ be a bimeromorphic holomorphic map of complex spaces. Then $F^{-1}(B)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ for every nowhere dense analytic subset $B\subset X$. Consequently, the set $E$ in the definition may be enlarged by any nowhere dense analytic subset of $X$; if $U\subset X$ is the complement of a nowhere dense analytic subset, then $F^{-1}(U)$ is dense in $Y$; and every nonempty open subset of $Y$ contains a nonempty open set that $F$ maps isomorphically onto an open subset of $X$. Proof. Let $E$ be as in the definition, and let $G\subset F^{-1}(B)$ be open in $Y$. Then $G\setminus F^{-1}(E)$ is an open subset of $Y\setminus F^{-1}(E)$ contained in $F^{-1}(B\setminus E)$, which corresponds under the isomorphism $Y\setminus F^{-1}(E)	o X\setminus E$ to the nowhere dense subset $B\setminus E$ of $X\setminus E$; so $G\setminus F^{-1}(E)$ is empty, and $G$, an open subset of the nowhere dense set $F^{-1}(E)$, is empty as well. In particular $F$ is also an isomorphism over $X\setminus (E\cup B)$, and $F^{-1}(E\cup B)=F^{-1}(E)\cup F^{-1}(B)$ is nowhere dense, as the union of two closed nowhere dense sets; so $E$ may be replaced by $E\cup B$. If $U=X\setminus B$, then $F^{-1}(U)$ is the complement of the closed nowhere dense set $F^{-1}(B)$, hence dense. Finally, a nonempty open set $G\subset Y$ meets the dense open set $Y\setminus F^{-1}(E)$, and $F$ maps the nonempty open set $G\setminus F^{-1}(E)$ isomorphically onto an open subset of $X\setminus E$. $\square$ A weakly holomorphic function on an open set $U\subset X$ is a holomorphic function on $U\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ that is locally bounded near $U\cap X_{\mathrm{sing}}$: every point of $U$ has a neighborhood $V$ such that the function is bounded on $V\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. These functions form a sheaf of rings $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_ X$, which contains $\mathcal O_ X$ because $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is dense in $X$ (corollary 9.3.16 ).
