C3781B231934 A subharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: 06D657B81863 $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; 2BAC570CEF93 $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; 249F615C259B $\varphi $ satisfies the sub-mean value inequality : For any $a\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ such that $\overline{B_1(a,r)}\subseteq \Omega $, we have \[  \varphi (a)\leq \frac{1}{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi } \varphi (a+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })\, \mathrm{d}\theta .{}^{\href{#sgpt-a0000001456}{1}} \] We will denote the set of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ by $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. 1. ↩ Condition 2 guarantees that $\varphi $ is measurable and locally bounded from above, and hence the integral in Condition 3 makes sense. Here, $B_1(a,r)\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:|z-a|<r\} $ denotes the open ball with center $a$ and radius $r$. In fact, for each $a\in \Omega $, in 3 , it suffices to require the sub-mean value inequality for all small enough $r>0$. Intuitively, at a specific point $a\in \Omega $, Condition 2 says $\varphi (a)$ is no smaller than the upper limit of nearby values, while Condition 3 says $\varphi (a)$ is no larger than the mean. This intuition leads to the following rigidity theorem: Theorem 5.13.3 . FDD1E63B4457 Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: E03504FC9B0D $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\Delta \varphi \geq 0$. D517D85A39B6 $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a subharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $. Moreover, the subharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique. Proof. Suppose first that $\varphi\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and $\Delta\varphi\geq0$. Apply the distributional characterization of subharmonic functions to the distribution defined by $\varphi$. It gives a subharmonic representative $\psi$ of this distribution. Equality of the distributions defined by two locally integrable functions is equality almost everywhere, so $\varphi=\psi$ almost everywhere. Conversely, a subharmonic function on the connected domain $\Omega$ is locally integrable and has positive distributional Laplacian by the same theorem. Replacing it on a null set changes neither its distribution nor its local integrability. Finally, two subharmonic representatives that agree almost everywhere agree at every point: their values are the limits of their averages over shrinking balls. This also proves uniqueness. Multiplying the usual planar Laplacian by a fixed positive normalization constant does not change positivity. Here in Condition 1 , $\Delta \varphi =2\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \varphi $ is the Laplacian in the sense of currents. This is a special case of theorem 5.13.8 below. This theorem gives a very useful way of constructing subharmonic functions.

title: 5.13.4 The higher dimensional case
text:
We will fix $n\in \mathbb {N}$ and a domain $\Omega $ (a connected open subset) in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Definition 5.8.1 . 6070D2D83EC6 When $n\geq 1$, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: 1E4DADA74A2A $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; 62EDD3578A72 $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; B250529A16B9 for any complex line $L\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and any connected component $U$ of $L\cap \Omega $, the restriction $\varphi |_ U$ is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $. 1 When $n=0$, the only domain $\Omega $ is the singleton. In this case, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a real-valued function on $\Omega $. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. 1. ↩ An extremely common mistake in the literature is to replace 3 by the condition that $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ in the sense of currents. For a concrete counterexample, consider a function $\varphi $ that takes a constant value $0$ at all but one single point, at which the value of $\varphi $ is $1$. A plurisubharmonic function is also called a psh function for short. The relevant notations are indicated in 5.13.5 . 2 2. ↩ Recall that most figures here are somewhat misleading: We usually draw a complex dimension as a real dimension. The figures should not be read literally! B2EF8B3CC1DB 5.13.5 A domain $\Omega $ cut by a complex line $L$. Example 5.13.6 . DD77B8A4B7A7 When $n=0$, we have a canonical bijection $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )\cong \mathbb {R}$. Example 5.13.7 . 1C9711BBE591 When $n=1$, we have $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )=\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. Similar to theorem 5.13.3 , we have a rigidity theorem for plurisubharmonic functions as well. Theorem 5.13.8 . 2CB6F65A67EE Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: AD9F1D874ACA $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$; B21823D3C183 $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $. Moreover, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ is unique. Proof. In positive dimension, regard a locally integrable $\varphi$ as a real distribution. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\varphi\geq0$, the plurisubharmonic representative theorem supplies a plurisubharmonic function $\psi$ representing this distribution, hence equal to $\varphi$ almost everywhere. Conversely, that theorem proves local integrability and positivity of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\psi$ for every plurisubharmonic $\psi$; these properties are unchanged by almost-everywhere equality. Uniqueness follows from the shrinking-ball formula for the subharmonic representative. This is essential: an arbitrary pointwise representative of a positive distribution need not itself be plurisubharmonic. In dimension zero the domain is a point, with its counting measure; local integrability is finiteness, so both conditions simply say that the value is finite. Here, the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is normalized so that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }.  \] For the proof, we refer to [ Proposition 1.43 , GZ17 ] . Plurisubharmonic functions have nice functorialities: Proposition 5.13.9 . 5DCB508EA9AD Let $n'\in \mathbb {N}$ and $\Omega '\subseteq \mathbb {C}^{n'}$ be a domain. Given any holomorphic map $f\colon \Omega \rightarrow \Omega '$ and any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$, exactly one of the following cases occurs: 11DBE4FA0035 $f^*\varphi \equiv -\infty $; EEDAC90E09ED $f^*\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. For positive source and target dimensions, apply the holomorphic pullback theorem . Its conclusion is precisely that $\varphi\circ f$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty$ on each connected component. Here the source is connected, so there is just one alternative to consider. They are disjoint because the definition of plurisubharmonicity excludes the function identically $-\infty$. If the source has dimension zero, it is a point: the pullback is either a finite number or $-\infty$. If the target has dimension zero, $\varphi$ is finite and constant, and so is its pullback. Thus these cases satisfy the same assertion. We refer to [ Proposition 1.44 , GZ17 ] for the proof 3 . 3. ↩ Recall that the statement of [ Proposition 1.44 , GZ17 ] is flawed. One has to reduce to the case where Case 1 does not occur before following their proof. For each $n\in \mathbb {N}$, $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $r>0$, we write 7D0D660F11F8 5.13.10 \begin{equation}  B_ n(a,r)=\left\{  z\in \mathbb {C}^ n: |z-a|<r \right\} . \end{equation} Proposition 5.13.11 . 2FF7CC0E8132 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ n(a,r_0))$ for some $r_0>0$. Then the function \[  (-\infty ,\log r_0)\rightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad \log r\mapsto \sup _{B_ n(a,r)}\varphi  \] is convex and increasing. Proof. Write $M(r)=\sup_{B_n(a,r)}\varphi$. This is finite: upper semicontinuity bounds $\varphi$ above on the closure of each smaller ball, and a plurisubharmonic function not identically $-\infty$ cannot equal $-\infty$ on a ball. It is increasing by inclusion of balls. In dimension zero it is constant. Assume $n\geq1$ and fix $0<r_1<r_2<r_0$. Let $A\log r+B$ interpolate $M(r_1)$ and $M(r_2)$. On every complex line through $a$, comparison with this harmonic function on the annulus gives
\[\varphi(z)\leq A\log|z-a|+B\qquad(r_1\leq|z-a|\leq r_2).\]
The boundary bounds also hold on the spheres: if its value at a sphere point exceeded the interior supremum by $\delta>0$, upper semicontinuity would bound nearby values by that value plus $\delta/4$. A sufficiently small centered circle has at least one third of its length on the interior side, so its average would be strictly below the center value, contradicting the submean inequality. For $|z-a|<r_1$, the bound $\varphi(z)\leq M(r_1)$ suffices, because $A\geq0$. Taking the supremum over $|z-a|<r$, where $r_1<r<r_2$, yields
\[M(r)\leq \frac{\log r_2-\log r}{\log r_2-\log r_1}M(r_1)+\frac{\log r-\log r_1}{\log r_2-\log r_1}M(r_2).\]
This is convexity in $\log r$. See [ Theorem 4.1.13 , Hor07 ] for the case $n>1$ and [ Corollary 2.4 , Bou17 ] for the general case. Proposition 5.13.12 . D8BC10548372 Let $a<b$ be two real numbers. Let $f\colon (a,b)\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Define \[  g\colon \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto f(\operatorname{Re}z).  \] Suppose that $g$ is subharmonic. Then $f$ is convex. In particular, $f$ takes real values only. Proof. Convolve $g$ on smaller strips with a nonnegative smooth radial approximate identity. The regularizations $g_\varepsilon$ are smooth and subharmonic and decrease pointwise to $g$ by subharmonic regularization . They are still invariant under imaginary translations, hence have the form $g_\varepsilon(z)=f_\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}z)$. Therefore $f_\varepsilon''=\Delta g_\varepsilon\geq0$, and each $f_\varepsilon$ is convex on its interval of definition. Passing to the decreasing limit in the convexity inequality proves convexity of $f$ in the extended sense. This limit is finite everywhere: it is bounded above locally because $g$ is subharmonic, and if it were $-\infty$ at an interior point, convexity with a point beyond any other given point would force it to be $-\infty$ throughout $(a,b)$. That would make $g\equiv-\infty$, which is excluded. Thus $f$ is a real-valued convex function.

title: 5.13.13 The manifold case
text:
Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Here, complex manifolds are assumed to be paracompact, namely, all connected components have countable bases. Definition 5.13.14 . D072C98719AA A plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for any $x\in X$, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$, an integer $n\in \mathbb {N}$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a biholomorphic map $F\colon \Omega \rightarrow U$ such that $F^*(\varphi |_ U)\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Example 5.13.15 . 67A5152A77BC When $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, the notions of plurisubharmonic functions in definition 5.13.14 and in definition 5.8.1 coincide. Example 5.13.16 . 399FC71A61E3 Write $\{ X_ i\} _{i\in I}$ for the set of connected components of $X$. Then we have a natural bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X) \cong \prod _{i\in I} \mathrm{PSH}(X_ i).  \] Here the product is in the category of sets. In particular, if $X=\varnothing $, then $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ is a singleton. This example allows us to reduce to the case of connected manifolds when studying general plurisubharmonic functions. Proposition 5.13.17 . 726DDFDDA8F2 Let $Y$ be a complex manifold and $f\colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic map. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, exactly one of the following cases occurs: CAAB826BFF14 $f^*\varphi $ is identically $-\infty $ on some connected component of $Y$; 13566C9390E6 $f^*\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y)$. Proof. Work on one connected component $Y_0$ of $Y$. In coordinate neighborhoods of $Y$ and $X$, holomorphic pullback says that $\varphi\circ f$ is either plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty$. A plurisubharmonic function cannot be identically $-\infty$ on a nonempty open subset of a connected domain, by its local integrability. Thus a neighborhood on which the pullback is identically $-\infty$ cannot overlap a neighborhood on which it is plurisubharmonic. The two types form disjoint open subsets of $Y_0$; connectedness leaves only one type. If the first type never occurs on any component, the pullback is plurisubharmonic on $Y$. Zero-dimensional charts are covered by the finite-value convention. This proposition follows from proposition 5.13.9 applied separately on each connected component of $Y$. 


theorem 5.13.8 implies immediately the general form of the rigidity theorem: Theorem 5.13.18 . FEFFC91695E0 Let $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: 3BB9EAC495FC $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$; FB5BA344B4A3 $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $X$. Moreover, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique. Proof. Restrict a locally integrable $\varphi$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\varphi\geq0$ to each coordinate chart and apply the local representative theorem . The resulting plurisubharmonic representatives agree almost everywhere on overlaps, hence everywhere there by the uniqueness part of the same theorem. They therefore glue to a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ representing $\varphi$. Conversely, local integrability and positivity hold in every chart for a plurisubharmonic function and are preserved by almost-everywhere equality. The same overlap argument proves uniqueness globally. On a zero-dimensional component all assertions reduce to finiteness at each point. Definition 5.47.2 . 5458CA6608A5 A subset $E\subseteq X$ is pluripolar if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ and a function $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \psi |_{E\cap U}\equiv -\infty .  \] A subset $E\subseteq X$ is non-pluripolar if $E$ is not pluripolar. A subset $F\subseteq X$ is co-pluripolar if $X\setminus F$ is pluripolar. When $X$ has dimension $1$, a pluripolar set is called a polar set . We say some property about objects on $X$ holds quasi-everywhere if it holds outside a pluripolar set. Theorem 5.13.19 (Josefson's theorem) . DB05CEAF06C1 Let $E\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pluripolar set. Then there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $. Proof. Apply Josefson's theorem, proved earlier in the collection to $E$. It constructs a function $V\in\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb C^n)$ with $E\subset\{V=-\infty\}$, in fact with the additional bound $V(z)\leq\log^+|z|$. Taking $\varphi=V$ gives the assertion. The earlier construction is a proof of this stronger statement, so no additional external theorem is being invoked here. In dimension zero a pluripolar set is empty and a finite constant suffices. See [ Corollary 4.41 , GZ17 ] for the proof of a more general result. 


There is also a global version of Josefson's theorem: Theorem 5.13.20 . 0ED3DB1BD7C2 Assume that $X$ is a compact complex manifold and $E\subseteq X$ is a pluripolar set. Then there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ with $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $. For a proof, see [ Vu19 ] . The notion of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions will be recalled in definition 5.17.1 below.

title: 5.14 Properties of plurisubharmonic functions
text:
In this section, we explore the basic properties of plurisubharmonic functions. Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Proposition 5.14.1 . 0372195E73A0 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then for any $p\geq 1$, $\varphi \in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. Proof. It suffices to work near a point $x$ in a positive-dimensional chart. The Lelong number $
u(\varphi,x)$ is finite. Choose $c>0$ with $c
u(\varphi,x)<1$. The upper bound in the multiplier-ideal order estimate gives
\[0\leq\operatorname{ord}_x\mathcal I(c\varphi)\leq c
u(\varphi,x)<1.\]
This integral order is zero; hence the ideal contains a germ nonvanishing at $x$, so $\exp(-c\varphi)$ is integrable on a neighborhood of $x$. After subtracting a local upper bound for $\varphi$, assume $\varphi\leq0$. For every finite $p\geq1$, the elementary bound $t^p\leq C_{p,c}\exp(ct)$ for $t\geq0$ now proves local integrability of $|\varphi|^p$. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover each compact set. In dimension zero the function is finite at every point, so the assertion is immediate. See [ Theorem 1.46, Theorem 1.48 , GZ17 ] . Proposition 5.14.2 . 01C3654494E2 8BD4DEED7DA3 Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. 567577F8D619 Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Furthermore, $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}} \varphi $. Proof. For the upper envelope, the upper-envelope theorem applies exactly to the given nonempty, locally uniformly upper-bounded family; its conclusion is that the upper semicontinuous regularization of its supremum is plurisubharmonic. For a decreasing net, the decreasing-net theorem gives, on each connected component, either a plurisubharmonic limit or the limit identically $-\infty$, with the local convergence asserted there. Applying these results in charts and using uniqueness of representatives on overlaps proves the statements on a manifold. No passage from an arbitrary net to a supposedly cofinal sequence is needed. Here $\operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum. When $I$ is a finite family, observe that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i= \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] When $I=\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, we write \[  \varphi _1\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _ m\coloneqq \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] We refer to [ Proposition 1.28, Proposition 1.40 , GZ17 ] . Proposition 5.14.3 (Choquet's lemma) . 1D624ECF05E9 Assume that $X$ has countably many connected components. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. There exists a countable subset $J\subseteq I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in J}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j.  \] In the sequel, we say a subset $B\subseteq X$ is a holomorphic ball if $B$ has smooth boundary in $X$, and $B$ is biholomorphic to an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Since by our convention, the complex manifold $X$ is paracompact, it can be covered by countably many holomorphic balls, so we can easily reduce to the case where $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. In this case, the result is proved in [ Lemma 4.31 , GZ17 ] . $\square$ Proposition 5.14.4 . E2A24FD63150 A pluripolar set $E\subseteq X$ is a Lebesgue null set. Proof. This is a trivial consequence of proposition 5.14.1 . $\square$ Proposition 5.14.5 . E10B5F00D3ED Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i<\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i ight\}   \] is pluripolar and hence Lebesgue null. Proof. Put $u=\sup_i\varphi_i$ and $v=u^*$. By the pluripolar discrepancy theorem , $\{u<v\}$ is pluripolar. The stronger local conclusion in the upper-envelope theorem says that the same discrepancy set is real polar in each coordinate chart. Thus both asserted notions of polarity follow from the proved envelope construction, rather than from an assumed measurability of an arbitrary supremum. The conclusion is local, as are the definitions of polar and pluripolar subsets of $X$. See [ Corollary 4.28 , GZ17 ] . Proposition 5.14.6 . FA3AF40B9A0A Suppose that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. If $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi \leq \psi $ everywhere. In particular, if $\varphi =\psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi =\psi $ everywhere. Proof. Replace $\varphi $ by $\varphi \lor \psi $. Then $\varphi ,\psi $ are two plurisubharmonic functions that coincide almost everywhere. The uniqueness statement in theorem 5.13.18 gives $\varphi =\psi $. $\square$ Proposition 5.14.7 . 459E68F98F06 Let $(E_ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence of pluripolar sets in $X$. Then \[  E\coloneqq  igcup _{i=1}^{\infty }E_ i  \] is also pluripolar. Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a bounded domain. In this case, by theorem 5.13.19 for each $i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ we can choose $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \psi _ i|_{E_ i}\equiv -\infty ,\quad \psi _ i|_ X\leq 0  \] for all $i>0$. By proposition 5.14.1 , we have $\psi _ i|_ X\in L^1(X)$ for all $i>0$. After rescaling, we may also assume that $\| \psi _ i\| _{L^1(X)}\leq 1$ for all $i>0$. We then define \[  \psi =\sum _{i=1}^{\infty }2^{-i} \psi _ i|_ X.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ according to proposition 5.14.2 and $\psi |_{E}=-\infty $. $\square$ Corollary 5.14.8 . Then 02A6B28E8E8F 5.14.9  egin{equation}  \varphi =\mathop{\vphantom {\operatorname {sup}^{*}}\inf }\limits _{j>0} \operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k, \end{equation} and the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \varphi (x)
eq \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\varphi _ j(x)ight\}   \] is pluripolar. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. We first observe that $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This follows from [ Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] . For each $j\geq 1$, let \[  \psi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k.  \] Then $\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 5.14.2 . Moreover, $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is a decreasing sequence and $\psi _ j\geq \varphi _ j$ for all $j$. After considering a subsequence of $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ which converges to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, we get $\varphi \leq \psi \coloneqq \inf _ j \psi _ j$ almost everywhere. In particular, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 5.14.2 . On the other hand, by proposition 5.14.5 , there exist pluripolar sets $Z_ j\subseteq X$ such that \[  \psi _ j=\sup _{k\geq j}\varphi _ k  \] on $X\setminus Z_ j$. Let \[  Z= igcup _{j=1}^{\infty } Z_ j.  \] Then $Z$ is a pluripolar set by proposition 5.14.7 , and for any $x\in X\setminus Z$, we have $\psi (x)=\varlimsup _ j \varphi _ j(x)$. Moreover, $\psi =\varphi $ almost everywhere by [ Theorem 1.46 , GZ17 ] , and hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . Hence we conclude ( 5.14.9 ). Moreover, for all $x\in X\setminus Z$, \[  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{j	o \infty } \varphi _ j(x).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 5.14.10 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert) . Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: A8DA4460C6EC The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. Then there exist $z\in Z$ and a sequence $(x_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ in $X\setminus Z$ converging to $z$ such that CD940E826F95 5.14.13  egin{equation}  \lim _{j	o \infty } \varphi (x_ j)=\infty . \end{equation} Since $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ 2 , we may choose a complex line $L$ through $z$ which meets $Z$ in a discrete set; after shrinking $X$ we may further assume that \[  L\cap Z=\{ z\} .  \] Pick an open ball $B_ n(z,r)\Subset X$. Since $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X\setminus Z$ of $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$ such that \[  \varphi |_ U<0.  \] For each $j\geq 1$ we now choose a complex line $L_ j$ through $x_ j$, disjoint from $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$, with $L_ j	o L$ as $j	o \infty $ (the convergence being in the Grassmannian of affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^ n$). The existence of such $L_ j$ is precisely where the assumption $\operatorname {codim} Z\geq 2$ enters: after replacing $B_ n(z,r)$ by a slightly smaller ball if necessary, the closure of $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$ is analytic in a neighborhood of the closed ball. The projection to the space of directions is proper on this compact analytic set, so by Remmert's theorem its image is contained in a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb {P}^{n-1}$. Hence its complement contains directions arbitrarily close to that of $L$. For $j$ large enough we now have \[  L_ j\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)\subseteq U,  \] so applying the maximum principle to $\varphi |_{L_ j\cap X}$ at $x_ j$ yields $\varphi (x_ j)<0$, contradicting ( 5.14.13 ). $\square$ 2. ↩ In fact, codimension at least $1$ suffices for this step. Lemma 5.14.14 . 741322DD572F Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}((\Delta ^*)^ n)$ be an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function. Then $\varphi $ is finite everywhere. Here \[  \Delta ^*\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: 0<|z|<1\}   \] denotes the punctured unit disk. Proof. It clearly suffices to handle the case $n=1$. In this case, by [ Theorem 2.12 , HK76 ] , the map \[  \log r\mapsto \int _{0}^{1} \varphi \left(r\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i}	heta }ight)\, \mathrm{d}	heta =\varphi (r)  \] is a convex function of $\log r$. So, the set $\{ r\in (0,1): \varphi (r)=-\infty \} $ is convex. But $\varphi $ is almost everywhere finite by proposition 5.14.1 . Since $\varphi $ is $S^1$-invariant, $\varphi |_{(0,1)}$ is almost everywhere finite. It follows from the convexity that it is everywhere finite. $\square$ Proposition 5.14.15 (Kiselman's principle) . BB26476C13FA Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m	imes \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pseudoconvex domain. Assume that for each $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$, the set \[  \Omega _ z\coloneqq  igl \{ w\in \mathbb {C}^ n: (z,w)\in \Omega  igr \}   \] has the form $E+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ n$, where $E\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ is a subset. Let $\Omega '$ be the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$. Define $\psi \colon \Omega 'ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ as follows: \[  \psi (z)=\inf _{w\in \Omega _ z}\varphi (z,w).  \] Then either $\psi \equiv -\infty $ or $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that 504311AA3518 5.14.17  egin{equation}  \varliminf _{\substack {\Omega '

Define \[  \eta (z)=\left\{   egin{aligned}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega ',\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{aligned} ight.  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. This is essentially [ Proposition 1.30 , GZ17 ] . Since the statement in the reference is slightly misleading for our purposes, we include the proof for clarification. 660980D172BD 5.14.18 Gluing procedure Proof. See 5.14.18 for the notations used in the proof. Take $\epsilon >0$. We first define \[  \eta _{\epsilon }(z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor (\psi (z)-2\epsilon ),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] We claim that \[  \eta _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] By our assumption, for each $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, we can find an open neighborhood $U_ x\subseteq \Omega $ such that for any $y\in U_ x\cap \Omega '$, we have $\varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon $. Therefore, by taking a union of the $U_ x$'s for various $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that \[  \varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon ,\quad  orall y\in U\cap \Omega '.  \] Since $U$ contains $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, the set $(\Omega \setminus \Omega ')\cup U$ is open in $\Omega $. On this open set we have $\eta _{\epsilon }=\varphi $, hence $\eta _{\epsilon }$ is plurisubharmonic there. It is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega '$ by proposition 5.14.2 . These two descriptions agree on the overlap $U\cap \Omega '$, so our claim follows from the local nature of plurisubharmonicity. Next we observe that as $\epsilon $ decreases to $0$, the functions $\eta _{\epsilon }$ increase to $\eta $. The family $(\eta _\epsilon )_{0<\epsilon \leq 1}$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This is clear away from $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Near $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, applying the previous estimate with $\epsilon =1$ gives an open neighborhood $U_1$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that $\psi \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1\cap \Omega '$, hence $\eta _\epsilon \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1$ for all $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. Therefore, $\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ by proposition 5.14.2 . It remains to observe that $\eta $ is upper semicontinuous. This is only non-trivial on the boundary of $\Omega '$. We first show that 19FE6DB3F44A 5.14.19  egin{equation}  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x). \end{equation} We may assume that $\psi (y_ i)
eq -\infty $ for all $i>0$ and the left-hand side of ( 5.14.19 ) is not $-\infty $. Then we can compute \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)+\varliminf _{i	o \infty }  igl (\varphi (y_ i)-\psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty }\varphi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x).  \] Combining this with the upper semicontinuity of $\varphi $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } igl (\varphi (y_ i)\lor \psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varphi (x)=\eta (x).  \] This proves upper semicontinuity across $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Therefore, $\eta =\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$ Note that the boundary condition ( 5.14.17 ) enters the proof only through ( 5.14.19 ), therefore, we can formulate a variant of 5.14.16 : Corollary 5.14.20 . 79C564A098F9 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{\Omega '
i y	o x}\psi (y)\leq \varphi (x)  \] for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. Let $u$ be the function equal to $\max\{\varphi,\psi\}$ on $\Omega'$ and to $\varphi$ elsewhere. The boundary limsup hypothesis is exactly the gluing condition in the maximum gluing proposition . Hence $u$ is plurisubharmonic. This argument is local near each point of $\partial\Omega'\cap\Omega$; no relative compactness of $\Omega'$ in $\Omega$ is required. Away from that boundary, the assertion is simply stability under the maximum or the original plurisubharmonicity of $\varphi$. Using the ideas of 5.14.16 and the solution of the homogeneous Monge–Ampère equations on a strong pseudoconvex domain, one can prove the following: Proposition 5.14.21 . 3EDBDD31B3F1 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, let $D \Subset \Omega $ be a strongly pseudoconvex domain, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Then there exists a unique locally bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that \[   egin{cases}  \left(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ight)^ n = 0&  	extup{on } D,\  \psi = \varphi &  	extup{on } \Omega \setminus D. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. See [ Proposition 9.1 , BT82 ] for the proof. We sometimes say $\psi $ is the balayage of $\varphi $ on $D$. 


Let us also recall the following domination principle: Proposition 5.14.22 . EFFC20773E2E Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a bounded domain. Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Assume that 32392BCFEA58 for each $z\in \partial \Omega $, we have \[  \varliminf _{\Omega 
i w	o z} \Bigl (\psi (w)-\varphi (w)\Bigr )\geq 0;  \] 8FB9E09F9A4A $\varphi \leq \psi $ a.e. with respect to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, Then $\varphi \leq \psi $. Proof. Apply the local Bedford--Taylor domination principle with $u=\varphi$ and $v=\psi$. Its hypotheses are exactly $\liminf_{\Omega
i w	o z}(v-u)\geq0$ on the boundary and $u\leq v$ almost everywhere for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}v)^n$. Thus its conclusion is $\varphi\leq\psi$. The earlier proof uses bounded strict comparison sets and local boundedness; continuity on the boundary and a uniform bound on the whole domain are not required. This is [ Corollary 3.31 , GZ17 ] . 1 1. ↩ The statement in the reference is flawed, but the proof is correct.

title: Proposition 5.14.1
text:
Proposition 5.14.1 . 0372195E73A0 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then for any $p\geq 1$, $\varphi \in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. Proof. It suffices to work near a point $x$ in a positive-dimensional chart. The Lelong number $
u(\varphi,x)$ is finite. Choose $c>0$ with $c
u(\varphi,x)<1$. The upper bound in the multiplier-ideal order estimate gives
\[0\leq\operatorname{ord}_x\mathcal I(c\varphi)\leq c
u(\varphi,x)<1.\]
This integral order is zero; hence the ideal contains a germ nonvanishing at $x$, so $\exp(-c\varphi)$ is integrable on a neighborhood of $x$. After subtracting a local upper bound for $\varphi$, assume $\varphi\leq0$. For every finite $p\geq1$, the elementary bound $t^p\leq C_{p,c}\exp(ct)$ for $t\geq0$ now proves local integrability of $|\varphi|^p$. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover each compact set. In dimension zero the function is finite at every point, so the assertion is immediate.

title: Proposition 5.14.2
text: Proposition 5.14.2 . 01C3654494E2 8BD4DEED7DA3 Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. 567577F8D619 Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Furthermore, $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}} \varphi $. Proof. For the upper envelope, the upper-envelope theorem applies exactly to the given nonempty, locally uniformly upper-bounded family; its conclusion is that the upper semicontinuous regularization of its supremum is plurisubharmonic. For a decreasing net, the decreasing-net theorem gives, on each connected component, either a plurisubharmonic limit or the limit identically $-\infty$, with the local convergence asserted there. Applying these results in charts and using uniqueness of representatives on overlaps proves the statements on a manifold. No passage from an arbitrary net to a supposedly cofinal sequence is needed.

title: Proposition 5.14.3 (Choquet's lemma)
text: Proposition 5.14.3 (Choquet's lemma) . 1D624ECF05E9 Assume that $X$ has countably many connected components. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. There exists a countable subset $J\subseteq I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in J}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j.  \] Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Since by our convention, the complex manifold $X$ is paracompact, it can be covered by countably many holomorphic balls, so we can easily reduce to the case where $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. In this case, the result is proved in [ Lemma 4.31 , GZ17 ] . $\square$

title: Proposition 5.14.4
text: Proposition 5.14.4 . E2A24FD63150 A pluripolar set $E\subseteq X$ is a Lebesgue null set. Proof. This is a trivial consequence of proposition 5.14.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 5.14.5
text: Proposition 5.14.5 . E10B5F00D3ED Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i<\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i \right\}   \] is pluripolar and hence Lebesgue null. Proof. Put $u=\sup_i\varphi_i$ and $v=u^*$. By the pluripolar discrepancy theorem , $\{u<v\}$ is pluripolar. The stronger local conclusion in the upper-envelope theorem says that the same discrepancy set is real polar in each coordinate chart. Thus both asserted notions of polarity follow from the proved envelope construction, rather than from an assumed measurability of an arbitrary supremum. The conclusion is local, as are the definitions of polar and pluripolar subsets of $X$.

title: Proposition 5.14.6
text: Proposition 5.14.6 . FA3AF40B9A0A Suppose that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. If $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi \leq \psi $ everywhere. In particular, if $\varphi =\psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi =\psi $ everywhere. Proof. Replace $\varphi $ by $\varphi \lor \psi $. Then $\varphi ,\psi $ are two plurisubharmonic functions that coincide almost everywhere. The uniqueness statement in theorem 5.13.18 gives $\varphi =\psi $. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.14.7
text: Proposition 5.14.7 . 459E68F98F06 Let $(E_ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence of pluripolar sets in $X$. Then \[  E\coloneqq \bigcup _{i=1}^{\infty }E_ i  \] is also pluripolar. Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a bounded domain. In this case, by theorem 5.13.19 for each $i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ we can choose $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \psi _ i|_{E_ i}\equiv -\infty ,\quad \psi _ i|_ X\leq 0  \] for all $i>0$. By proposition 5.14.1 , we have $\psi _ i|_ X\in L^1(X)$ for all $i>0$. After rescaling, we may also assume that $\| \psi _ i\| _{L^1(X)}\leq 1$ for all $i>0$. We then define \[  \psi =\sum _{i=1}^{\infty }2^{-i} \psi _ i|_ X.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ according to proposition 5.14.2 and $\psi |_{E}=-\infty $. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.14.8
text: Corollary 5.14.8 . E23F3D6154AB Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then 02A6B28E8E8F 5.14.9 \begin{equation}  \varphi =\mathop{\vphantom {\operatorname {sup}^{*}}\inf }\limits _{j>0} \operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k, \end{equation} and the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \varphi (x)\neq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\varphi _ j(x)\right\}   \] is pluripolar. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. We first observe that $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This follows from [ Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] . For each $j\geq 1$, let \[  \psi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k.  \] Then $\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 5.14.2 . Moreover, $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is a decreasing sequence and $\psi _ j\geq \varphi _ j$ for all $j$. After considering a subsequence of $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ which converges to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, we get $\varphi \leq \psi \coloneqq \inf _ j \psi _ j$ almost everywhere. In particular, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 5.14.2 . On the other hand, by proposition 5.14.5 , there exist pluripolar sets $Z_ j\subseteq X$ such that \[  \psi _ j=\sup _{k\geq j}\varphi _ k  \] on $X\setminus Z_ j$. Let \[  Z=\bigcup _{j=1}^{\infty } Z_ j.  \] Then $Z$ is a pluripolar set by proposition 5.14.7 , and for any $x\in X\setminus Z$, we have $\psi (x)=\varlimsup _ j \varphi _ j(x)$. Moreover, $\psi =\varphi $ almost everywhere by [ Theorem 1.46 , GZ17 ] , and hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . Hence we conclude ( 5.14.9 ). Moreover, for all $x\in X\setminus Z$, \[  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{j\to \infty } \varphi _ j(x).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.14.10 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert)
text: Theorem 5.14.10 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert) . DAE812E1A818 Let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: A8DA4460C6EC The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. F3ED7BD4ED03 The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by 09298412E7CE 5.14.11 \begin{equation}  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z\ni y\to x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in Z. \end{equation} Proof. The extension is unique thanks to proposition 5.14.6 . We shall prove the existence. 2 Thanks to the uniqueness of the extension, the problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n>0$ and there is a non-zero holomorphic function $f$ on $X$ vanishing on $Z$. For each $\epsilon >0$, we claim that the function $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ defined by \[  \varphi _{\epsilon }(x)\coloneqq \left\{  \begin{aligned}  \varphi (x)+\epsilon \log |f(x)|^2,& \quad x\in X\setminus Z;\\  -\infty ,& \quad x\in Z \end{aligned} \right.  \] is plurisubharmonic on $X$. By definition 5.8.1 , it suffices to verify the case $n=1$. In this case, we may assume that $Z=\{ 0\} $. It is clear that $ \varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{SH}(X\setminus Z)$. It suffices to verify the sub-mean value inequality at $0$, which is immediate. Next observe that the net $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is increasing as $\epsilon \searrow 0$ and $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. It follows from proposition 5.14.2 that $\tilde{\varphi }\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Moreover, $\tilde{\varphi }$ clearly extends $\varphi $. Note that ( 5.14.11 ) follows from the construction. 1 We invite the reader to consult 5.14.12 for the notations used in the proof. Thanks to 2 , it suffices to verify that $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n\geq 2$. Suppose the assertion fails. Then there exist $z\in Z$ and a sequence $(x_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ in $X\setminus Z$ converging to $z$ such that CD940E826F95 5.14.13 \begin{equation}  \lim _{j\to \infty } \varphi (x_ j)=\infty . \end{equation} Since $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ 2 , we may choose a complex line $L$ through $z$ which meets $Z$ in a discrete set; after shrinking $X$ we may further assume that \[  L\cap Z=\{ z\} .  \] Pick an open ball $B_ n(z,r)\Subset X$. After adding a constant to $\varphi $, we may arrange $\varphi <0$ on $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$. Since $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X\setminus Z$ of $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$ such that \[  \varphi |_ U<0.  \] For each $j\geq 1$ we now choose a complex line $L_ j$ through $x_ j$, disjoint from $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$, with $L_ j\to L$ as $j\to \infty $ (the convergence being in the Grassmannian of affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^ n$). The existence of such $L_ j$ is precisely where the assumption $\operatorname {codim} Z\geq 2$ enters: after replacing $B_ n(z,r)$ by a slightly smaller ball if necessary, the closure of $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$ is analytic in a neighborhood of the closed ball. The projection to the space of directions is proper on this compact analytic set, so by Remmert's theorem its image is contained in a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb {P}^{n-1}$. Hence its complement contains directions arbitrarily close to that of $L$. For $j$ large enough we now have \[  L_ j\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)\subseteq U,  \] so applying the maximum principle to $\varphi |_{L_ j\cap X}$ at $x_ j$ yields $\varphi (x_ j)<0$, contradicting ( 5.14.13 ). $\square$ 2. ↩ In fact, codimension at least $1$ suffices for this step.

title: Lemma 5.14.14
text: Lemma 5.14.14 . 741322DD572F Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}((\Delta ^*)^ n)$ be an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function. Then $\varphi $ is finite everywhere. Proof. It clearly suffices to handle the case $n=1$. In this case, by [ Theorem 2.12 , HK76 ] , the map \[  \log r\mapsto \int _{0}^{1} \varphi \left(r\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i}\theta }\right)\, \mathrm{d}\theta =\varphi (r)  \] is a convex function of $\log r$. So, the set $\{ r\in (0,1): \varphi (r)=-\infty \} $ is convex. But $\varphi $ is almost everywhere finite by proposition 5.14.1 . Since $\varphi $ is $S^1$-invariant, $\varphi |_{(0,1)}$ is almost everywhere finite. It follows from the convexity that it is everywhere finite. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.14.15 (Kiselman's principle)
text: Proposition 5.14.15 (Kiselman's principle) . BB26476C13FA Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pseudoconvex domain. Assume that for each $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$, the set \[  \Omega _ z\coloneqq \bigl \{ w\in \mathbb {C}^ n: (z,w)\in \Omega \bigr \}   \] has the form $E+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ n$, where $E\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ is a subset. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, assume that $\varphi $ is independent of the imaginary part of the variable in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Let $\Omega '$ be the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$. Define $\psi \colon \Omega '\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ as follows: \[  \psi (z)=\inf _{w\in \Omega _ z}\varphi (z,w).  \] Then either $\psi \equiv -\infty $ or $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$.

title: Lemma 5.14.16
text:
Lemma 5.14.16 . 49CC56CB484C Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that 504311AA3518 5.14.17  egin{equation}  \varliminf _{\substack {\Omega '
i y	o x,\ \psi (y)
eq -\infty }} igl (\varphi (y)-\psi (y) igr )\geq 0 \end{equation} for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)=\left\{   egin{aligned}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega ',\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{aligned} ight.  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. See 5.14.18 for the notations used in the proof. Take $\epsilon >0$. We first define \[  \eta _{\epsilon }(z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor (\psi (z)-2\epsilon ),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] We claim that \[  \eta _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] By our assumption, for each $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, we can find an open neighborhood $U_ x\subseteq \Omega $ such that for any $y\in U_ x\cap \Omega '$, we have $\varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon $. Therefore, by taking a union of the $U_ x$'s for various $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that \[  \varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon ,\quad  orall y\in U\cap \Omega '.  \] Since $U$ contains $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, the set $(\Omega \setminus \Omega ')\cup U$ is open in $\Omega $. On this open set we have $\eta _{\epsilon }=\varphi $, hence $\eta _{\epsilon }$ is plurisubharmonic there. It is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega '$ by proposition 5.14.2 . These two descriptions agree on the overlap $U\cap \Omega '$, so our claim follows from the local nature of plurisubharmonicity. Next we observe that as $\epsilon $ decreases to $0$, the functions $\eta _{\epsilon }$ increase to $\eta $. The family $(\eta _\epsilon )_{0<\epsilon \leq 1}$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This is clear away from $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Near $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, applying the previous estimate with $\epsilon =1$ gives an open neighborhood $U_1$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that $\psi \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1\cap \Omega '$, hence $\eta _\epsilon \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1$ for all $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. Therefore, $\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ by proposition 5.14.2 . It remains to observe that $\eta $ is upper semicontinuous. This is only non-trivial on the boundary of $\Omega '$. Take $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ and let $(y_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence in $\Omega '$ with limit $x$. We first show that 19FE6DB3F44A 5.14.19  egin{equation}  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x). \end{equation} We may assume that $\psi (y_ i)
eq -\infty $ for all $i>0$ and the left-hand side of ( 5.14.19 ) is not $-\infty $. Then we can compute \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)+\varliminf _{i	o \infty }  igl (\varphi (y_ i)-\psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty }\varphi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x).  \] Combining this with the upper semicontinuity of $\varphi $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } igl (\varphi (y_ i)\lor \psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varphi (x)=\eta (x).  \] This proves upper semicontinuity across $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Therefore, $\eta =\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$

text: Corollary 5.14.20 . 79C564A098F9 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{\Omega '\ni y\to x}\psi (y)\leq \varphi (x)  \] for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)=\begin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad \textup{if }z\in \Omega ';\\  \varphi (z),& \quad \textup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. Let $u$ be the function equal to $\max\{\varphi,\psi\}$ on $\Omega'$ and to $\varphi$ elsewhere. The boundary limsup hypothesis is exactly the gluing condition in the maximum gluing proposition . Hence $u$ is plurisubharmonic. This argument is local near each point of $\partial\Omega'\cap\Omega$; no relative compactness of $\Omega'$ in $\Omega$ is required. Away from that boundary, the assertion is simply stability under the maximum or the original plurisubharmonicity of $\varphi$.

title: Proposition 5.14.21
text: Proposition 5.14.21 . 3EDBDD31B3F1 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, let $D \Subset \Omega $ be a strongly pseudoconvex domain, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Then there exists a unique locally bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that \[  \begin{cases}  \left(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \right)^ n = 0&  \textup{on } D,\\  \psi = \varphi &  \textup{on } \Omega \setminus D. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $.

text: Proposition 5.14.22 . EFFC20773E2E Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a bounded domain. Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Assume that 32392BCFEA58 for each $z\in \partial \Omega $, we have \[  \varliminf _{\Omega \ni w\to z} \Bigl (\psi (w)-\varphi (w)\Bigr )\geq 0;  \] 8FB9E09F9A4A $\varphi \leq \psi $ a.e. with respect to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, Then $\varphi \leq \psi $. Proof. Apply the local Bedford--Taylor domination principle with $u=\varphi$ and $v=\psi$. Its hypotheses are exactly $\liminf_{\Omega\ni w\to z}(v-u)\geq0$ on the boundary and $u\leq v$ almost everywhere for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}v)^n$. Thus its conclusion is $\varphi\leq\psi$. The earlier proof uses bounded strict comparison sets and local boundedness; continuity on the boundary and a uniform bound on the whole domain are not required.

title: 5.15 Plurifine topology
text: The plurifine topology is the coarsest topology making all local plurisubharmonic functions continuous. The results below describe its neighborhoods, thin sets, and local connectedness.

title: 5.15.1 Plurifine topology on domains
Proposition 5.15.2
text: Proposition 5.15.2 . 0E4FD8AF1256 The plurifine topology on $\Omega $ is finer than the Euclidean topology. Proof. It suffices to show that the unit ball $\{ z\in \mathbb {C}^ n:|z|<1\} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. This follows from the observation that this set can be written as \[  \{ \psi <0\}  \quad \textup{with}\quad \psi (z)\coloneqq (\log |z|) \lor (-1).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Example 5.15.3
text: Example 5.15.3 . 28F2383E9245 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Then the sets $\{ \varphi >C\} $ and $\{ \varphi <C\} $ are both $\mathcal{F}$-open. In fact, the latter case follows from proposition 5.15.2 , while the former follows from the observation \[  \{ \varphi >C\} =\{ \varphi \lor (C-1)>C\} .  \]

title: Definition 5.15.4
text: Definition 5.15.4 . EC0662753F9C A subset $E\subseteq \Omega $ is thin 1 at $x\in \Omega $ if one of the following conditions holds: 2F25DFCC541C $x\not\in \overline{E}$; 9A680A93372A $x\in \overline{E}$ and there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{(U\cap E)\setminus \{ x\}  \ni y\to x} \varphi (y)<\varphi (x).  \] We say $E$ is thin if it is thin at all $x\in \Omega $. 1. ↩ Here “thin” means plurithin . Classical thinness, defined using subharmonic functions, is treated separately.

title: Remark 5.15.5

title: Lemma 5.15.9
text: Lemma 5.15.9 . D3F2BF3D82BD Let $E_1,E_2\subseteq \Omega $. Assume that $E_1$, $E_2$ are both thin at $x\in \Omega $. Then so is $E_1\cup E_2$. Proof. We may assume that $x\in \overline{E_1}\cap \overline{E_2}$. Take an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in E_ i\setminus \{ x\} } \varphi _ i(y)<\varphi _ i(x),\quad i=1,2.  \] Then $\varphi _1+\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ and \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in (E_1\cup E_2)\setminus \{ x\} } (\varphi _1+\varphi _2)(y)<\varphi _1(x)+\varphi _2(x).  \] In particular, $E_1\cup E_2$ is thin at $x$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.15.10 (H.Cartan)
text: Theorem 5.15.10 (H. Cartan) . 458C93F5F6CD Consider a set $E\subseteq \Omega $ and $x\in E$. Then the following are equivalent: 15B95CB674C7 $E$ is an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood of $x$; 53048930270F $\Omega \setminus E$ is thin at $x$. Proof. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Assume 2 . We may assume that $x\in \overline{\Omega \setminus E}$. Otherwise, our assertion follows from proposition 5.15.2 . By proposition 5.15.6 , there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $\Omega $ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \varphi (x)>\sup _{y\in U\cap (\Omega \setminus E)} \varphi (y)\eqqcolon \lambda .  \] Let $F=\{ y\in \Omega : \varphi (y)>\lambda \} $. Then $x\in F$ and $F$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open by example 5.15.3 . Moreover, $U\cap F\subseteq E$. By proposition 5.15.2 , we conclude 1 . 1 $\implies $ 2 . Assume 1 . We may always replace $E$ by smaller $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhoods of $x$. In particular, we may assume that $E$ has the following form \[  \{ y\in U:\varphi _1(y)>\lambda _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ m(y)>\lambda _ m\} ,  \] where $U\subseteq \Omega $ is an open neighborhood of $x$, and $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ m$ are $\mathbb {R}$-valued psh functions on $\Omega $, and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ m\in \mathbb {R}$. Since $x\in U$, the set $\Omega \setminus U$ is thin at $x$. Moreover, \[  \Omega \setminus E=(\Omega \setminus U)\cup \bigcup _{i=1}^ m\{ y\in U:\varphi _ i(y)\leq \lambda _ i\} .  \] By 5.15.9 , it is enough to prove that each set $\{ y\in U:\varphi _ i(y)\leq \lambda _ i\} $ is thin at $x$. Thus we may assume $m=1$. In this case, $\Omega \setminus E$ is clearly thin at $x$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.15.11
text: Theorem 5.15.11 . 4388B85DDD67 A base of the plurifine topology on $\Omega $ is given by sets of the following form: E3CEA68870B6 5.15.12 \begin{equation}  \left\{ x\in U: \varphi (x)>0\right\} , \end{equation} where $U\subseteq \Omega $ is an open subset and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. Proof. Observe that sets of the form ( 5.15.12 ) are $\mathcal{F}$-open. 2 By theorem 5.15.10 , it suffices to show its complement in $\Omega $ is thin at each point of ( 5.15.12 ), which is obvious. Now consider $x\in \Omega $ and an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood $V\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$. We want to find a set of the form ( 5.15.12 ) contained in $V$ and containing $x$. Write $E=\Omega \setminus V$. In case $x\in \operatorname{Int}V$, there is nothing to prove. So we may assume that $x\in \overline{E}$. By theorem 5.15.10 , $E$ is thin at $x$. By definition, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in U\cap (E\setminus \{ x\} )}\varphi (y)<\varphi (x).  \] We may assume that $\varphi |_{E\cap U}\leq 0<\varphi (x)$. Then the set $\{ y\in U:\varphi (y)>0\} $ suffices for our purpose. $\square$ 2. ↩ This is not entirely obvious by definition, as $\varphi $ is not defined on the whole $\Omega $.

title: Remark 5.15.13
text: Remark 5.15.13 . 2EDAD1EF1694 Recall that in general, an $\mathcal{F}$-open set is not a countable union of sets of the form ( 5.15.12 ). In fact, an $\mathcal{F}$-open set is not a Borel set in general. See [ EK23 ] for a concrete example.

title: Corollary 5.15.14
text: Corollary 5.15.14 . 49909C9A34E2 Let $\Omega _1\subseteq \Omega _2\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be two non-empty open subsets. Then the plurifine topology on $\Omega _1$ is the same as the subspace topology induced from the plurifine topology on $\Omega _2$.

title: Corollary 5.15.15
text: Corollary 5.15.15 . C94ADCA6E19D Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open subset and $x\in \Omega $. Then $x$ has a compact $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood contained in $\Omega $. Proof. By theorem 5.15.11 , it suffices to prove the assertion after replacing $\Omega $ by a smaller $\mathcal F$-open neighborhood of $x$. Thus we may assume that \[  \Omega =\{ y\in U:\varphi (y)>0\}   \] for some open set $U\subseteq \mathbb C^ n$ and some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. Take a compact neighborhood $K$ of $x$ in $U$. Now $\{ y\in K: \varphi (y)\geq \varphi (x)/2\} $ is a compact $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\Omega $. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.15.16
text: Corollary 5.15.16 . DF37542BAB03 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$, $\Omega '\subseteq \mathbb {C}^{n'}$ be two domains and $F\colon \Omega '\rightarrow \Omega $ be a holomorphic map. Then $F$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that the inverse image $F^{-1}(U)$ of each $\mathcal{F}$-open subset $U\subseteq \Omega $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. By theorem 5.15.11 , after possibly shrinking $\Omega $ and $\Omega '$, we may assume that $U$ has the form $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)>0\} $, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Clearly, we may assume that $F^{-1}(U)$ is non-empty. Then $F^*\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$ by proposition 5.13.17 , we find that \[  F^{-1}(U)=\{ y\in \Omega ': F^*\psi (y)>0\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$

title: 5.15.17 Plurifine topology on manifolds
text:
Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 5.47.14 . 09A00D4B8096 The plurifine topology on $X$ is the topology with a base consisting of sets of the form $F^{-1}(V)$, where $U\subseteq X$ is an open subset, $F\colon Uightarrow \Omega $ is a biholomorphic map, $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain for some $n\in \mathbb {N}$, and $V\subseteq \Omega $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Note that these sets form a topological base thanks to corollary 5.15.16 . Moreover, it also follows from corollary 5.15.16 that the plurifine topologies on domains defined in definition 5.47.14 and in definition 5.47.14 coincide. 


We refer to definition 5.17.1 for the notion of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. Proposition 5.15.18 . E49CF7960E4C Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi |_{\{ \varphi 
eq -\infty \} }$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous, since $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-closed. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\varphi =\psi +g$, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$ and $|g|\leq C$ for some $C>0$. For an open interval $(a,b)\subseteq \mathbb {R}$, it suffices to show that \[  U\coloneqq \left\{  x\in X:a<\varphi (x)<bight\} =\left\{  x\in X:a-g(x)<\psi (x)<b-g(x)ight\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Take $x\in U$. We can find an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $U$ such that \[  \sup _{y\in V} \left( a-g(y)ight)<\psi (x)< \inf _{y\in V} \left( b-g(y) ight).  \] Therefore, \[  \left\{ z\in V:\sup _{y\in V} \left(a-g(y)ight)<\psi (z)<\inf _{y\in V} \left(b-g(y)ight)ight\}   \] is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $U$. We conclude that $U$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$ Corollary 5.15.19 . 030D740FC9C6 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then the set \[  \{ x\in X: \varphi (x)>\psi (x)\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Proof. It suffices to show that for any $x\in X$ such that $\varphi (x)>\psi (x)$, the same holds on an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Observe that $\varphi (x)
eq -\infty $. If $\psi (x)
eq -\infty $, then it suffices to apply proposition 5.15.18 . Otherwise, take \[  U\coloneqq \{ y\in X: \varphi (y)>\varphi (x)-1\} \cap \{ y\in X: \psi (y)<\varphi (x)-1\} .  \] This is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\{ \varphi >\psi \} $. $\square$ Lemma 5.15.20 . 4014761D7A8A Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar subset. Then \[  \overline{X\setminus Z}^{\mathcal{F}}=X.  \] Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ and that there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ with $Z\subseteq \{ \varphi =-\infty \} $. It suffices to show that $\{ \varphi >-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-dense. Let $x\in X$ be a point with $\varphi (x)=-\infty $ and $U\subseteq X$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $X$. We need to show that $U\cap \{ \varphi >-\infty \} 
eq \varnothing $. Thanks to theorem 5.15.11 , after shrinking $U$, we may assume that there is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $U=\{ \psi >0\} $. Observe that $U$ is not a pluripolar set: Otherwise, $\psi \leq 0$ almost everywhere by proposition 5.14.4 , and hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . So $\varphi |_ U
ot\equiv -\infty $. We conclude that $U\cap \{ \varphi >-\infty \} 
eq \varnothing $, as desired. $\square$ Corollary 5.15.21 . 31032260EF62 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Set \[  W=\left\{ x\in X:\varphi (x)=-\infty ight\} 	extup{ or }W=\left\{ x\in X:\psi (x)=-\infty ight\} .  \] Then for any pluripolar set $Z\subseteq X$, we have \[  \sup _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\sup _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ),\quad \inf _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\inf _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ).  \] In particular, taking $\psi =0$, we find that \[  \sup _{X\setminus Z}\varphi =\sup _ X \varphi .  \] Proof. This is an immediate consequence of 5.15.20 and proposition 5.15.18 . $\square$ In the literature about pluripotential theory, one often finds the careless expressions like $\sup _ X (\varphi -\psi )$. The issue is that $\varphi -\psi $ is not defined everywhere, and hence this expression does not make sense if you read it literally. corollary 5.15.21 tells you that you do not have to worry too much about the details on a pluripolar set. In other words, $\sup $ and $\inf $ could always be understood as a kind of essential supremum and essential infimum modulo pluripolar sets. There is a convenient way to fix this issue in the literature — just replace the suprema by quasi-suprema: Definition 5.15.22 . 8485EC5E3BC1 Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar set, and $f\colon X\setminus Zightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. We define the quasi-supremum and the quasi-infimum of $f$ as follows: \[   egin{split}  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X f\coloneqq & \inf \left\{ \sup _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W 	extup{ is pluripolar}ight\} ,\  \operatorname *{q-inf}_ X f\coloneqq & \sup \left\{ \inf _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W 	extup{ is pluripolar}ight\} . \end{split}  \] For two functions $f$ and $g$ equal quasi-everywhere, the quasi-suprema and quasi-infima of them are equal, as is clear from the definition. For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $, we have \[  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X \varphi =\sup _ X \varphi ,  \] as a consequence of corollary 5.15.21 .

title: Proposition 5.15.18
text: Proposition 5.15.18 . E49CF7960E4C Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi |_{\{ \varphi \neq -\infty \} }$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous, since $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-closed. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\varphi =\psi +g$, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$ and $|g|\leq C$ for some $C>0$. For an open interval $(a,b)\subseteq \mathbb {R}$, it suffices to show that \[  U\coloneqq \left\{  x\in X:a<\varphi (x)<b\right\} =\left\{  x\in X:a-g(x)<\psi (x)<b-g(x)\right\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Take $x\in U$. We can find an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $U$ such that \[  \sup _{y\in V} \left( a-g(y)\right)<\psi (x)< \inf _{y\in V} \left( b-g(y) \right).  \] Therefore, \[  \left\{ z\in V:\sup _{y\in V} \left(a-g(y)\right)<\psi (z)<\inf _{y\in V} \left(b-g(y)\right)\right\}   \] is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $U$. We conclude that $U$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.15.19
text: Corollary 5.15.19 . 030D740FC9C6 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then the set \[  \{ x\in X: \varphi (x)>\psi (x)\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Proof. It suffices to show that for any $x\in X$ such that $\varphi (x)>\psi (x)$, the same holds on an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Observe that $\varphi (x)\neq -\infty $. If $\psi (x)\neq -\infty $, then it suffices to apply proposition 5.15.18 . Otherwise, take \[  U\coloneqq \{ y\in X: \varphi (y)>\varphi (x)-1\} \cap \{ y\in X: \psi (y)<\varphi (x)-1\} .  \] This is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\{ \varphi >\psi \} $. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.15.20
Corollary 5.15.21
text: Corollary 5.15.21 . 31032260EF62 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Set \[  W=\left\{ x\in X:\varphi (x)=-\infty \right\} \textup{ or }W=\left\{ x\in X:\psi (x)=-\infty \right\} .  \] Then for any pluripolar set $Z\subseteq X$, we have \[  \sup _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\sup _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ),\quad \inf _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\inf _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ).  \] In particular, taking $\psi =0$, we find that \[  \sup _{X\setminus Z}\varphi =\sup _ X \varphi .  \] Proof. This is an immediate consequence of 5.15.20 and proposition 5.15.18 . $\square$

title: Definition 5.15.22
text: Definition 5.15.22 . 8485EC5E3BC1 Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar set, and $f\colon X\setminus Z\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. We define the quasi-supremum and the quasi-infimum of $f$ as follows: \[  \begin{split}  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X f\coloneqq & \inf \left\{ \sup _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W \textup{ is pluripolar}\right\} ,\\  \operatorname *{q-inf}_ X f\coloneqq & \sup \left\{ \inf _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W \textup{ is pluripolar}\right\} . \end{split}  \]

section: 5.16 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves
text:
Lelong numbers measure logarithmic growth of plurisubharmonic singularities. Multiplier ideal sheaves record which holomorphic germs are square integrable against their weights. Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 5.16.1 . A8F9CC5C117D Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $x\in X$. The Lelong number $
u (\varphi ,x)$ of $\varphi $ at $x$ is defined as follows: If $x$ is a point on a $0$-dimensional connected component of $X$, we set \[  
u (\varphi ,x)=0.  \] Otherwise, take an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ and a biholomorphic map $F\colon Uightarrow \Omega $, where $\Omega $ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Then we define D4BCC2E76B62 5.16.2  egin{equation}  
u (\varphi ,x)\coloneqq \sup \left\{  \gamma \in \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}: \varphi (F^{-1}(y))\leq \gamma \log |y-F(x)|^2+\mathcal{O}(1)	extup{ as }y	o F(x) ight\} . \end{equation} Observe that $
u (\varphi ,x)$ does not depend on the choices of $U$ and $F$, see [ Page 167, Corollary 7.2 , DemBook ] . Furthermore, it follows from proposition 5.16.4 below that the supremum in ( 5.16.2 ) is a maximum. Remark 5.16.3 . 9ADE309D4F8B Our definition of the Lelong number is not standard. It differs from the standard definition by a factor of $2$. As a mnemonic, just remember \[  
u \left(\log |z|^2,0ight)=1 \quad (	ext{instead of } 2).  \] Our convention of the Lelong numbers together with the convention of the multiplier ideal sheaves below make sure that ( 5.16.16 ) has no extra factors. Proposition 5.16.4 . 61D6716B27F1 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ n(0,1))$. Then F9F65BFBF525 5.16.5  egin{equation}  
u (\varphi ,0)=\lim _{r 	o 0+}  rac{\sup _{B_ n(0,r)}\varphi }{\log r^2}\in [0,\infty ). \end{equation} Proof. Note that ( 5.16.5 ) is trivial when $n=0$, so we may assume that $n>0$ in the proof. It follows from proposition 5.13.11 that the limit in ( 5.16.5 ) exists and is finite. We shall denote the limit by $

u (\varphi ,x)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the Zariski topology. Proof. For every $c>0$, the analytic Lelong-level-set theorem proves that $\{x:

These are exactly the upper level sets needed for upper semicontinuity in the analytic Zariski topology. The normalization is the same in both statements: $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm i\partial ar\partial/(2\pi)$ and $

All properties follow directly from proposition 5.16.4 . $\square$ Corollary 5.16.9 . F3F797E97E9D Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ locally uniformly bounded from above and $x\in X$. Then \[  
u \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i,xight)=\inf _{i\in I}
u (\varphi _ i,x).  \] Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Write $\varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 5.14.2 . We observe that the $\leq $ inequality is trivial. It remains to argue the reverse inequality. It follows from proposition 5.14.3 that we may assume that $I$ is countable. When $I$ is finite, this is already proved in proposition 5.16.8 . Otherwise, we may further assume that $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Thanks to proposition 5.16.8 , we may further assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ is an increasing sequence. Furthermore, since the problem is local, we may assume that $x=0$, that $X=B_ n(0,1)$ for some $n\in \mathbb {N}$, and that $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is uniformly bounded from above on some ball $B_ n(0,r_1)$ with $0<r_1<1$. Since the sequence $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is increasing, the sequence $

u (\varphi _ i,0)\log |x|^2+C  \] for all $x\in B_ n(0,r_1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ and all $i\geq 1$, where $C$ is a constant independent of $i$. In particular, thanks to proposition 5.14.5 , for almost all $x\in B_ n(0,r_1)$, we have \[  \varphi (x)\leq \lim _{i	o \infty }
u (\varphi _ i,0)\log |x|^2+C.  \] Thanks to proposition 5.14.6 , the same holds for all $x
eq 0$ near $0$, and hence \[

u (\varphi _ i,0).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Definition 5.16.10 . 6777DFC31EF1 Let $F\subseteq X$ be a non-empty irreducible analytic subset. Then we define the generic Lelong number of $\varphi $ along $F$ as \[  
u (\varphi ,F)\coloneqq \min _{x\in F}
u (\varphi ,x).  \] Note that the minimum is attained by Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 5.16.7 . Definition 5.16.11 . E9EA7799080C Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Let $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$ (see definition 9.10.2 ). Take a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ from a complex manifold $Y$ such that $E$ is a prime divisor on $Y$, then we define the generic Lelong number of $\varphi $ along $E$ as \[  
u (\varphi ,E)\coloneqq 
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,E).  \] It follows from theorem 5.16.7 that $
u (\varphi ,E)$ does not depend on the choice of $\pi $. Definition 6.8.5 . 990C506B7D25 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, the multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$  of $\varphi $ is by definition the ideal sheaf given by \[  \Gamma \left(U,\mathcal{I}(\varphi )ight)=\left\{  f\in \mathcal{O}_ X(U) : |f|^2\exp (-\varphi )\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) ight\}   \] for any open subset $U\subseteq X$. Remark 5.16.12 . 4E2D4F8663A3 This definition is different from a few references, where instead of $\exp (-\varphi )$, they use $\exp (-2\varphi )$. The conventions adopted in the current book are the most convenient ones as far as I know. They simplify a number of formulae. As a mnemonic, for any real $\lambda >0$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \log |z|^2)=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {C}}\left(-\lfloor \lambda floor \{ 0\} ight)\quad \Bigl (	extup{instead of }\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {C}}\left(-\lfloor 2\lambda floor \{ 0\} ight)\Bigr ),  \] where $z$ is a variable in $\mathbb {C}$ and $\{ 0\} $ is the divisor defined by $0\in \mathbb {C}$. Proposition 5.16.13 (Nadel) . 926B8027EE55 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then $\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$ is coherent. Proof. On each coordinate ball, the multiplier-ideal coherence theorem proves that the germs $f$ for which $|f|^2\exp(-\varphi)$ is locally integrable form a coherent analytic ideal sheaf. This is exactly the definition of $\mathcal I(\varphi)$ used here.
