title: Theorem 5.16.26 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi)
section: 5.16 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves
text: Theorem 5.16.26 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . 151D57BCA31B Let $Y$ be a connected submanifold of $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then \[  \mathcal{I}\left(\varphi |_ Y\right)\subseteq \operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}(\varphi ).  \] Proof. This is local on $Y$. In coordinates in which $Y$ is a coordinate subspace, take a germ $f\in\mathcal I(\varphi|_Y)$. The weighted restriction theorem extends $f$ to a holomorphic germ $F$ in the ambient coordinates with $|F|^2\exp(-\varphi)$ integrable. Thus $F\in\mathcal I(\varphi)$ and its restriction is $f$. This is precisely the inclusion in the image ideal $\operatorname{Res}_Y\mathcal I(\varphi)$. The hypothesis that the restricted weight is not identically $-\infty$ ensures that its multiplier ideal has the intended nontrivial local definition; the earlier theorem also covers the zero-ideal case.

title: 5.17 Quasi-plurisubharmonic functions
text:
In practice, it is important to consider a variant of plurisubharmonic functions. We will fix a complex manifold $X$. Definition 5.17.1 . 3DC2C56EBB31 Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function or $\theta $-psh function for short on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ satisfying the condition that $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some smooth function $g$ on $U$, we have $g+\varphi |_ U\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. The set of $\theta $-psh functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that there exists a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta '$ on $X$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$. The set of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. There is a natural preorder on $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ defined as follows: Definition 16.7.1 . 3E4D57445698 Assume that $X$ is compact. Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $ and write $\varphi \preceq \psi $ 1 if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $\varphi \leq \psi +C$. We also say $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $ and write $\psi \succeq \varphi $. In case $\varphi \preceq \psi $ and $\psi \preceq \varphi $, we say $\varphi $ and $\psi $ have the same singularity type . We write $\varphi \sim \psi $  in this case. 1. ↩ Some people write $\psi \preceq \varphi $. It is sometimes convenient to include the constant function $-\infty $ as well. Then we always write $-\infty \preceq \varphi $ for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Formally, we write $-\infty \sim -\infty $ as well. 


When $X$ is not compact, one can still define similar notions, but the generalization is not unique, and we shall not consider them here. Remark 5.17.2 . 8B989AE345C3 The preceding results concerning plurisubharmonic functions can be extended mutatis mutandis to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. We will apply these extensions without further explanations. Proposition 5.17.3 . EC4B3805B84D Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then for any $a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$, the set \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \sup _ X \varphi \in [a,b]\right\}   \] is compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Moreover, $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X \varphi $ is $L^1$-continuous for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Qualification and proof. The compactness assertion needs connectedness of $X$, or a separate normalization on every connected component. Indeed, take the disjoint union of two compact connected complex manifolds, put $\theta=0$, and let $u_j$ equal $0$ on the first component and $-j$ on the second. Then $\sup_Xu_j=0$, but the $L^1$ norms tend to infinity, so this sequence has no convergent subsequence. Thus a proof for the stated disconnected case would be impossible. For connected $X$ of positive dimension, normalized global plurisubharmonic compactness proves the assertion, including continuity of $u\mapsto\sup_Xu$. In dimension zero, connected $X$ is a point and the assertion is compactness of $[a,b]$. More generally a compact manifold has finitely many connected components. Requiring $a_l\leq\sup_{X_l}u\leq b_l$ on every component gives a finite product of these compact sets, hence a compact set in $L^1(X)$. The global supremum is then the maximum of finitely many continuous component suprema and is continuous. This is an immediate consequence of [ Proposition 8.5, Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] . Remark 5.17.4 . 0CEC6D75820C More generally, if $K\subseteq X$ is a closed non-pluripolar subset, then \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \sup _ K \varphi \in [a,b]\right\}   \] is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. See [ Corollary 4.3 , GZ05 ] . As a consequence, if $\sup _ K \varphi \leq C_0$ for some $C_0\in \mathbb {R}$, then $\sup _ X \varphi \leq C_1$ for some $C_1\in \mathbb {R}$ as well. To see this, we may assume that $C_0>0$. When $\sup _ K \varphi \in [0,C_0]$, our assertion follows from the above. If $\sup _ K \varphi <0$, it suffices to observe that \[  \varphi \leq \varphi -\sup _ K \varphi .  \] Corollary 5.17.5 . B5E91AB35965 Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\sup _ X \varphi _ i$ is uniformly bounded from below. Then $\varphi =\inf _{i\in I} \varphi _ i$ is a $\theta $-psh function and 88BE4BEDE25D 5.17.6 \begin{equation}  \adjustlimits \lim _{i\in I}\sup _ X \varphi _ i=\sup _ X \varphi ,\quad \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi . \end{equation} Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. It suffices to show that $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $. From this, it follows that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1$ by proposition 5.14.2 . The $L^1$-continuity of $\eta \mapsto \sup _ X\eta $ on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ from proposition 5.17.3 then gives the first equality in ( 5.17.6 ). Fix $i_0\in I$ and replace $I$ by the cofinal tail $I_{\geq i_0}$. This does not change the infimum. On this tail we have \[  \sup _ X\varphi _ i\leq \sup _ X\varphi _{i_0},  \] while the suprema are bounded from below by assumption. Hence proposition 5.17.3 shows that the net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We may therefore take a subnet $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ converging in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ is a Willard subnet of $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, we know that it is also decreasing. Therefore, $\psi =\inf _{j\in J} \varphi _ j$ due to proposition 5.14.2 and proposition 5.14.6 . Fix $i_0\in I$. For all sufficiently large $j\in J$, the corresponding index of the subnet dominates $i_0$, hence \[  \varphi _ j\leq \varphi _{i_0}.  \] Therefore, $\psi \leq \varphi _{i_0}$. As $i_0$ was arbitrary, $\psi \leq \varphi $ everywhere. In particular, $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 5.17.7 . A1D8E7565DF1 Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then \[  \sup \Bigl \{  \nu (\varphi ,E): \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ) \Bigr \} <\infty .  \] Proof. It follows from the proof of [ Exercise 2.7 , GZ17 ] that $\nu (\bullet ,E)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since adding a constant does not change Lelong numbers, we may restrict to the compact set $\{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ X\varphi =0\} $ from proposition 5.17.3 . The desired upper bound follows. $\square$ Proposition 5.17.8 . AF2A3F35959C Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then the pull-back gives a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. Injectivity holds because $\pi$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset, and plurisubharmonic representatives are determined by their values almost everywhere. For surjectivity, descent across a smooth-target modification proves that every $\pi^*\theta$-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$ descends to a $\theta$-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. Locally, the descended function is defined off the exceptional image using the inverse map, extended by its upper semicontinuous regularization, and the removable-singularity argument in that proposition proves positivity and equality of its pullback with the original function. Thus every function on the right is a pullback, uniquely. This follows from a more general result theorem 9.10.5 . Since we shall constantly need the balayage argument of proposition 5.14.21 , we explain explicitly the global version of it. Proposition 5.17.9 . 5F9E17A436E9 Fix a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $B\Subset B' \subseteq X$ be two holomorphic balls. Assume that $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $B'$. Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that $\psi $ is bounded on an open neighborhood of $\overline{B}$, and \[  \begin{cases}  \left( \theta |_ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi |_ B \right)^ n = 0,\\  \psi = \varphi \quad \textup{on } X\setminus B. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. We shall call $\psi $ the balayage of $\varphi $ on $B$. Proof. By the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma, after possibly shrinking $B'$, we may write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some bounded function $g\in C^{\infty }(B')$. We can then use $g$ to translate $\theta $-psh functions to psh functions, and our assertion follows immediately from proposition 5.14.21 . $\square$

title: Definition 16.7.1
text: Definition 16.7.1 . 3E4D57445698 Assume that $X$ is compact. Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $ and write $\varphi \preceq \psi $ 1 if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $\varphi \leq \psi +C$. We write $\varphi \sim \psi $  in this case. 1. ↩ Some people write $\psi \preceq \varphi $. Definition 16.7.1 . 3E4D57445698 Let $u,v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$. We write $u\preceq v$ if there is a constant $C\in \mathbb R$ such that $u\leq v+C$ on $X$, and $u\sim v$ if both $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$; in the latter case $u$ and $v$ have the same singularity type . When this has to be distinguished from the multiplier-ideal type introduced below, we speak of the ordinary singularity type , or simply the ordinary type .

title: Proposition 5.17.7
text: Proposition 5.17.7 . A1D8E7565DF1 Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then \[  \sup \Bigl \{  \nu (\varphi ,E): \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ) \Bigr \} <\infty .  \] Proof. It follows from the proof of [ Exercise 2.7 , GZ17 ] that $\nu (\bullet ,E)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since adding a constant does not change Lelong numbers, we may restrict to the compact set $\{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ X\varphi =0\} $ from proposition 5.17.3 . The desired upper bound follows. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.17.8
text: Proposition 5.17.8 . AF2A3F35959C Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then the pull-back gives a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. Injectivity holds because $\pi$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset, and plurisubharmonic representatives are determined by their values almost everywhere. For surjectivity, descent across a smooth-target modification proves that every $\pi^*\theta$-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$ descends to a $\theta$-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. Locally, the descended function is defined off the exceptional image using the inverse map, extended by its upper semicontinuous regularization, and the removable-singularity argument in that proposition proves positivity and equality of its pullback with the original function. Thus every function on the right is a pullback, uniquely.

title: Proposition 5.17.9
text: Proposition 5.17.9 . 5F9E17A436E9 Fix a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $B\Subset B' \subseteq X$ be two holomorphic balls. Assume that $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $B'$. Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that $\psi $ is bounded on an open neighborhood of $\overline{B}$, and \[  \begin{cases}  \left( \theta |_ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi |_ B \right)^ n = 0,\\  \psi = \varphi \quad \textup{on } X\setminus B. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. Proof. By the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma, after possibly shrinking $B'$, we may write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some bounded function $g\in C^{\infty }(B')$. We can then use $g$ to translate $\theta $-psh functions to psh functions, and our assertion follows immediately from proposition 5.14.21 . $\square$

title: 5.18 Analytic singularities
text:
The simplest type of plurisubharmonic singularities is given by the so-called analytic singularities . The notion is fairly subtle and there are several mutually incompatible definitions in the literature, as we shall explain below. Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 6.14.5 . 6A7E913297D5 We say $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities if for each $x\in X$, we can find a connected open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $\varphi |_ U$ has the form: 90744C0CCE8E 5.18.1 \begin{equation}  c\log (|f_1|^2+\cdots +|f_ N|^2)+R, \end{equation} where $f_1,\ldots ,f_ N$ are holomorphic functions on $U$, $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $R$ is a bounded function on $U$. 1 When $R$ can be taken to be smooth 2 , we say $\varphi $ has neat analytic singularities . Suppose that there is a coherent ideal $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathcal{O}_ X$ on $X$ such that we can choose $U$ so that the $f_1,\ldots ,f_ N$ can be chosen as the generators of $\Gamma (U,\mathcal{I})$ and $c$ is independent of the choice of $U$. Then we say $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$. 1. ↩ Note that since $\varphi |_ U\not\equiv -\infty $ by assumption, it is implicit in the definition that $\{ f_1=\cdots =f_ N=0\} \subseteq U$ is a proper subset. 2. ↩ The decomposition ( 5.18.1 ) is highly non-unique. Here we mean for any $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ and a decomposition of the form ( 5.18.1 ) with $R$ smooth. In the non-trivial cases, $R$ cannot be smooth for all decompositions ( 5.18.1 ). If $X$ is compact, each potential with analytic singularities has a type. The type is not uniquely determined. We refer to [ Bou02 ] and [ Bou02b ] for the details. 


Some authors allow $c\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$ in ( 5.18.1 ). We keep $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ because the following closure property, which is essential in constructing Demailly approximations, would otherwise fail. Proposition 5.18.2 . AB08C5138082 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be potentials with analytic singularities. Then so are $\lambda \varphi $ ($\lambda \in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$), $\varphi +\psi $ and $\varphi \lor \psi $. Proof. The assertion for $\lambda \varphi $ follows by multiplying the rational coefficient in ( 5.18.1 ). The assertion for $\lor $ is proved in [ Proposition 4.1.8 , Dem15 ] . For the addition assertion, take local presentations as in ( 5.18.1 ) and multiply the corresponding finite systems of holomorphic generators. $\square$ Definition 5.18.3 . 670832106E8E Let $D$ be an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor 1 on $X$. We say $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has log singularities (along $D$) on $X$ if for each $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that 05DF50833BB0 $D|_ U$ has finitely many irreducible components and can be written as \[  D|_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i D_ i  \] with $D_ i$ prime divisors on $U$, $a_ i\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $s_ i$ holomorphic functions on $U$ defining $D_ i$, and B8CC79988714 we have C6AC1C84A3B3 5.18.4 \begin{equation}  \varphi |_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i\log |s_ i|^2+R, \end{equation} where $R$ is a bounded function on $U$. 1. ↩ Divisors and $\mathbb {Q}$-divisors are implicitly assumed to have locally finite coefficients as usual. By proposition 5.18.2 , $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. Lemma 5.18.5 . 3B54149D4222 Suppose that $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$ on $X$. Then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. Moreover, if in addition $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current 2 , then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. 2. ↩ That is, there is a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ in the sense of currents. Here and in the sequel, we write $\theta _{\varphi }$ for $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. Proof. The current $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]$ has bounded local potentials. Therefore, the class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. If $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, say $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ for a Kähler form $\omega $, then $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]-\omega $ is positive and has bounded local potentials, and therefore represents a nef class. We conclude that $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. $\square$ The following proposition follows immediately from the definitions: Proposition 5.18.6 . 4A902295BB8C Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a complex manifold $Y$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$). Then $\pi ^*\varphi $ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along $\pi ^*D$). Definition 5.18.7 . 239591DA9F90 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. A log resolution of $\varphi $ is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities along a simple normal crossing effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor. See definition 9.10.6 for the notion of modifications. Theorem 5.18.8 . D6BDA051B7C1 Assume that $X$ is compact. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities. Then there is a log resolution of $\varphi $. For a proof, we refer to the arguments on [ Page 104 , MM07 ] . 


A general quasi-plurisubharmonic function can be nicely approximated by those with analytic singularities. We need a few preliminary definitions. Definition 6.17.5 . 165F88FAE668 Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ in $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ if 46C84A9DAE79 $\varphi _ j$ has analytic singularities for each $j$; B059E004A0A9 $\varphi _ j$ is decreasing with limit $\varphi $; E413383CB676 there is a decreasing sequence $\epsilon _ j\geq 0$ with limit $0$ and a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$; 82DBC1A3025C for each $\lambda '>\lambda >0$, there is $j>0$ such that EF5655B5F536 5.18.9 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(\lambda ' \varphi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi ). \end{equation} We also say $(\theta _{\varphi _ j})_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\theta _{\varphi }$. Definition 5.18.10 . FFAA7E68EEC1 Let $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathcal O_ X$ be a coherent ideal sheaf and $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$. A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is said to have gentle analytic singularities (of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$) if 802BF78106AD $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$; 99804F1A8886 $\mathrm{e}^{{\varphi }/{c}}\colon X\to \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ is a smooth function; 78E694C022AB there is a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon \widetilde{X}\to X$ from a Kähler manifold $\widetilde{X}$ and an effective $\mathbb {Z}$-divisor $D$ on $\widetilde{X}$ such that one can write $\pi ^*\varphi $ locally as \[  \pi ^*\varphi =c\log |g|^2+h,  \] where $g$ is a local equation of the divisor $D$ and $h$ is smooth. Theorem 5.18.11 . 9348BF57481B Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$. Moreover, we can guarantee that for all $j>0$, $\varphi _ j$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $\left(2^{-j},\mathcal{I}(2^ j\varphi )\right)$. Proof. Apply the gentle quasi-equisingular approximation theorem to $(X,\theta,\varphi)$. It constructs approximants of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^j\varphi))$, with a curvature error tending to zero, convergence in $L^1$, and the required multiplier-ideal inclusions. These are the defining conditions of a quasi-equisingular approximation in this section. Its approximants have gentle analytic singularities, so they also supply the additional regularity asserted here. The powers $2^j$ fix a subsequence of Bergman approximations; they impose no extra assumption on $\varphi$. We refer to [ Dem92reg , DPS01 ] for the proof. 


Quasi-equisingular approximations are essentially unique in the following sense: Proposition 5.18.12 . 36EC36A38FAB Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ be two quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $. Then for any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any $j>0$, we can find $k_0>0$ such that for any $k\geq k_0$, we have \[  \psi _ k\preceq (1-\epsilon )\varphi _ j.  \] Proof. The final assertion of the comparison theorem for analytic approximants applies to the two given quasi-equisingular approximations. Its hypotheses are precisely compact Kähler $X$, a smooth closed background $\theta$, a $\theta$-plurisubharmonic limit, and the multiplier-ideal inclusions in the definition of quasi-equisingularity. For every fixed $j$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$ it yields $\psi_k\preceq(1-\varepsilon)\varphi_j$ for every sufficiently large $k$. The index is allowed to depend on $j$ and $\varepsilon$. In particular, no global pointwise ordering of two unrelated approximation sequences is being assumed. See [ Corollary 4.1.7 , Dem15 ] . Definition 5.18.13 . 99446B95B55B Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. Then we define $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$  as the ideal sheaf consisting of germs $f$ of holomorphic functions such that $\log |f|^2\leq \varphi +C$ for some $C\in \mathbb {R}$. By definition, $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\varphi )$. Lemma 5.18.14 . D9F25876A735 Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. The sheaf $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$ is coherent. Proof. By theorem 5.18.8 , we may find a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities. Observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\pi _*\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\pi ^*\varphi ),  \] so we may replace $X$ and $\varphi $ by $Y$ and $\pi ^*\varphi $ and assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$. We decompose $D$ into its irreducible components: \[  D=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ iD_ i.  \] In this case, observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\mathcal{O}_ X\left(-\sum _{i=1}^ N\left(\lceil a_ i \rceil D_ i\right)\right)  \] is clearly coherent. $\square$ The multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$ and the sheaf $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }$ are not very different in the asymptotic sense, as shown by the following lemma: Lemma 5.18.15 . 2E0432C779A0 Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. Then for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find $k_0>0$ such that for each $k\geq k_0$, we have 35E0DBB664F7 5.18.16 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}\left(k(1+\epsilon )\varphi \right)\subseteq \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(k\varphi ). \end{equation} Proof. We shall prove a more precise local result. Take $x\in X$, take an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X$ of $x$, on which \[  \varphi =c\log \left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)+\mathcal{O}(1),  \] where $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ are holomorphic functions on $U$. Then we claim that for any $\lambda >0$, we have D1A302A4CDD6 5.18.17 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )_ x\subseteq \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left( \left( \lambda -c^{-1}n \right)_+\varphi \right)_ x, \end{equation} where for any $a\in \mathbb {R}$, $a_+$ means $a\lor 0$. Note that ( 5.18.16 ) is a straightforward consequence of ( 5.18.17 ). The global result follows easily from the local result by the compactness of $X$. Fix a smooth volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$. Take $f\in \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )$. By strong openness theorem 5.16.21 , we can find $\epsilon >0$ so that $f\in \mathcal{I}((\lambda +\epsilon /c)\varphi )$. Therefore, we can find an open neighborhood $W\subseteq U$ of $x$ so that \[  \int _ W |f|^2\left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)^{-c\lambda -\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}V<\infty .  \] But it follows from the Briançon–Skoda division theorem ( [ Sko72 ] , [ SB74 ] , [ Theorem 11.17 , Dem12 ] ) that \[  f_ x\in \left(g_{1,x},\ldots ,g_{N,x} \right)^\alpha ,  \] where $\alpha =\left(\lfloor c \lambda \rfloor -n+1\right)_+$. Here $\left(g_{1,x},\ldots ,g_{N,x} \right)$ denotes the ideal in $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ generated by the germs of $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ at $x$. Note that $\alpha \geq (c\lambda -n)_+$. It follows that on a neighborhood of $x$, we have \[  \log |f|^2\leq \alpha \log \left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)+\mathcal{O}(1)\leq c^{-1}\alpha \varphi +\mathcal{O}(1).  \] Hence ( 5.18.17 ) follows. $\square$ Theorem 5.18.18 . 2D610C4DD6AD Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega |_ Y)$ such that $\omega |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current and $\mathrm{e}^{\varphi }$ is a Hölder continuous function on $Y$. Then there exists $\tilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying 1E31A11A83C4 $\tilde{\varphi }|_ Y=\varphi $; 2229D01A1A95 $\omega _{\tilde{\varphi }}$ is a Kähler current. In addition, if $\varphi $ has analytic singularities, then so does $\tilde{\varphi }$. See [ Theorem 6.1 , DRWNXZ ] .

title: Lemma 5.18.5
text: Lemma 5.18.5 . 3B54149D4222 Suppose that $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$ on $X$. Then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. Moreover, if in addition $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current 2 , then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. 2. ↩ That is, there is a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ in the sense of currents. Proof. The current $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]$ has bounded local potentials. Therefore, the class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. If $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, say $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ for a Kähler form $\omega $, then $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]-\omega $ is positive and has bounded local potentials, and therefore represents a nef class. We conclude that $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. $\square$
