title: 5.19 The space of currents
text:
Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$. Definition 5.19.1 . DF4FCB370781 Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$ and $m\in \mathbb {N}$. We say an $(m,m)$-current $T$ on $Y$ is positive 1 if either $m>N$ or for any smooth $(1,0)$-forms $ eta _1,\ldots , eta _{N-m}$ on $Y$, the measure \[  T\wedge \mathrm{i} eta _1\wedge \overline{ eta _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{i} eta _{N-m}\wedge \overline{ eta _{N-m}}  \] is positive. 1. ↩ This notion is sometimes known as weak positivity . The basic properties of positive currents can be found in [ Section III.1 , DemBook ] . Recall that a positive current is necessarily real. Definition 5.19.2 . AE4F30A1999E We say $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current in $\alpha $. We say $\alpha $ is big if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ in $\alpha $ dominating a Kähler form. Such currents are called Kähler currents . Given classes $\alpha , eta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, we say $\alpha \leq  eta $ if $ eta -\alpha $ is pseudo-effective. Definition 5.19.3 . 49CF4A9C5660 We introduce the following notations: 9DEEC889C347 $\mathcal{Z}_+(X)$  denotes the space of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$; 146392D01DAE given a pseudo-effective $(1,1)$-class $\alpha $ on $X$, we write $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$  for the set of $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ such that $\{ T\} =\alpha $. Here $\{ T\} $ denotes the cohomology class represented by $T$. definition 16.7.1 has a natural analogue for currents. Definition 5.19.4 . 0909012E7F31 Given $T,T'\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, we write $T\preceq T'$ and say $T$ is more singular than $T'$ if when we write $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $, $T'=	heta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi '$, we have $\varphi \preceq \varphi '$. We write $T\sim T'$ if $T\preceq T'$ and $T'\preceq T$. In this case, we say $T$ and $T'$ have the same singularity type . Remark 5.19.5 . 877B9D0BDD26 Observe that \[  \mathcal{Z}_+(X)/\sim \cong \mathrm{QPSH}(X)/\sim  \] canonically. The correspondence sends the class of a closed positive current $	heta _{\varphi }=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ to the class of $\varphi $. We will adopt the following convention: Whenever we have a notion for quasi-plurisubharmonic functions which depends only on the singularity type, we use the same notation and the same definition for closed positive $(1,1)$-currents. Example 5.19.6 . AAD0C8775B34 As an important example of 5.19.5 , given $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ and $x\in X$, we define 3E19B5D1CC32 5.19.7  egin{equation}  
u (T,x)=
u (\varphi ,x). \end{equation} Again, as in 5.16.3 , this differs from the definitions in some literature by a factor of $2$. But given our normalization \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}= rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial },  \] ( 5.19.7 ) seems to be the most natural choice. The key example to keep in mind is the following: \[  
u ([0],0)=1,  \] where $[0]$ is the current of integration at $0\in \mathbb {P}^1$. In fact, as a simple application of the Green's second identity, one can verify that \[   rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }\log |z|^2=\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side is the Dirac delta distribution at $0\in \mathbb {C}$. Definition 5.19.8 . 4A951ED7EEE8 Given $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, represent $T$ as $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The polar locus of $T$ is defined as the set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $. It is clear that the polar locus of $T$ is independent of the choices of $	heta $ and $\varphi $. We also call the set $\{ -\infty \} $ the polar locus of $\varphi $. Definition 5.19.9 . AEE3AF4068CD Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-Kähler locus $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the intersection of the polar loci of all Kähler currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha $. Theorem 5.19.10 (Boucksom) . 847815EFB4FE Assume that $\alpha $ is big. There is a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ with analytic singularities, such that the polar locus of $T$ is exactly $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. In particular, $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ is a proper Zariski closed subset of $X$. Proof. The big-class part of the theorem on positivity loci constructs a single Kähler current with analytic singularities whose pole set is $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha)$. This set is the same as $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha)$ here, by the defining intersection of singular loci of Kähler currents in $\alpha$. The same theorem proves that this pole set is a proper analytic subset. Thus its constructed current has all the required properties, including equality, rather than just containment, of the polar locus. See [ Théorème 2.1.20 , Bou02 ] . Definition 5.19.11 . 1AA67767FB84 Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-nef locus $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the following set: \[  \operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\coloneqq \{ x\in X :
u (T_{\min },x)>0\} ,  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Note that $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\subseteq \operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. Thanks to theorem 5.16.7 , $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ is a countable union of proper Zariski closed subsets of $X$. The non-Kähler locus and non-nef locus are studied in detail in [ Bou02 ] . Lemma 5.19.12 (Siu's decomposition) . F956E74CD8C5 Let $E$ be a prime divisor on $X$. Then for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, the difference $T-
u (T,E)[E]$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current. Proof. By the proved divisorial decomposition ,
\[T=R+\sum_D
u(T,D)[D],\qquad R\geq0,\]
where the series converges weakly and every summand is positive. Remove the summand with $D=E$; the remaining weakly convergent sum together with $R$ is positive and closed. It is exactly $T-
u(T,E)[E]$. If $
u(T,E)=0$, the assertion reduces to positivity of $T$. Here $[E]$ is the current of integration associated with $E$, while $\{ E\} $ denotes the cohomology class of $E$. See [ Page 386, Example 1 , GH14 ] for the precise definition. See [ Lemma 2.17 , Dem12 ] for the proof. As a consequence, for each closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, we can write 6720366F8D5B 5.19.13  egin{equation}  T=\operatorname{Reg}T+\sum _{i} c_ i [E_ i], \end{equation} where $\{ E_ i\} $ is a countable collection of prime divisors on $X$, $c_ i>0$. Definition 5.19.14 . 5545837BA9C1 A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ is non-divisorial (resp. divisorial ) if $T=\operatorname{Reg}T$ (resp. $\operatorname{Reg}T=0$). It is helpful to check that our conventions are always consistent: There is no extra factor of $2$ or $1/2$ anywhere. One can verify this using our favorite example as in example 5.19.6 . Next we recall the notion of modified nef classes. Definition 5.19.15 . 4DFBEC43A4B0 A class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ is modified nef if the following condition holds: after fixing a reference Kähler metric $\omega $ on $X$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find a closed $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ such that EEF77CF757EA $T+\epsilon \omega \geq 0$; AEF6FAE47DAC $
u (T+\epsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for any prime divisor $D$ on $X$. This definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $. These classes are called nef en codimension $1$ in Boucksom's thesis [ Bou02 ] , where they were introduced for the first time. They are also known as movable classes in other references. Modified nef classes form a closed convex cone in $\mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$. Note that a modified nef class is necessarily pseudo-effective. A nef class is obviously modified nef. 


Recall the multiplicity of a cohomology class as defined in [ Section 2.1.3 , Bou02 ] : Definition 5.19.16 . 0EB97717F408 Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class and $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. We define the Lelong number $
u (\alpha ,D)$ as follows: C6833F83A5C1 When $\alpha $ is big, define $
u (\alpha ,D)=
u (T,D)$ for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ with minimal singularities. 3CE6AD34390C In general, define \[  
u (\alpha ,D)\coloneqq \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}
u (\alpha +\epsilon \{ \omega \} ,D).  \] When $\alpha $ is big, 2 is compatible with 1 and the definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $. By definition, a pseudo-effective class $\alpha $ is modified nef if and only if $
u (\alpha ,D)=0$ for all prime divisors $D$ on $X$. Let us recall the behavior of several cones under modifications. Proposition 5.19.17 . 191D96316EC3 Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. 4F00658A644B For any nef class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is nef. 98B07470D933 For any modified nef class $ eta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _* eta $ is modified nef. Proof. Only 2 requires a proof. Fix a Kähler class $\gamma $ on $Y$. Since the modified nef cone is closed, replacing $ eta $ by $ eta +\epsilon \gamma $ and then letting $\epsilon 	o 0+$ reduces the proof to the case where $ eta $ is big as well. Let $T$ (resp. $S$) be a current with minimal singularities in $\pi _* eta $ (resp. in $ eta $), and let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It suffices to show that \[  
u (T,D)=0.  \] Since $ eta $ is modified nef, $S$ is non-divisorial. Hence by 5.19.18 below, $
u (\pi _*S,D)=0$. Since $T$ has minimal singularities in $\pi _* eta $, we have $T\succeq \pi _*S$, and the desired equality follows. $\square$ Recall that non-divisorial currents are introduced in definition 5.19.14 . Lemma 5.19.18 . 9F062B47A2B4 Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $T$ be a non-divisorial current on $Y$. Then $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. Conversely, if $S$ is a non-divisorial current on $X$, $\pi ^*S$ could have divisorial part. As a simple example, consider $S$ on $\mathbb {P}^2$, whose local potential near $0\in \mathbb {C}^2_{z,w}$ looks like $\log (|z|^2+|w|^2)$. Proof. Let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It follows from Zariski's main theorem theorem 9.10.5 that $D$ is not contained in the exceptional locus of $\pi $. Let $D'$ be the strict transform of $D$. Thanks to Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 5.16.7 , we have \[  
u (\pi _*T,D)=
u (T,D')=0.  \] Hence $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. $\square$

title: Definition 5.19.1
text: Definition 5.19.1 . DF4FCB370781 Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$ and $m\in \mathbb {N}$. We say an $(m,m)$-current $T$ on $Y$ is positive 1 if either $m>N$ or for any smooth $(1,0)$-forms $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _{N-m}$ on $Y$, the measure \[  T\wedge \mathrm{i}\beta _1\wedge \overline{\beta _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{i}\beta _{N-m}\wedge \overline{\beta _{N-m}}  \] is positive. 1. ↩ This notion is sometimes known as weak positivity .

title: Definition 5.19.2
text: Definition 5.19.2 . AE4F30A1999E We say $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current in $\alpha $. We say $\alpha $ is big if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ in $\alpha $ dominating a Kähler form. Such currents are called Kähler currents .

title: Definition 5.19.3
text: Definition 5.19.3 . 49CF4A9C5660 We introduce the following notations: 9DEEC889C347 $\mathcal{Z}_+(X)$  denotes the space of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$; 146392D01DAE given a pseudo-effective $(1,1)$-class $\alpha $ on $X$, we write $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$  for the set of $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ such that $\{ T\} =\alpha $.

title: Definition 5.19.4
text: Definition 5.19.4 . 0909012E7F31 Given $T,T'\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, we write $T\preceq T'$ and say $T$ is more singular than $T'$ if when we write $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $, $T'=\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi '$, we have $\varphi \preceq \varphi '$. We write $T\sim T'$ if $T\preceq T'$ and $T'\preceq T$. In this case, we say $T$ and $T'$ have the same singularity type .

title: Remark 5.19.5
text: Remark 5.19.5 . 877B9D0BDD26 Observe that \[  \mathcal{Z}_+(X)/\sim \cong \mathrm{QPSH}(X)/\sim  \] canonically. The correspondence sends the class of a closed positive current $\theta _{\varphi }=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ to the class of $\varphi $. We will adopt the following convention: Whenever we have a notion for quasi-plurisubharmonic functions which depends only on the singularity type, we use the same notation and the same definition for closed positive $(1,1)$-currents.

title: Example 5.19.6
text:
Example 5.19.6 . AAD0C8775B34 As an important example of 5.19.5 , given $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ and $x\in X$, we define 3E19B5D1CC32 5.19.7  egin{equation}  
u (T,x)=
u (\varphi ,x). \end{equation} Again, as in 5.16.3 , this differs from the definitions in some literature by a factor of $2$. But given our normalization \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}= rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial },  \] ( 5.19.7 ) seems to be the most natural choice. The key example to keep in mind is the following: \[  
u ([0],0)=1,  \] where $[0]$ is the current of integration at $0\in \mathbb {P}^1$. In fact, as a simple application of the Green's second identity, one can verify that \[   rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }\log |z|^2=\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side is the Dirac delta distribution at $0\in \mathbb {C}$.

title: Equation 5.19.7
text: 3E19B5D1CC32 5.19.7 \begin{equation}  \nu (T,x)=\nu (\varphi ,x). \end{equation}

title: Definition 5.19.8
text: Definition 5.19.8 . 4A951ED7EEE8 Given $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, represent $T$ as $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The polar locus of $T$ is defined as the set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $.

title: Definition 5.19.9
text: Definition 5.19.9 . AEE3AF4068CD Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-Kähler locus $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the intersection of the polar loci of all Kähler currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha $.

title: Theorem 5.19.10 (Boucksom)
text: Theorem 5.19.10 (Boucksom) . 847815EFB4FE Assume that $\alpha $ is big. There is a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ with analytic singularities, such that the polar locus of $T$ is exactly $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. In particular, $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ is a proper Zariski closed subset of $X$. Proof. The big-class part of the theorem on positivity loci constructs a single Kähler current with analytic singularities whose pole set is $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha)$. This set is the same as $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha)$ here, by the defining intersection of singular loci of Kähler currents in $\alpha$. The same theorem proves that this pole set is a proper analytic subset. Thus its constructed current has all the required properties, including equality, rather than just containment, of the polar locus.

title: Definition 5.19.11
text: Definition 5.19.11 . 1AA67767FB84 Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-nef locus $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the following set: \[  \operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\coloneqq \{ x\in X :\nu (T_{\min },x)>0\} ,  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $.

title: Lemma 5.19.12 (Siu's decomposition)
text:
Lemma 5.19.12 (Siu's decomposition) . F956E74CD8C5 Let $E$ be a prime divisor on $X$. Then for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, the difference $T-
u (T,E)[E]$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current. Proof. By the proved divisorial decomposition ,
\[T=R+\sum_D
u(T,D)[D],\qquad R\geq0,\]
where the series converges weakly and every summand is positive. Remove the summand with $D=E$; the remaining weakly convergent sum together with $R$ is positive and closed. It is exactly $T-
u(T,E)[E]$. If $
u(T,E)=0$, the assertion reduces to positivity of $T$.

title: Equation 5.19.13
text: 6720366F8D5B 5.19.13 \begin{equation}  T=\operatorname{Reg}T+\sum _{i} c_ i [E_ i], \end{equation}

title: Definition 5.19.14
text: Definition 5.19.14 . 5545837BA9C1 A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ is non-divisorial (resp. divisorial ) if $T=\operatorname{Reg}T$ (resp. $\operatorname{Reg}T=0$).

title: Definition 5.19.15
text: Definition 5.19.15 . 4DFBEC43A4B0 A class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ is modified nef if the following condition holds: after fixing a reference Kähler metric $\omega $ on $X$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find a closed $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ such that EEF77CF757EA $T+\epsilon \omega \geq 0$; AEF6FAE47DAC $\nu (T+\epsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for any prime divisor $D$ on $X$. This definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $.

title: Definition 5.19.16
text:
Definition 5.19.16 . 0EB97717F408 Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class and $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. We define the Lelong number $
u (\alpha ,D)$ as follows: C6833F83A5C1 When $\alpha $ is big, define $
u (\alpha ,D)=
u (T,D)$ for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ with minimal singularities. 3CE6AD34390C In general, define \[  
u (\alpha ,D)\coloneqq \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}
u (\alpha +\epsilon \{ \omega \} ,D).  \]

title: Proposition 5.19.17
text: Proposition 5.19.17 . 191D96316EC3 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. 4F00658A644B For any nef class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is nef. 98B07470D933 For any modified nef class $\beta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _*\beta $ is modified nef. Proof. Only 2 requires a proof. Fix a Kähler class $\gamma $ on $Y$. Since the modified nef cone is closed, replacing $\beta $ by $\beta +\epsilon \gamma $ and then letting $\epsilon \to 0+$ reduces the proof to the case where $\beta $ is big as well. Let $T$ (resp. $S$) be a current with minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $ (resp. in $\beta $), and let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It suffices to show that \[  \nu (T,D)=0.  \] Since $\beta $ is modified nef, $S$ is non-divisorial. Hence by 5.19.18 below, $\nu (\pi _*S,D)=0$. Since $T$ has minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $, we have $T\succeq \pi _*S$, and the desired equality follows. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.19.18
text: Lemma 5.19.18 . 9F062B47A2B4 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $T$ be a non-divisorial current on $Y$. Then $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. Proof. Let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It follows from Zariski's main theorem theorem 9.10.5 that $D$ is not contained in the exceptional locus of $\pi $. Let $D'$ be the strict transform of $D$. Thanks to Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 5.16.7 , we have \[  \nu (\pi _*T,D)=\nu (T,D')=0.  \] Hence $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. $\square$

title: 5.20 Plurisubharmonic metrics on line bundles
text:
A natural source of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions is the metrics on line bundles. Let $X$ be a connected Kähler manifold and $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Usually, we do not distinguish $L$ from the associated invertible sheaf $\mathcal{O}_ X(L)$. Definition 5.20.1 . C5880C6F61FA Let $V$ be a $1$-dimensional complex linear space. A Hermitian form $h$ on $V$ is a map $h\colon V\times V\rightarrow \mathbb {C}$ such that CF86155BCCFB $h$ is $\mathbb {C}$-linear in the second variable and conjugate linear in the first, and B8DA9F74F30F \[  |v|_ h^2\coloneqq h(v,v)\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}  \] for each $v\in V\setminus \{ 0\} $. We usually identify $h$ with the quadratic form $V\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ sending $v$ to $|v|_ h^2$. We write $|v|_ h=\sqrt{|v|_ h^2}$ for any $v\in V$. The singular Hermitian form on $V$ is the map $V\rightarrow \{ 0,\infty \} $ sending $0$ to $0$ and other elements to $\infty $. Definition 5.20.2 . 90891EB78EA0 Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be $1$-dimensional complex linear spaces. Given two maps $h_ i\colon V_ i\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ ($i=1,2$), each of which is either a Hermitian form or a singular Hermitian form, we define the tensor product $h_1\otimes h_2\colon V_1\otimes V_2\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ as follows: F0878993B90B If either $h_1$ or $h_2$ is singular, we define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the singular Hermitian form; 6CC728E84DA0 otherwise, define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the usual tensor product: For any $v_1\in V_1$, $v_2\in V_2$, set \[  h_1\otimes h_2(v_1\otimes v_2)=h_1(v_1)h_2(v_2).  \] Definition 5.20.3 . 293669D813B8 A Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ is a family of Hermitian forms $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$, such that 8F75F9950CF9 for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is a Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and 56AE61E47B2A for each local holomorphic section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}_ X(L)$, the map $x\mapsto |s(x)|^2_{h_ x}$ is smooth. The pair $(L,h)$ is called a Hermitian line bundle . We shall write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$ 2 for the first Chern form of $h$ 3 , normalized so that \[  [c_1(L,h)]=c_1(L).  \] The map $x\mapsto |s(x)|_{h_ x}$ will be denoted by $|s|_ h$. To be more precise, if $U\subseteq X$ is an open subset on which $L$ admits a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$, then we define \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left(-\log |s|_ h^2\right).  \] 2. ↩ The unusual notation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is sometimes referred to as the Göteborg notation because it is widely used by complex geometers in Göteborg (usually spelled as Gothenburg in English, the second largest (yet very poorly known) city in Sweden). As I identify myself as Göteborgare , I do not feel guilty about this notation. 3. ↩ In the literature, people sometimes define the curvature form of $(L,h)$ as $\Theta _{h}=-2\pi \mathrm{i}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Proposition 5.20.4 (Lelong–Poincaré) . 0C02CD3B5D59 Let $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ be non-zero and $h$ be a Hermitian metric on $L$. Then 1322FD7BDF4F 5.20.5 \begin{equation}  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $Z(s)$ is the zero divisor defined by $s$ and $[\bullet ]$ denote the associated current of integration. Proof. In a holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$, write $s=fe$ and $|e|_h^2=\exp(-\rho)$. Then $\log|s|_h^2=\log|f|^2-\rho$ and $c_1(L,h)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\rho$. The normalized Poincaré--Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\log|f|^2=[Z(f)]$. Substitution proves
\[c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\log|s|_h^2=[Z(s)].\]
Changing the frame multiplies $f$ by a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic function; its logarithmic squared modulus is pluriharmonic, so the local identities agree on overlaps. This also checks the factor $1/(2\pi)$ in the normalization. See [ (3.11) , Dem12 ] . Again, we want to check that our conventions are compatible by investigating the following simple example. Example 5.20.6 . 0D9E7B0EE3DC Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. The homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb {P}^1$ will be denoted by $[X_0:X_1]$. At a point $x=[X_0:X_1]\in \mathbb {P}^1$, the fiber $L_ x$ is identified with the dual of $[x]$, where $[x]\subseteq \mathbb {C}^2$ is the line represented by $x$. In order to introduce the Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$, we fix the standard Hermitian norm $\| \bullet \| $ on $\mathbb {C}^2$. Then given $\lambda \in L_ x=[x]^{\vee }$, we introduce \[  |\lambda |_{h_ x}=\frac{|\lambda (\tilde{x})|}{\| \tilde{x}\| },  \] where $\tilde{x}$ is an arbitrary non-zero element in $[x]$. The reader can easily verify that $h$ is indeed a Hermitian metric on $L$. The Hermitian metric $h$ is known as the Fubini–Study metric . A holomorphic section $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ can be formally identified with a linear form $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$: At $x\in X$, the corresponding linear form on $[x]$ is given by sending $(X_0,X_1)$ to $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$. Next we compute $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$. For this purpose, we cover $\mathbb {P}^1$ by $\mathbb {C}=\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ \infty \} $ and $\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ 0\} $. Both are holomorphic coordinate charts with coordinate function $z=X_0/X_1$ and $z^{-1}=X_1/X_0$ respectively. We claim that on $\mathbb {C}$, 3C9B623060E7 5.20.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation} In fact, let $t$ be the nowhere vanishing section of $L$ on $\mathbb {C}$ corresponding to $X_1$. Then for $z\in \mathbb {C}$, we have an obvious lift $(z,1)\in [z]$, so \[  |t|_ h^2(z)=\frac{1}{|z|^2+1}.  \] So ( 5.20.7 ) follows. In order to obtain a non-trivial case of the Lelong–Poincaré formula, we need to consider a section which vanishes at some points in $\mathbb {C}$. Let $s$ be the holomorphic section of $L$ corresponding to $X_0$. Then \[  \log |s|_ h^2(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for any $z\in \mathbb {C}$ using the same argument as above. Therefore, we find that restricted to $\mathbb {C}$, we have \[  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=[0],  \] where $f(z)=\log |z|^2$. So the Lelong–Poincaré formula ( 5.20.5 ) is verified in this case. The Kähler form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$ is also known as the Fubini–Study metric . Definition 5.20.8 . A43467D63B4A A (singular) plurisubharmonic metric (or psh metric for short) 4 $h$ on $L$ is a family $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$ such that DCF7D606ADB1 for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is either a Hermitian form on $L_ x$ or the singular Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and 32709CF6AC92 there is a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each $v\in L_ x$, we have 6C8BC3AC251D 5.20.9 \begin{equation}  |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation} The (first) Chern current of $h$ is by definition \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)\coloneqq c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] The set of psh metrics on $L$ will be denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$. 4. ↩ In the literature, people usually refer to such metrics as positively curved singular Hermitian metrics . I dislike this terminology, as having positive curvature only determines a plurisubharmonic metric almost everywhere, not everywhere. We shall write the plurisubharmonic metric defined by ( 5.20.9 ) as $h_0\exp (-\varphi )$ 1 . With these conventions, $c_1(L,h)$ does not depend on the choice of $h_0$. 1. ↩ Be careful, this is not $h_0^2\exp (-\varphi )$, as I prefer to think of $h_0$ as a quadratic form. Given a local holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we shall use the following notations interchangeably to denote the map $x\mapsto h_ x(s)$: \[  |s|^2_ h=h(s)=h(s,s).  \] Remark 5.20.10 . D2F8C4BB2BD4 In the literature, some people prefer the convention that in ( 5.20.9 ), neither side has the square. Our choice seems to be the most natural one given our normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Observe that once a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ is given, the construction in 2 gives a bijection between $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ and the set of plurisubharmonic metrics on $L$. Based on this correspondence, plurisubharmonic metrics have the same functoriality property as quasi-plurisubharmonic functions in proposition 5.13.17 . In particular, given a connected closed submanifold $Y$ of $X$, $h|_ Y$ is a plurisubharmonic metric as long as it is not singular everywhere. Definition 5.20.11 . 9834FE8F2B0D Given two holomorphic line bundles $L_1$, $L_2$ on $X$ and plurisubharmonic metrics $h_1$ on $L_1$ and $h_2$ on $L_2$, we define the tensor product plurisubharmonic metric $h_1\otimes h_2$ on $L_1\otimes L_2$ as follows: for each $x\in X$, define \[  (h_1\otimes h_2)_ x=h_{1,x}\otimes h_{2,x}  \] in the sense of definition 5.20.2 . We can easily verify that $h_1\otimes h_2$ is indeed a plurisubharmonic metric on $L_1\otimes L_2$. Example 5.20.12 . CC1C409253F3 We continue with our example example 5.20.6 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. Let $h^0$ denote the Fubini–Study metric on $L$ as defined in example 5.20.6 . Note that we have changed the notation from $h$ to $h^0$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h^0$. We construct $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ as follows: On $\mathbb {C}$, define 6B76079BBD9C 5.20.13 \begin{equation}  \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation} Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C},\omega |_{\mathbb {C}})$ by ( 5.20.7 ). Setting $\varphi (\infty )=0$, we can easily verify that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {P}^1,\omega )$. 5 We then get a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h^0\exp (-\varphi )$. To be more explicit, the fiber metric $h$ at $0$ is singular, $h_{\infty }=h^0_{\infty }$, while for $z\in \mathbb {C}\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $\lambda \in [z]^{\vee }$, we have \[  |\lambda |_{h_ z}=\frac{|\lambda (z,1)|}{|z|}.  \] 5. ↩ This can also be verified using the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem theorem 5.14.10 . In the remainder of this section, we assume that $X$ is compact. Definition 5.20.14 . 9FE903B6E5A8 Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a psh metric $h$ on $L$ of the following form: There exists $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ m)$ and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ N\in \mathbb {Q}$ such that for any local nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we have \[  |s|_ h^2=\min _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left| \frac{s^{\otimes m}}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ i/2}s_ i}\right|^{2m^{-1}}.  \] We write $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ for the set of Fubini–Study metrics on $L$. If we fix a reference smooth Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ with $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_0$, we can write $h=h_0\exp (-\varphi )$ with \[  \varphi =\frac{1}{m}\max _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left(\log |s_ i|^2_{h_0^{m}}+\lambda _ i\right).  \] Similarly, we write $\mathrm{FS}(X,\theta )$ for the set of such functions. Definition 5.20.15 . 8FCD7BEEDD56 Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. The set $\widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$ containing $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ which is closed under the following two operations: B253418A2EBA $\mathbb {Q}$-convex combinations: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ and $t\in (0,1)$, then \[  h_1^ t \otimes h_2^{1-t}\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L);  \] CCB3DD349505 minima: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$, then \[  \min \{ h_1,h_2\} \in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L).  \] We shall need the following Ohsawa–Takegoshi type extension theorem. Theorem 5.20.16 . 2985932B2B64 Assume that $L$ is big and $T$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h_ T$ on $T$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ and let $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Let $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold of dimension $m$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta - \delta \omega )$ for some $\delta >0$ and $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then there exists $k_0(\delta ,h_ T)>0$ such that for all $k \geq k_0$ and $s \in \mathrm{H}^0(Y, T\otimes L|_ Y^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi |_ Y))$ 6 , there exists an extension $\tilde s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X, T\otimes L^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ such that \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \leq C \int _ Y |s|^2_{(h^ k\otimes h_ T)|_ Y} \mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi |_ Y}\, \omega |_ Y^ m,  \] where $C>0$ is an absolute constant, independent of the data $(\varphi ,s,k)$. 6. ↩ Here and in the sequel, we usually abbreviate $\otimes k$ in the superscript as $k$ to save space. This is a special case of [ Theorem 1.4 , His12 ] . 


Let us also recall a simple result about the Bergman kernel approximations: Proposition 5.20.17 . 2DDBBF280789 Let $(L,h)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$ and set $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $(T,h_ T)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a potential with analytic singularities such that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. For each $k\geq 1$, we let 1EE7A6DB1803 5.20.18 \begin{equation}  \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation} Then for all sufficiently large $k$, \[  \varphi \preceq \varphi _ k\preceq \alpha _ k \varphi ,  \] where $\alpha _ k\in (0,1)$ is an increasing sequence with limit $1$. Proof. First we prove $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, there is $\delta >0$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Applying theorem 5.20.16 to the point $Y=\{ x\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$ and every unit vector $e_ x\in (L^ k\otimes T)_ x$, there is a section $\tilde{s}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ with $\tilde{s}(x)=e_ x$ and \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\omega ^ n\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi (x)}.  \] After rescaling $\tilde{s}$, the definition of $\varphi _ k$ gives \[  \varphi _ k(x)\geq \varphi (x)-\frac{\log C}{k}.  \] This proves $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. The other part of the inequality follows from 5.18.15 and ( 5.18.17 ). More precisely, if $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$, with respect to the $L^2$-norm: \[  s\mapsto \left( \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \right)^{1/2},  \] then by ( 5.18.17 ), \[  s_ i\in \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left((k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi \right)\right),  \] where $c>0$ depends only on $\varphi $. So there is $C_ k>0$ so that \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N |s_ i|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-(k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi }\leq C_ k\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] In other words, \[  \varphi _ k\preceq \frac{1}{k}\left( k-c^{-1}n \right)_+ \varphi .  \] It suffices to take $\alpha _ k=(1-k^{-1}c^{-1}n)_+$. $\square$

title: Definition 5.20.1
text: Definition 5.20.1 . C5880C6F61FA Let $V$ be a $1$-dimensional complex linear space. A Hermitian form $h$ on $V$ is a map $h\colon V\times V\rightarrow \mathbb {C}$ such that CF86155BCCFB $h$ is $\mathbb {C}$-linear in the second variable and conjugate linear in the first, and B8DA9F74F30F \[  |v|_ h^2\coloneqq h(v,v)\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}  \] for each $v\in V\setminus \{ 0\} $. We usually identify $h$ with the quadratic form $V\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ sending $v$ to $|v|_ h^2$. We write $|v|_ h=\sqrt{|v|_ h^2}$ for any $v\in V$. The singular Hermitian form on $V$ is the map $V\rightarrow \{ 0,\infty \} $ sending $0$ to $0$ and other elements to $\infty $.

title: Definition 5.20.2
text: Definition 5.20.2 . 90891EB78EA0 Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be $1$-dimensional complex linear spaces. Given two maps $h_ i\colon V_ i\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ ($i=1,2$), each of which is either a Hermitian form or a singular Hermitian form, we define the tensor product $h_1\otimes h_2\colon V_1\otimes V_2\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ as follows: F0878993B90B If either $h_1$ or $h_2$ is singular, we define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the singular Hermitian form; 6CC728E84DA0 otherwise, define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the usual tensor product: For any $v_1\in V_1$, $v_2\in V_2$, set \[  h_1\otimes h_2(v_1\otimes v_2)=h_1(v_1)h_2(v_2).  \]

title: Definition 5.20.3
text: Definition 5.20.3 . 293669D813B8 A Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ is a family of Hermitian forms $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$, such that 8F75F9950CF9 for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is a Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and 56AE61E47B2A for each local holomorphic section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}_ X(L)$, the map $x\mapsto |s(x)|^2_{h_ x}$ is smooth. The pair $(L,h)$ is called a Hermitian line bundle . We shall write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$ 2 for the first Chern form of $h$ 3 , normalized so that \[  [c_1(L,h)]=c_1(L).  \] The map $x\mapsto |s(x)|_{h_ x}$ will be denoted by $|s|_ h$. To be more precise, if $U\subseteq X$ is an open subset on which $L$ admits a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$, then we define \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left(-\log |s|_ h^2\right).  \] 2. ↩ The unusual notation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is sometimes referred to as the Göteborg notation because it is widely used by complex geometers in Göteborg (usually spelled as Gothenburg in English, the second largest (yet very poorly known) city in Sweden). As I identify myself as Göteborgare , I do not feel guilty about this notation. 3. ↩ In the literature, people sometimes define the curvature form of $(L,h)$ as $\Theta _{h}=-2\pi \mathrm{i}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$.

title: Proposition 5.20.4 (Lelong–Poincaré)
text:
Proposition 5.20.4 (Lelong–Poincaré) . 0C02CD3B5D59 Let $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ be non-zero and $h$ be a Hermitian metric on $L$. Then 1322FD7BDF4F 5.20.5 \begin{equation}  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $Z(s)$ is the zero divisor defined by $s$ and $[\bullet ]$ denote the associated current of integration. Proof. In a holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$, write $s=fe$ and $|e|_h^2=\exp(-\rho)$. Then $\log|s|_h^2=\log|f|^2-\rho$ and $c_1(L,h)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\rho$. The normalized Poincaré--Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\log|f|^2=[Z(f)]$. Substitution proves
\[c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}\log|s|_h^2=[Z(s)].\]
Changing the frame multiplies $f$ by a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic function; its logarithmic squared modulus is pluriharmonic, so the local identities agree on overlaps. This also checks the factor $1/(2\pi)$ in the normalization.

title: Equation 5.20.5
text: 1322FD7BDF4F 5.20.5 \begin{equation}  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation}

title: Example 5.20.6
text: Example 5.20.6 . 0D9E7B0EE3DC Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. The homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb {P}^1$ will be denoted by $[X_0:X_1]$. At a point $x=[X_0:X_1]\in \mathbb {P}^1$, the fiber $L_ x$ is identified with the dual of $[x]$, where $[x]\subseteq \mathbb {C}^2$ is the line represented by $x$. In order to introduce the Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$, we fix the standard Hermitian norm $\| \bullet \| $ on $\mathbb {C}^2$. Then given $\lambda \in L_ x=[x]^{\vee }$, we introduce \[  |\lambda |_{h_ x}=\frac{|\lambda (\tilde{x})|}{\| \tilde{x}\| },  \] where $\tilde{x}$ is an arbitrary non-zero element in $[x]$. The reader can easily verify that $h$ is indeed a Hermitian metric on $L$. The Hermitian metric $h$ is known as the Fubini–Study metric . A holomorphic section $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ can be formally identified with a linear form $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$: At $x\in X$, the corresponding linear form on $[x]$ is given by sending $(X_0,X_1)$ to $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$. Next we compute $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$. For this purpose, we cover $\mathbb {P}^1$ by $\mathbb {C}=\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ \infty \} $ and $\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ 0\} $. Both are holomorphic coordinate charts with coordinate function $z=X_0/X_1$ and $z^{-1}=X_1/X_0$ respectively. We claim that on $\mathbb {C}$, 3C9B623060E7 5.20.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation} In fact, let $t$ be the nowhere vanishing section of $L$ on $\mathbb {C}$ corresponding to $X_1$. Then for $z\in \mathbb {C}$, we have an obvious lift $(z,1)\in [z]$, so \[  |t|_ h^2(z)=\frac{1}{|z|^2+1}.  \] So ( 5.20.7 ) follows. In order to obtain a non-trivial case of the Lelong–Poincaré formula, we need to consider a section which vanishes at some points in $\mathbb {C}$. Let $s$ be the holomorphic section of $L$ corresponding to $X_0$. Then \[  \log |s|_ h^2(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for any $z\in \mathbb {C}$ using the same argument as above. Therefore, we find that restricted to $\mathbb {C}$, we have \[  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=[0],  \] where $f(z)=\log |z|^2$. So the Lelong–Poincaré formula ( 5.20.5 ) is verified in this case. The Kähler form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$ is also known as the Fubini–Study metric .

title: Equation 5.20.7
text: 3C9B623060E7 5.20.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation}

title: Definition 5.20.8
text: Definition 5.20.8 . A43467D63B4A A (singular) plurisubharmonic metric (or psh metric for short) 4 $h$ on $L$ is a family $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$ such that DCF7D606ADB1 for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is either a Hermitian form on $L_ x$ or the singular Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and 32709CF6AC92 there is a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each $v\in L_ x$, we have 6C8BC3AC251D 5.20.9 \begin{equation}  |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation} The (first) Chern current of $h$ is by definition \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)\coloneqq c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] The set of psh metrics on $L$ will be denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$. 4. ↩ In the literature, people usually refer to such metrics as positively curved singular Hermitian metrics . I dislike this terminology, as having positive curvature only determines a plurisubharmonic metric almost everywhere, not everywhere.

title: Equation 5.20.9
text: 6C8BC3AC251D 5.20.9 \begin{equation}  |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}

title: Remark 5.20.10
text: Remark 5.20.10 . D2F8C4BB2BD4 In the literature, some people prefer the convention that in ( 5.20.9 ), neither side has the square. Our choice seems to be the most natural one given our normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$.

title: Definition 5.20.11
text: Definition 5.20.11 . 9834FE8F2B0D Given two holomorphic line bundles $L_1$, $L_2$ on $X$ and plurisubharmonic metrics $h_1$ on $L_1$ and $h_2$ on $L_2$, we define the tensor product plurisubharmonic metric $h_1\otimes h_2$ on $L_1\otimes L_2$ as follows: for each $x\in X$, define \[  (h_1\otimes h_2)_ x=h_{1,x}\otimes h_{2,x}  \] in the sense of definition 5.20.2 .

title: Example 5.20.12
text: Example 5.20.12 . CC1C409253F3 We continue with our example example 5.20.6 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. Let $h^0$ denote the Fubini–Study metric on $L$ as defined in example 5.20.6 . Note that we have changed the notation from $h$ to $h^0$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h^0$. We construct $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ as follows: On $\mathbb {C}$, define 6B76079BBD9C 5.20.13 \begin{equation}  \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation} Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C},\omega |_{\mathbb {C}})$ by ( 5.20.7 ). Setting $\varphi (\infty )=0$, we can easily verify that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {P}^1,\omega )$. 5 We then get a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h^0\exp (-\varphi )$. To be more explicit, the fiber metric $h$ at $0$ is singular, $h_{\infty }=h^0_{\infty }$, while for $z\in \mathbb {C}\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $\lambda \in [z]^{\vee }$, we have \[  |\lambda |_{h_ z}=\frac{|\lambda (z,1)|}{|z|}.  \] 5. ↩ This can also be verified using the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem theorem 5.14.10 .

title: Equation 5.20.13
text: 6B76079BBD9C 5.20.13 \begin{equation}  \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation}

title: Definition 5.20.14
text: Definition 5.20.14 . 9FE903B6E5A8 Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a psh metric $h$ on $L$ of the following form: There exists $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ m)$ and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ N\in \mathbb {Q}$ such that for any local nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we have \[  |s|_ h^2=\min _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left| \frac{s^{\otimes m}}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ i/2}s_ i}\right|^{2m^{-1}}.  \] We write $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ for the set of Fubini–Study metrics on $L$.

title: Definition 5.20.15
text: Definition 5.20.15 . 8FCD7BEEDD56 Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. The set $\widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$ containing $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ which is closed under the following two operations: B253418A2EBA $\mathbb {Q}$-convex combinations: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ and $t\in (0,1)$, then \[  h_1^ t \otimes h_2^{1-t}\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L);  \] CCB3DD349505 minima: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$, then \[  \min \{ h_1,h_2\} \in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L).  \]

title: Theorem 5.20.16
text: Theorem 5.20.16 . 2985932B2B64 Assume that $L$ is big and $T$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h_ T$ on $T$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ and let $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Let $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold of dimension $m$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta - \delta \omega )$ for some $\delta >0$ and $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then there exists $k_0(\delta ,h_ T)>0$ such that for all $k \geq k_0$ and $s \in \mathrm{H}^0(Y, T\otimes L|_ Y^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi |_ Y))$ 6 , there exists an extension $\tilde s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X, T\otimes L^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ such that \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \leq C \int _ Y |s|^2_{(h^ k\otimes h_ T)|_ Y} \mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi |_ Y}\, \omega |_ Y^ m,  \] where $C>0$ is an absolute constant, independent of the data $(\varphi ,s,k)$. 6. ↩ Here and in the sequel, we usually abbreviate $\otimes k$ in the superscript as $k$ to save space.

title: Proposition 5.20.17
text: Proposition 5.20.17 . 2DDBBF280789 Let $(L,h)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$ and set $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $(T,h_ T)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a potential with analytic singularities such that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. For each $k\geq 1$, we let 1EE7A6DB1803 5.20.18 \begin{equation}  \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation} Then for all sufficiently large $k$, \[  \varphi \preceq \varphi _ k\preceq \alpha _ k \varphi ,  \] where $\alpha _ k\in (0,1)$ is an increasing sequence with limit $1$. Proof. First we prove $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, there is $\delta >0$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Applying theorem 5.20.16 to the point $Y=\{ x\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$ and every unit vector $e_ x\in (L^ k\otimes T)_ x$, there is a section $\tilde{s}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ with $\tilde{s}(x)=e_ x$ and \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\omega ^ n\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi (x)}.  \] After rescaling $\tilde{s}$, the definition of $\varphi _ k$ gives \[  \varphi _ k(x)\geq \varphi (x)-\frac{\log C}{k}.  \] This proves $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. The other part of the inequality follows from 5.18.15 and ( 5.18.17 ). More precisely, if $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$, with respect to the $L^2$-norm: \[  s\mapsto \left( \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \right)^{1/2},  \] then by ( 5.18.17 ), \[  s_ i\in \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left((k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi \right)\right),  \] where $c>0$ depends only on $\varphi $. So there is $C_ k>0$ so that \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N |s_ i|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-(k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi }\leq C_ k\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] In other words, \[  \varphi _ k\preceq \frac{1}{k}\left( k-c^{-1}n \right)_+ \varphi .  \] It suffices to take $\alpha _ k=(1-k^{-1}c^{-1}n)_+$. $\square$

title: Equation 5.20.18
text: 1EE7A6DB1803 5.20.18 \begin{equation}  \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation}

title: Equation 13.1.1
text: 82D27D8CAD36 13.1.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \end{equation}

title: 13.10 Bedford–Taylor theory
text: Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ ($p\in \mathbb {N}$) be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ 1 . In this case, there is a canonical definition of the Monge–Ampère type product ( 13.1.1 ). Definition 13.10.1 . F6CEAE1224B7 We define the closed positive $(p,p)$-current ( 13.1.1 ) on $X$ as follows: We proceed by induction on $p\geq 0$. When $p=0$, we define ( 13.1.1 ) as the $(0,0)$-current $[X]$. When $p>0$, we let \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _1\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \right).  \] We call this product the Bedford–Taylor product . 1. ↩ In the literature, some people use $\mathrm{PSH}(X)\cap L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to denote the set of such functions, which is an abuse of notation. However, this is legitimate thanks to the rigidity theorem 5.13.18 . Remark 13.10.2 . 918938F52375 There is also a slightly more general version of this construction. Given a closed positive current $T$, one can also define the product \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \wedge T  \] in a very similar way. Proposition 13.10.3 . E1938BA48A2F The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Moreover, the product is symmetric in the $\varphi _ i$'s. Proof. The recursive construction here is the same as the one in the positive Bedford--Taylor recursion . That result proves that each step is a positive current of order zero, so multiplication by the next locally bounded potential is defined; applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}$ makes the next product closed. Symmetry is proved, together with monotone continuity, in the Bedford--Taylor continuity theorem . Its proof uses the common-collar integration-by-parts identity and the Chern--Levine--Nirenberg bound, not the incorrect claim that $\mathrm du\wedge\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge T$ is closed. Since all constructions agree in overlapping charts, they define the stated global current. See [ Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.12 , GZ17 ] . The proof relies crucially on an important estimate, known as the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality . See [ CLN69 ] or [ Theorem 3.9 , GZ17 ] . The Bedford–Taylor theory has many satisfactory properties. Theorem 13.10.4 . 032A3F745585 Let $(\varphi _ i^ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be decreasing sequences (resp. increasing sequences) of locally bounded psh functions on $X$ converging (resp. converging a.e.) to locally bounded psh functions $\varphi _ i$'s, where $i=0,\ldots ,p$. Then \[  \varphi _0^ j\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \varphi _0\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p  \] as $j\to \infty $. In particular, if $(\varphi _0^ j)_ j$ is the constant sequence $1$, we have \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p.  \] Proof. On a relatively compact coordinate ball, the decreasing case, including the factor $\varphi_0^j$, is weighted Bedford--Taylor decreasing continuity . The increasing case is weighted increasing continuity , which allows almost-everywhere convergence to the specified locally bounded representatives. The local bounds needed in these results hold on a slightly larger compact set: in the decreasing case they are bounded below by the limit and above by the first term; in the increasing case they are bounded below by the first term and above by the limit, using almost-everywhere order and uniqueness of plurisubharmonic representatives. For a compactly supported test form on $X$, use a finite partition of unity subordinate to such balls and sum the local limits. This proves weak convergence of the currents globally. Taking the auxiliary factor constantly equal to $1$ gives the unweighted assertion. Here the notation $\rightharpoonup $ denotes the weak-* convergence of currents. We refer to [ Theorem 3.18, Theorem 3.23 , GZ17 ] for the proofs. By contrast, we emphasize that the Bedford–Taylor product is not continuous with respect to the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-convergence in general. A simple example can be found in [ Example 3.25 , GZ17 ] . Lemma 13.10.5 . 10BB181E99E0 Let $Q\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $D\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m$ be domains, let $p_2\colon Q\times D\to D$ be the second projection, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(m,m)$-form on $D$. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded psh functions on $Q\times D$, and put \[  M=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n,\qquad M_ z=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1)_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n)_ z.  \] Here $(u_ r)_ z(x)=u_ r(x,z)$. For every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support in $Q\times D$, E7F106829576 13.10.6 \begin{equation}  \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_2^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z), \qquad h_ z(x)=h(x,z). \end{equation} Proof. By linearity, it suffices to consider $\eta \geq 0$. We first prove ( 13.10.6 ) when $h$ is continuous. On a product neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}h$, choose smooth psh functions $u_ r^{(l)}\searrow u_ r$, $1\leq r\leq n$. For the smooth approximants, decompose each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r^{(l)}$ according to the $x$- and $z$-directions. After wedging with $p_2^*\eta $, every term containing a factor $\mathrm{d}z_\alpha $ or $\mathrm{d}\bar z_\beta $ vanishes; hence only the factors $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ r^{(l)})_ z$ remain, and ( 13.10.6 ) follows from the usual Fubini theorem. As $l\to \infty $, the Bedford–Taylor monotone continuity theorem theorem 13.10.4 gives convergence on $Q\times D$ and on every fibre. Fix $K\Subset Q$ and $L\Subset D$ containing the projections of $\operatorname{Supp}h$. The Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate [ Theorem 3.9 , GZ17 ] , together with the local uniform bounds for $u_ r^{(l)}$, bounds the masses of the fibre products on $K$ uniformly for $z\in L$ and $l$. Since $h_ z=0$ for $z\notin L$, dominated convergence proves ( 13.10.6 ). It remains to pass from continuous to bounded Borel functions. Fix relatively compact open sets $U\Subset Q$ and $V\Subset D$. If $\chi \in C_ c(U)$, then \[  F_\chi (z)\coloneqq \int _ U\chi \, M_ z, \qquad z\in V,  \] is Borel measurable. Indeed, choose the smooth decreasing approximations on a neighborhood of $\overline U\times \overline V$ and set \[  M_ z^{(l)}\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1^{(l)})_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n^{(l)})_ z.  \] The functions $z\mapsto \int _ U\chi \, M_ z^{(l)}$ are continuous on $V$ and converge pointwise to $F_\chi $ by theorem 13.10.4 . Let $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $\chi $ on $U$ for which $F_\chi $ is Borel measurable on $V$. It is closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions by the monotone convergence theorem. Taking compactly supported continuous cut-off functions increasing to $1$ on $U$ shows that $1\in \mathcal{A}_{U,V}$. Thus $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains the algebra $\mathbb {R}+C_ c(U)$, which generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U$. The functional monotone class theorem therefore shows that $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U$. Next, let $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $g$ on $U\times V$ such that \[  z\longmapsto \int _ U g_ z\, M_ z, \qquad g_ z(x)=g(x,z),  \] is Borel measurable on $V$. This space is again closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions. It contains every product $g(x,z)=\chi (x)\psi (z)$ of bounded Borel functions, by the preceding paragraph. Finite sums of such products form an algebra containing the indicators of all Borel rectangles $A\times B\subseteq U\times V$; hence this algebra generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U\times V$. A second application of the functional monotone class theorem shows that $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U\times V$. To pass from $U\times V$ to $Q\times D$, choose exhaustions $U_ j\Subset Q$ and $V_ j\Subset D$ by relatively compact open sets. For a Borel set $E\subseteq Q\times D$, the preceding paragraph, applied to the restriction of $\mathds {1}_ E$ to $U_ j\times V_ j$, shows that \[  G_ j(z)\coloneqq \mathds {1}_{V_ j}(z)\int _{U_ j}\mathds {1}_ E(x,z)\, M_ z  \] is Borel measurable on $D$. We may take both exhaustions increasing, so $G_ j\nearrow M_ z(E_ z)$ pointwise, where \[  E_ z\coloneqq \{ x\in Q:(x,z)\in E\} .  \] Thus $z\mapsto M_ z(E_ z)$ is Borel measurable on $D$. We may therefore define \[  \lambda (E)\coloneqq \int _ D M_ z(E_ z)\, \eta (z).  \] The monotone convergence theorem, first on each fibre and then on $D$, shows that $\lambda $ is a Borel measure on $Q\times D$. The local uniform mass bound above shows that $\lambda $ is locally finite and hence Radon. Approximation by non-negative simple functions gives \[  \int _{Q\times D}h\, \mathrm{d}\lambda =\int _ D\left(\int _ Qh_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z)  \] for every non-negative Borel function $h$. For continuous compactly supported $h$, the first part of the proof shows that $\lambda $ agrees with $p_2^*\eta \wedge M$. The uniqueness of Radon measures then gives the same equality for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. $\square$

title: Definition 13.10.1
text: Definition 13.10.1 . F6CEAE1224B7 We define the closed positive $(p,p)$-current ( 13.1.1 ) on $X$ as follows: We proceed by induction on $p\geq 0$. When $p=0$, we define ( 13.1.1 ) as the $(0,0)$-current $[X]$. When $p>0$, we let \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _1\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \right).  \] We call this product the Bedford–Taylor product .

title: Remark 13.10.2
text: Remark 13.10.2 . 918938F52375 There is also a slightly more general version of this construction. Given a closed positive current $T$, one can also define the product \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \wedge T  \] in a very similar way.

title: Proposition 13.10.3
text: Proposition 13.10.3 . E1938BA48A2F The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Moreover, the product is symmetric in the $\varphi _ i$'s. Proof. The recursive construction here is the same as the one in the positive Bedford--Taylor recursion . That result proves that each step is a positive current of order zero, so multiplication by the next locally bounded potential is defined; applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}$ makes the next product closed. Symmetry is proved, together with monotone continuity, in the Bedford--Taylor continuity theorem . Its proof uses the common-collar integration-by-parts identity and the Chern--Levine--Nirenberg bound, not the incorrect claim that $\mathrm du\wedge\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge T$ is closed. Since all constructions agree in overlapping charts, they define the stated global current.
