title: 16.6.6 The definition of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope
text: Fix a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Definition 16.6.7 . E94E1B7F9193 Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define its $\mathcal{I}$-envelope as follows: FA4D3373FBAE 16.6.8 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}\{ \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \psi \leq 0,\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi \} . \end{equation} If $\varphi =P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$, we say $\varphi $ is an $\mathcal{I}$-model potential (in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$). Note that by proposition 5.14.2 , $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proposition 16.6.9 . 708B2E9B2EF0 Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have $\varphi '\coloneqq \varphi -g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. By symmetry, it suffices to show that \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] After replacing $g$ by $g+C$ for a suitable constant $C$, which only changes $\varphi '$ by an additive constant, we may assume that $g\geq 0$. Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be such that $\psi \leq 0$ and $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Then $\psi '\coloneqq \psi -g$ lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$, satisfies $\psi '\leq 0$, and is $\mathcal{I}$-equivalent to $\varphi '$ since adding a smooth function does not change multiplier ideals. Hence \[  \psi -g=\psi '\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] It follows that \[  \psi -\sup _ X g\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Taking the upper envelope over all such $\psi $ gives \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}-\sup _ X g\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}},  \] which proves the desired comparison. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.10 . E535E4DC5384 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$ to $X$. Then for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have \[  P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=\pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. Let \[  \eta =P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] First take a candidate $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in ( 16.6.8 ), so that $\psi \leq 0$ and $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Then $\pi ^*\psi \leq 0$ and $\pi ^*\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $ by proposition 16.6.4 ; hence $\pi ^*\psi \leq \eta $. Taking the upper envelope over all such $\psi $ gives \[  \pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta .  \] Conversely, let $\chi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$ be a candidate in the definition of $\eta $, so that $\chi \leq 0$ and $\chi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $. By proposition 5.17.8 , there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\chi =\pi ^*\psi $. Since $\pi $ is surjective, $\psi \leq 0$. By proposition 16.6.4 , the relation $\chi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $ implies $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Thus $\psi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$, and hence \[  \chi \leq \pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Taking the upper envelope over all such $\chi $ gives the reverse inequality. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.11 . 363E28FF4A61 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, \[  P_{\theta }\Bigl [ P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}  \] and the upper semicontinuous regularization in ( 16.6.8 ) is not necessary. Proof. In view of proposition 16.6.2 , it suffices to show that for $k \in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have 5888DEC3C930 16.6.12 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}). \end{equation} By proposition 5.14.3 , we can find $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ ($i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$) such that $\psi _ i\leq 0$, $\psi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $ for all $i\geq 1$ and \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i>0}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _ i=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] By proposition 16.6.5 , we may replace $\psi _ i$ by $\psi _1\lor \cdots \lor \psi _ i$ and assume that the sequence $\psi _ i$ is increasing. In this case, it follows from the strong openness theorem theorem 5.16.21 that for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi _ j)=\mathcal{I} (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})  \] for $j$ large enough. $\square$ Definition 16.6.13 . 1D9577F4ECC2 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define the volume 1 $\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )$ as \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )=\int _ X \Bigl (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr )^ n.  \] 1. ↩ We choose to call this quantity the volume instead of the $\mathcal{I}$-volume so that the terminology is consistent with the line bundle case. Proposition 16.6.14 . 8DF15E9E1928 Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have $\varphi '=\varphi -g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )= \operatorname{vol}\left(\theta ',\varphi '\right).  \] Proof. By proposition 16.6.9 , the currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal I}$ have the same singularity type in the same cohomology class. Applying the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.13.11 gives equality of their non-pluripolar masses. $\square$ In view of proposition 16.6.14 , the volume $\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )$ depends only on the current $\theta _{\varphi }$, and we may write 3535B0853CBC 16.6.15 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }=\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi ). \end{equation} Definition 16.6.16 . 202451F22A2A Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class. The volume $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ of $\alpha $ is defined as \[  \operatorname{vol}\alpha =\operatorname{vol}T_{\min },  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Note that $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ is independent of the choice of $T_{\min }$, thanks to theorem 13.13.11 . Let us recall the following elementary result for later use. Proposition 16.6.17 . 12DD9B82F232 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. 7C6266FB792D For any big class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi ^*\alpha =\operatorname{vol}\alpha $. FDD4AF241C61 For any big class $\beta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _*\beta $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. Proof. 1 Take a current $T_{\min }$ with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Then $\pi ^*T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\pi ^*\alpha $. Our assertion follows from proposition 13.13.4 . 2 Let $S_{\min }$ be a current with minimal singularities in $\beta $. Then $\pi _*S_{\min }$ is a positive current in the cohomology class $\pi _*\beta $. A current with minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $ is less singular than $\pi _*S_{\min }$, hence by the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.13.11 \[  \operatorname{vol}(\pi _*\beta )\geq \int _ X\left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n.  \] By proposition 13.13.4 , \[  \int _ X \left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n\geq \int _ Y S_{\min }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\beta .  \] We conclude $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. $\square$ The $\mathcal{I}$-envelope and the $P$-envelope are related in a simple manner. Proposition 16.6.18 . 8AE79B76D6D2 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}},\quad \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ].  \] As a consequence, 0BC2A1135095 16.6.19 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }\Bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$. Namely, for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have EA49AC910A56 16.6.20 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ). \end{equation} Fix $k$ for now. It follows from ( 16.3.7 ) and the strong openness theorem theorem 5.16.21 that \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr ),  \] when $C$ is large enough. Since $(k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\sim k\varphi $, we have \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}(k\varphi )  \] and ( 16.6.20 ) follows. $\square$ In particular, we obtain an interesting relation between the non-pluripolar mass and the volume. Corollary 16.6.21 . FB21F0385323 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n\leq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] The reverse inequality fails in general, see example 16.8.19 . Proof. This follows from proposition 16.6.18 , theorem 13.13.11 and proposition 16.3.10 . $\square$ We note the following special case: Proposition 16.6.22 . 10F9DDE25703 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. Then B621808C9E65 16.6.23 \begin{equation}  \varphi \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ] \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Hence, $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ and $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ both have analytic singularities. In particular, D91D171A0296 16.6.24 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n= \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }. \end{equation} Proof. First observe that ( 16.6.24 ) follows from ( 16.6.23 ) and theorem 13.13.11 . It remains to establish ( 16.6.23 ). In view of proposition 16.6.18 , it suffices to show that 9169FBAAFD41 16.6.25 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq \varphi . \end{equation} By proposition 16.6.10 , proposition 16.4.1 and theorem 5.18.8 , after passing to a log resolution we may assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb Q$-divisor $D$. This reduction does not change the assertion, since both the $P$- and the $\mathcal I$-envelope are compatible with bimeromorphic pull-back. After multiplying $\theta $ and $\varphi $ by a sufficiently divisible positive integer, and then dividing the final comparison by the same integer, we may assume that $D$ is integral. In this case the Bergman-type quasi-equisingular approximants of $\varphi $ associated to the ideals $\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi )$ have the same singularity type as $\varphi $. Since \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}\varphi  \] by proposition 16.6.11 , we have \[  \mathcal I(2^ jP_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I})=\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ).  \] Thus the quasi-equisingular approximants $\eta _ j$ of $P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\varphi _ j$ of $\varphi $ may be chosen with the same singularity type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ))$. Consequently $\eta _ j\sim \varphi _ j\sim \varphi $ for $j\gg 1$. Since $\eta _ j\searrow P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, choosing one such large $j$ gives \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\leq \eta _ j\leq \varphi +C_ j,  \] and hence ( 16.6.25 ) holds. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.11
text: Proposition 16.6.11 . 363E28FF4A61 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, \[  P_{\theta }\Bigl [ P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}  \] and the upper semicontinuous regularization in ( 16.6.8 ) is not necessary. Proof. In view of proposition 16.6.2 , it suffices to show that for $k \in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have 5888DEC3C930 16.6.12 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}). \end{equation} By proposition 5.14.3 , we can find $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ ($i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$) such that $\psi _ i\leq 0$, $\psi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $ for all $i\geq 1$ and \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i>0}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _ i=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] By proposition 16.6.5 , we may replace $\psi _ i$ by $\psi _1\lor \cdots \lor \psi _ i$ and assume that the sequence $\psi _ i$ is increasing. In this case, it follows from the strong openness theorem theorem 5.16.21 that for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi _ j)=\mathcal{I} (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})  \] for $j$ large enough. $\square$

title: Equation 16.6.12
text: 5888DEC3C930 16.6.12 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}). \end{equation}

title: Definition 16.6.13
text: Definition 16.6.13 . 1D9577F4ECC2 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define the volume 1 $\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )$ as \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )=\int _ X \Bigl (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr )^ n.  \] 1. ↩ We choose to call this quantity the volume instead of the $\mathcal{I}$-volume so that the terminology is consistent with the line bundle case.

title: Proposition 16.6.14
text: Proposition 16.6.14 . 8DF15E9E1928 Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have $\varphi '=\varphi -g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )= \operatorname{vol}\left(\theta ',\varphi '\right).  \] Proof. By proposition 16.6.9 , the currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal I}$ have the same singularity type in the same cohomology class. Applying the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.13.11 gives equality of their non-pluripolar masses. $\square$

title: Equation 16.6.15
text: 3535B0853CBC 16.6.15 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }=\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi ). \end{equation}

title: Definition 16.6.16
text: Definition 16.6.16 . 202451F22A2A Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class. The volume $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ of $\alpha $ is defined as \[  \operatorname{vol}\alpha =\operatorname{vol}T_{\min },  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Note that $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ is independent of the choice of $T_{\min }$, thanks to theorem 13.13.11 .

title: Proposition 16.6.17
text: Proposition 16.6.17 . 12DD9B82F232 Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. 7C6266FB792D For any big class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi ^*\alpha =\operatorname{vol}\alpha $. FDD4AF241C61 For any big class $\beta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _*\beta $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. Proof. 1 Take a current $T_{\min }$ with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Then $\pi ^*T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\pi ^*\alpha $. Our assertion follows from proposition 13.13.4 . 2 Let $S_{\min }$ be a current with minimal singularities in $\beta $. Then $\pi _*S_{\min }$ is a positive current in the cohomology class $\pi _*\beta $. A current with minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $ is less singular than $\pi _*S_{\min }$, hence by the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.13.11 \[  \operatorname{vol}(\pi _*\beta )\geq \int _ X\left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n.  \] By proposition 13.13.4 , \[  \int _ X \left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n\geq \int _ Y S_{\min }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\beta .  \] We conclude $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.18
text: Proposition 16.6.18 . 8AE79B76D6D2 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}},\quad \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ].  \] Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$. Namely, for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have EA49AC910A56 16.6.20 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ). \end{equation} Fix $k$ for now. It follows from ( 16.3.7 ) and the strong openness theorem theorem 5.16.21 that \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr ),  \] when $C$ is large enough. Since $(k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\sim k\varphi $, we have \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}(k\varphi )  \] and ( 16.6.20 ) follows. $\square$

title: Equation 16.6.19
text: 0BC2A1135095 16.6.19 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }\Bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation}

title: Equation 16.6.20
text: EA49AC910A56 16.6.20 \begin{equation}  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ). \end{equation}

title: Corollary 16.6.21
text: Corollary 16.6.21 . FB21F0385323 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n\leq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] Proof. This follows from proposition 16.6.18 , theorem 13.13.11 and proposition 16.3.10 . $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.22
text: Proposition 16.6.22 . 10F9DDE25703 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. Then B621808C9E65 16.6.23 \begin{equation}  \varphi \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ] \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Hence, $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ and $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ both have analytic singularities. In particular, D91D171A0296 16.6.24 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n= \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }. \end{equation} Proof. First observe that ( 16.6.24 ) follows from ( 16.6.23 ) and theorem 13.13.11 . It remains to establish ( 16.6.23 ). In view of proposition 16.6.18 , it suffices to show that 9169FBAAFD41 16.6.25 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq \varphi . \end{equation} By proposition 16.6.10 , proposition 16.4.1 and theorem 5.18.8 , after passing to a log resolution we may assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb Q$-divisor $D$. This reduction does not change the assertion, since both the $P$- and the $\mathcal I$-envelope are compatible with bimeromorphic pull-back. After multiplying $\theta $ and $\varphi $ by a sufficiently divisible positive integer, and then dividing the final comparison by the same integer, we may assume that $D$ is integral. In this case the Bergman-type quasi-equisingular approximants of $\varphi $ associated to the ideals $\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi )$ have the same singularity type as $\varphi $. Since \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}\varphi  \] by proposition 16.6.11 , we have \[  \mathcal I(2^ jP_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I})=\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ).  \] Thus the quasi-equisingular approximants $\eta _ j$ of $P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\varphi _ j$ of $\varphi $ may be chosen with the same singularity type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ))$. Consequently $\eta _ j\sim \varphi _ j\sim \varphi $ for $j\gg 1$. Since $\eta _ j\searrow P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, choosing one such large $j$ gives \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\leq \eta _ j\leq \varphi +C_ j,  \] and hence ( 16.6.25 ) holds. $\square$

title: Equation 16.6.23
text: B621808C9E65 16.6.23 \begin{equation}  \varphi \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ] \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation}

title: Equation 16.6.24
text: D91D171A0296 16.6.24 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n= \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }. \end{equation}

title: Equation 16.6.25
text: 9169FBAAFD41 16.6.25 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq \varphi . \end{equation}

title: 16.6.26 Properties of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope
text: Let $\theta ,\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. We have the following properties of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. Proposition 16.6.27 . F7C47263CB3C 6B3F6E8F1EC1 Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$. Then \[  P_{\lambda \theta }[\lambda \varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=\lambda P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 0F43574FD82C Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\geq P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 56C6F951EFD4 Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 14196330587C Suppose that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi _1\lor \varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor P_{\theta }[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. 1 This follows by rescaling the candidates in the definition of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. 2 Suppose that $\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\psi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ satisfy \[  \psi _ i\leq 0,\quad \psi _ i \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _ i  \] for $i=1,2$. Then thanks to proposition 16.6.5 , \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq 0,\quad \psi _1+\psi _2 \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _1+\varphi _2.  \] It follows that \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Since $\psi _1$ and $\psi _2$ are arbitrary, we conclude. 3 and 4 : These follow easily from proposition 16.6.11 and proposition 16.6.5 . $\square$ Lemma 16.6.28 . 2A3BCF353C03 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi \preceq \psi $. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. We may assume that $\psi \leq 0$. Observe that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $ as a consequence of proposition 5.16.8 and proposition 16.6.11 . So \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] The desired inequality follows. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.29 . 2D7AF550FFF7 Consider a decreasing net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ of model potentials, with $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $i\in I$. Set \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] Suppose that $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $ and $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0$. Then \[  \inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. We have $\eta \geq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 16.6.28 . In particular, $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By proposition 16.4.4 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n>\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $\varphi _ i=\varphi $ by theorem 16.3.15 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 16.6.19 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 13.13.30 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi _ i+\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi .  \] We can, for example, take \[  \epsilon _ i^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1+\left(\frac{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n}{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n}\right)^{1/n} \right).  \] By proposition 16.6.27 and 16.6.28 , we have \[  \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Each $P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$ has supremum $0$, so proposition 5.17.3 shows that the family is bounded in $L^1$. Hence $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$, and the preceding inequality gives $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ almost everywhere. By proposition 5.14.6 , the inequality holds everywhere. $\square$ Proposition 16.6.30 . 0C703BE43035 Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ uniformly bounded from above. Let $\varphi \coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i$. Then \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Then $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 16.6.28 . By corollary 13.13.12 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n<\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ by theorem 16.3.15 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 16.6.19 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 13.13.30 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) as in ( 16.4.10 ) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi +\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi _ i.  \] By proposition 16.6.27 and 16.6.28 , we have \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta .  \] As above, $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$. It follows that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . $\square$ Remark 16.6.31 . 0F2E59A9BE30 One could also define the following interpolation between the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope and the $P$-envelope: Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, $j\in \{ 0,\ldots ,n\} $. Then we let \[  \begin{split}  P_{\theta ,j}[\varphi ]\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}\left\{  \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \psi \leq 0,\varphi \preceq \psi , \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j}\right.\\  \left.=\int _ X \theta _{\psi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j} \right\} . \end{split}  \] Based on the techniques developed in section 16.7 , one could show that $P_{\theta ,j}[\bullet ]$ is a projection operator. The cases $j=0$ and $j=n$ recover the $\mathcal{I}$- and $P$-envelopes respectively; the intermediate operators $P_{\theta ,j}$ have not, to our knowledge, been systematically studied in the literature.

title: Proposition 16.6.27
text: Proposition 16.6.27 . F7C47263CB3C 6B3F6E8F1EC1 Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$. Then \[  P_{\lambda \theta }[\lambda \varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=\lambda P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 0F43574FD82C Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\geq P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 56C6F951EFD4 Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] 14196330587C Suppose that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi _1\lor \varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor P_{\theta }[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. 1 This follows by rescaling the candidates in the definition of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. 2 Suppose that $\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\psi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ satisfy \[  \psi _ i\leq 0,\quad \psi _ i \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _ i  \] for $i=1,2$. Then thanks to proposition 16.6.5 , \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq 0,\quad \psi _1+\psi _2 \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _1+\varphi _2.  \] It follows that \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Since $\psi _1$ and $\psi _2$ are arbitrary, we conclude. 3 and 4 : These follow easily from proposition 16.6.11 and proposition 16.6.5 . $\square$

title: Lemma 16.6.28
text: Lemma 16.6.28 . 2A3BCF353C03 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi \preceq \psi $. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. We may assume that $\psi \leq 0$. Observe that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $ as a consequence of proposition 5.16.8 and proposition 16.6.11 . So \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] The desired inequality follows. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.29
text: Proposition 16.6.29 . 2D7AF550FFF7 Consider a decreasing net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ of model potentials, with $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $i\in I$. Set \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] Suppose that $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $ and $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0$. Then \[  \inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. We have $\eta \geq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 16.6.28 . In particular, $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By proposition 16.4.4 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n>\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $\varphi _ i=\varphi $ by theorem 16.3.15 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 16.6.19 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 13.13.30 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi _ i+\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi .  \] We can, for example, take \[  \epsilon _ i^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1+\left(\frac{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n}{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n}\right)^{1/n} \right).  \] By proposition 16.6.27 and 16.6.28 , we have \[  \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Each $P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$ has supremum $0$, so proposition 5.17.3 shows that the family is bounded in $L^1$. Hence $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$, and the preceding inequality gives $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ almost everywhere. By proposition 5.14.6 , the inequality holds everywhere. $\square$

text: Proposition 16.6.30 . 0C703BE43035 Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ uniformly bounded from above. Then \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Then $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 16.6.28 . By corollary 13.13.12 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n<\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ by theorem 16.3.15 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 16.6.19 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 13.13.30 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) as in ( 16.4.10 ) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi +\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi _ i.  \] By proposition 16.6.27 and 16.6.28 , we have \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta .  \] As above, $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$. title: Remark 16.6.31
text: Remark 16.6.31 . 0F2E59A9BE30 One could also define the following interpolation between the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope and the $P$-envelope: Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, $j\in \{ 0,\ldots ,n\} $. Then we let \[  \begin{split}  P_{\theta ,j}[\varphi ]\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}\left\{  \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \psi \leq 0,\varphi \preceq \psi , \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j}\right.\\  \left.=\int _ X \theta _{\psi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j} \right\} . \end{split}  \] Based on the techniques developed in section 16.7 , one could show that $P_{\theta ,j}[\bullet ]$ is a projection operator. section: 17.10 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: When $\omega $ is a Kähler form, the space of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials carries the Mabuchi $L^2$-metric. Its geodesic equation is the homogeneous complex Monge–Ampère equation on $X\times \{ 0<\operatorname{Re}z<1\} $. Subsolutions of this equation are subgeodesics, and the geodesic between two boundary potentials is obtained as a Perron envelope. This construction continues to make sense for singular potentials, even when no smooth geodesic exists. The goal of this chapter is to further develop the corresponding theory for $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potentials, where $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form representing a big class. We define subgeodesics by requiring the complexification $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ to be plurisubharmonic. Geodesics are then defined as Perron envelopes of subgeodesics with prescribed boundary values. This point of view is flexible enough to handle unbounded potentials and singularity constraints. The first section sets up the basic properties of subgeodesics. We then construct geodesics with prescribed singular endpoints and study geodesic rays. The results are formulated relative to a model potential $\phi $, so that the endpoints and rays live in a fixed relative singularity class. The final part of the chapter studies the finite-energy space $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and the Darvas $d_1$-metric. We prove the basic metric properties needed later, including completeness and monotone convergence criteria. The radial version of the metric on geodesic rays will be used in the study of test curves and singularity types. This chapter provides the analytic bridge between envelopes and the later non-Archimedean theory. The space $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and the $d_1$-geometry developed here feed into the pseudometric $d_ S$ of section 16.7 , while geodesic rays will later be related to test curves and non-Archimedean potentials.

Proposition 17.10.7 . 1880C1FBD88F Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then for each $x\in X$, $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a convex function. Furthermore, \[  \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\quad \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1.  \] Proof. Let $\Phi $ be the complexification of $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. For each $x\in X$, the map \[  \Bigl \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1) \Bigr \} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto \Phi (x,z)  \] is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $, as follows from definition 17.10.2 1 and proposition 5.13.17 . In the latter case, the convexity of $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is trivial. In the former case, the convexity on the interval $(0,1)$ follows from proposition 5.13.12 . In order to verify the convexity at the boundary, let us fix $s\in (0,1)$. We need to show that 214F303DA2CC 17.10.8  egin{equation}  \varphi _ s(x)\leq s\varphi _1(x)+(1-s)\varphi _0(x) \end{equation} for all $x\in X$. Thanks to proposition 5.14.6 , it suffices to prove this for almost all $x$. Choose sequences $a_ j\searrow 0$ and $b_ j
earrow 1$ such that $\varphi _{a_ j}	o \varphi _0$ and $\varphi _{b_ j}	o \varphi _1$ almost everywhere. Outside a set $Z\subseteq X$ of zero Lebesgue measure, all these convergences hold and all the values involved are finite. For $x\in X\setminus Z$ and $j$ large enough that $a_ j<s<b_ j$, the convexity on $(0,1)$ gives \[  \varphi _ s(x)\leq  rac{b_ j-s}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{a_ j}(x)+ rac{s-a_ j}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{b_ j}(x).  \] Letting $j	o \infty $ gives ( 17.10.8 ) almost everywhere. Let us prove the last assertion. Let \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t.  \] By Kiselman's principle proposition 5.14.15 , we know that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. Since the complexification $\Phi $ is not identically $-\infty $, Fubini's theorem shows that for almost every $x\in X$, the function $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is finite for almost every $t\in (0,1)$. For such an $x$, the convexity just proved implies that $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a finite convex function on $(0,1)$, hence it is bounded from below on $(0,1)$. Thus $\varphi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, and so $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For any $t\in (0,1)$, using the convexity established above, we have \[  \varphi \leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1.  \] It follows that $\varphi \leq \varphi _0$ and $\varphi \leq \varphi _1$ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . Our assertion follows. $\square$

Then 3DF2DEE2C546 17.10.10 \begin{equation}  \lim _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t\to 1-}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _1. \end{equation} Moreover, \[  \lim _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t=\varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t\to 1-}\varphi _ t=\varphi _1\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] Proof. The inequalities in ( 17.10.10 ) and the existence of the limits follow from the convexity in proposition 17.10.7 . Let us prove the quasi-everywhere equality at $t=0$. Take a decreasing sequence $t_ j\searrow 0$ with $t_ j>0$. Then $\varphi _{t_ j}\to \varphi _0$ in $L^1(X)$ as $j\to \infty $. So by corollary 5.14.8 , we have \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\varphi _{t_ j}= \varphi _0\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] Therefore, we have \[  \varphi _0=\varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\varphi _{t_ j}=\lim _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] The assertion at $t=1$ is similar. $\square$

text: Proposition 17.10.13 . 5ECD747A7B0B Let $(\varphi ^ i_0)_{i\in I}$, $(\varphi ^ i_1)_{i\in I}$ be two non-empty uniformly bounded from above families in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be subgeodesics from $\varphi _0^ i$ to $\varphi _1^ i$ for each $i\in I$. Then \[  \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ i_ t\right)_{t\in (0,1)}  \] is a subgeodesic from $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_0$ to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_1$. Proof. We may assume that $\varphi _0^ i,\varphi _1^ i\leq 0$ for all $i\in I$. Then it follows that $\varphi _ t^ i\leq 0$ for all $t\in (0,1)$ and all $i\in I$ by proposition 17.10.7 . We define \[  \varphi _ t\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$. Observe that $[0,1] \ni t\mapsto \varphi _ t$ is convex by the same argument leading to ( 17.10.8 ). Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the subgeodesic whose complexification $\Phi _{\psi }$ corresponds to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$, where $\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$ is the complexification of $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. Then clearly, $\varphi _ t\leq \psi _ t$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. On the other hand, by proposition 5.14.5 , \[  \psi _ t=\sup _{i\in I}\varphi ^ i_ t=\varphi _ t\quad \textup{almost everywhere}  \] for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, using proposition 5.14.6 , we find $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Since both functions are convex in $t$, we conclude that $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. It remains to argue that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t\to 0+$ and $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$ as $t\to 1-$. By symmetry, it suffices to argue the former. By Choquet's lemma proposition 5.14.3 , applied to the uniformly bounded above family of complexifications $(\Phi _{\varphi ^ i})_{i\in I}$ on the strip, there is a countable subset $I'\subset I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}.  \] Applying Choquet's lemma proposition 5.14.3 once more to the endpoint families if necessary, and enlarging $I'$, we may also assume \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i,\quad \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i.  \] Thus, after replacing $I$ by $I'$, we may assume that $I$ is countable. We know that for any $t\in (0,1)$ and any $j\in I$, \[  \varphi ^ j_ t\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0.  \] Letting $t\to 0+$, we find that \[  \varphi _0^ j\leq \varlimsup _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0  \] almost everywhere. Since $I$ is countable, we conclude that BA313A9B1A1F 17.10.14 \begin{equation}  \varphi _0=\varlimsup _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t \end{equation} almost everywhere. Fix $i_0\in I$. Recall that by proposition 17.10.7 , for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi ^{i_0}_ t\geq \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi ^{i_0}_ t>-\infty ,  \] so the set $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology by proposition 5.17.3 . Let $\psi $ be a cluster point as $t\to 0+$. It suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. By corollary 5.14.8 and ( 17.10.14 ), this holds almost everywhere. Therefore, it holds everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . $\square$

text: Proposition 17.10.15 . E5064A497AB8 Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the segment $(\varphi _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. It suffices to show that \[  \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ a,\quad \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ b  \] as $t\to 0+$ and $t\to 1-$ respectively. In other words, we need to show that for any $c\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ c  \] as $t\to c$. For this purpose, observe that by proposition 17.10.7 , \[  \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{s\in (0,1)}\varphi _ s\leq \sup _{X}\varphi _ t\leq \left( \sup _ X \varphi _0 \right) \lor \left( \sup _ X\varphi _1 \right)  \] for any $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by proposition 5.17.3 . It suffices to show that any cluster point $\psi $ of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\to c$ is equal to $\varphi _ c$. By corollary 5.14.8 and the convexity proposition 17.10.7 , we have $\varphi _ c=\psi $ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . $\square$

title: Lemma 17.10.16

text: Lemma 17.10.16 . 3BEBB86C7F79 Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $0\leq a<b\leq 1$ and let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ be a subgeodesic such that $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$, $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, and \[  \psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (a,b).  \] Define \[  \gamma _ t= \begin{cases}  \psi _ t,& \textup{if }t\in (a,b),\\  \varphi _ t,& \textup{if }t\in [0,1]\setminus (a,b). \end{cases}  \] Then $(\gamma _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. The $L^1$-convergence of $\gamma _ t$ to $\varphi _0$ at $0$ and $\varphi _1$ at $1$ follows immediately from the corresponding property for $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$. It remains to prove that the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. Let \[  S=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:0<\operatorname{Re}z<1\} ,\quad S'=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} .  \] Let $\Phi $ and $\Psi $ be the complexifications of $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$ on the corresponding strips. Since $\Psi \geq \Phi $ on $X\times S'$, the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is equal to $\Phi \lor \Psi $ on $X\times S'$ and to $\Phi $ on $X\times (S\setminus S')$. By the gluing lemma corollary 5.14.20 , it is enough to verify that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {S'\ni z'\to z\\ x'\to x}}\Psi (x',z')\leq \Phi (x,z)  \] at every point $(x,z)\in X\times S$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ or $\operatorname{Re}z=b$. Suppose for instance that $a>0$, and let $(x_ j,z_ j)$ tend to $(x,z)$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ and $a<\operatorname{Re}z_ j<b$. Set $t_ j=\operatorname{Re}z_ j$. Since $(\psi _ t)_ t$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$, the sequence $\psi _{t_ j}$ converges to $\varphi _ a$ in $L^1$. Applying corollary 5.14.8 to this sequence gives \[  \varphi _ a=\inf _{m>0}\left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}\right).  \] For fixed $m$, the upper semicontinuity of $\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}\right)(x).  \] Letting $m\to \infty $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \varphi _ a(x).  \] Since $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _ a(x)$ when $\operatorname{Re}z=a$, this is the desired boundary inequality along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=a\} $. The same argument applies along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=b\} $ when $b<1$. Hence corollary 5.14.20 shows that the pasted complexification is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. $\square$

text: Definition 17.10.17 . 872270015CE7 A ray $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a subgeodesic ray in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ if for any $0\leq a\leq b$, the segment $(\ell _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We say $\ell $ emanates from $\ell _0$. The complexification of a subgeodesic ray $\ell $ is defined as the potential \[  \Phi \colon X\times \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad (x,z)\mapsto \ell _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x).  \] Note that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh, where $p_1\colon X\times \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} \rightarrow X$ is the natural projection.

Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Fix a model potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. See definition 16.3.18 for the definition. Definition 17.10.20 . 774DAAE2CF9E Let $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is the family of potentials $\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $ such that D0FE4F9BEB1B 17.10.21  egin{equation}   egin{split}  \varphi _ t=\operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}&  \left\{  \psi _ t: (\psi _{s})_ s 	extup{ is a subgeodesic from }\psi _0	extup{ to }\psi _1,ight.\ & \psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\left.\psi _0\leq \varphi _0,\psi _1\leq \varphi _1ight\} . \end{split} \end{equation} More generally, let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ ($a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$) be a curve in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. We say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic if the curve $(\varphi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is a geodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. The envelopes of the form ( 17.10.21 ) are usually referred to as the Perron envelopes . In general, the geodesic defined by ( 17.10.21 ) fails to have the correct limit when $t	o 0+$ or $t	o 1-$. Therefore, a priori it is not a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. In the sequel, we use the word geodesic only in situations where the endpoint behavior has been verified. Lemma 17.10.22 . BDEA4F06B7F1 Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Assume that there is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Proof. This is an immediate consequence of proposition 17.10.13 . $\square$ Example 17.10.23 . C16140E8B047 Let $\varphi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Then the subgeodesic $(\varphi _0+tC)_{t\in [0,1]}$ studied in example 17.10.6 is a geodesic. This follows easily from proposition 17.10.7 . In particular, when $C=0$, we find that the constant subgeodesic at $\varphi _0$ is indeed a geodesic, which we call the constant geodesic at $\varphi _0$. More generally, suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a geodesic and $C_1,C_2\in \mathbb {R}$, then $(\varphi _ t+C_1t+C_2)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a geodesic. This follows immediately from example 17.10.6 . Next we want to show that under mild assumptions, there exist subgeodesics between two potentials. The assumption below turns out to be necessary as well, as we shall prove in theorem 16.8.32 later. Proposition 17.10.24 . 8AB36536E36D Given $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ defined by ( 17.10.21 ) is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. Moreover, for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. If furthermore $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$), then $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. We refer to 16.5 for the definition of $\mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Our assumption means that $P_{	heta }[\varphi _0]=P_{	heta }[\varphi _1]=\phi $. As a consequence of this proposition, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is also a subgeodesic since $\varphi _ a,\varphi _ b\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ as well. Proof. After subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi _1$ and adding back the corresponding affine function of $t$, we may assume that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi $. It follows from proposition 17.10.7 that $\varphi _ t\leq \phi $ for all $t\in (0,1)$. In fact, we have the stronger estimate 991B9E91FD84 17.10.25  egin{equation}  \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} We first observe that when $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, so is $\varphi _0\land \varphi _1$, see proposition 16.5.49 . In particular, the constant subgeodesic $t\mapsto \varphi _0\land \varphi _1$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope ( 17.10.21 ). So C45355A6B32E 17.10.26  egin{equation}  \varphi _ t\geq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} By proposition 17.10.13 , $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic. 2 It follows from proposition 16.5.52 that $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. Next, we show that as $t	o 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. The corresponding result at $t=1$ is similar. We first argue the special case where $\varphi _0\preceq \varphi _1$. Take a constant $C>0$ such that \[  \varphi _0-C\leq \varphi _1.  \] Then $(\varphi _0-Ct)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is clearly a candidate in ( 17.10.21 ), see example 17.10.6 . Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, 431F43B008A4 17.10.27  egin{equation}  \varphi _0-Ct\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0. \end{equation} It follows that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t	o 0+$. Let us come back to the general case. By corollary 17.10.11 , $\{ \varphi _ t:t\in (0,1)\} $ is a relatively compact subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Let $\psi $ be an $L^1$-cluster point of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\searrow 0$, and it suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. For each $M\in \mathbb {N}$, we write \[  \varphi _0^ M=\varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M).  \] Observe that $\varphi _0^ M\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ by proposition 16.5.49 . Let $(\varphi _ t^ M)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$. Since $\varphi _0^ M\preceq \varphi _1$, the special case proved above applies to the geodesic $(\varphi _ t^ M)_ t$, and \[  \varphi _ t^ M\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0^ M \quad 	extup{as }t	o 0+.  \] Moreover, every candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$ is also a candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$, so \[  \varphi _ t^ M\leq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Letting $t	o 0+$ along a sequence for which $\varphi _ t	o \psi $ in $L^1$, and using corollary 5.14.8 , we obtain \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0^ M  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . On the other hand, by ( 17.10.25 ), $\psi \leq \varphi _0$. So it suffices to show that \[  \varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M)\xrightarrow {L^1} \varphi _0  \] as $M	o \infty $, which is shown in proposition 16.5.54 . Now we have shown that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Next, take $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$. We want to show that the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We may assume that $a<b$. The argument is the standard balayage argument. Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. The geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is the family of potentials $\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $ such that D0FE4F9BEB1B 17.10.21 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  \varphi _ t=\operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}&  \left\{  \psi _ t: (\psi _{s})_ s \textup{ is a subgeodesic from }\psi _0\textup{ to }\psi _1,\right.\\ & \psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\left.\psi _0\leq \varphi _0,\psi _1\leq \varphi _1\right\} . \end{split} \end{equation} More generally, let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ ($a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$) be a curve in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic if the curve $(\varphi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is a geodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$.

text: Proposition 17.10.24 . 8AB36536E36D Given $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ defined by ( 17.10.21 ) is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. Moreover, for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. If furthermore $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$), then $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. Proof. After subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi _1$ and adding back the corresponding affine function of $t$, we may assume that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi $. It follows from proposition 17.10.7 that $\varphi _ t\leq \phi $ for all $t\in (0,1)$. In fact, we have the stronger estimate 991B9E91FD84 17.10.25 \begin{equation}  \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} We first observe that when $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, so is $\varphi _0\land \varphi _1$, see proposition 16.5.49 . In particular, the constant subgeodesic $t\mapsto \varphi _0\land \varphi _1$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope ( 17.10.21 ). So C45355A6B32E 17.10.26 \begin{equation}  \varphi _ t\geq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} By proposition 17.10.13 , $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic. 2 It follows from proposition 16.5.52 that $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. Next, we show that as $t\to 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. The corresponding result at $t=1$ is similar. We first argue the special case where $\varphi _0\preceq \varphi _1$. Take a constant $C>0$ such that \[  \varphi _0-C\leq \varphi _1.  \] Then $(\varphi _0-Ct)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is clearly a candidate in ( 17.10.21 ), see example 17.10.6 . Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, 431F43B008A4 17.10.27 \begin{equation}  \varphi _0-Ct\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0. \end{equation} It follows that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t\to 0+$. Let us come back to the general case. By corollary 17.10.11 , $\{ \varphi _ t:t\in (0,1)\} $ is a relatively compact subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Let $\psi $ be an $L^1$-cluster point of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\searrow 0$, and it suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. For each $M\in \mathbb {N}$, we write \[  \varphi _0^ M=\varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M).  \] Observe that $\varphi _0^ M\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ by proposition 16.5.49 . Let $(\varphi _ t^ M)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$. Since $\varphi _0^ M\preceq \varphi _1$, the special case proved above applies to the geodesic $(\varphi _ t^ M)_ t$, and \[  \varphi _ t^ M\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0^ M \quad \textup{as }t\to 0+.  \] Moreover, every candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$ is also a candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$, so \[  \varphi _ t^ M\leq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Letting $t\to 0+$ along a sequence for which $\varphi _ t\to \psi $ in $L^1$, and using corollary 5.14.8 , we obtain \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0^ M  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 5.14.6 . On the other hand, by ( 17.10.25 ), $\psi \leq \varphi _0$. So it suffices to show that \[  \varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M)\xrightarrow {L^1} \varphi _0  \] as $M\to \infty $, which is shown in proposition 16.5.54 . Now we have shown that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Next, take $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$. We want to show that the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We may assume that $a<b$. The argument is the standard balayage argument. Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic by proposition 17.10.15 , we have $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (a,b)$. We define \[  \eta _ t= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  \psi _ t,& \quad \text{if }t\in (a,b),\\  \varphi _ t,& \quad \text{if }t\in (0,1)\setminus (a,b). \end{aligned} \right.  \] Extending it by setting $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$ and $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, the first part of the proof applied to the endpoints $\varphi _ a,\varphi _ b$ shows that $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for $t\in (a,b)$, the gluing lemma 17.10.16 shows that $(\eta _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t.  \] In particular, for $t\in (a,b)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t=\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t.  \] In other words, $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}=(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Finally, assume furthermore that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$). Thanks to ( 17.10.26 ), proposition 16.5.49 and proposition 16.5.52 , we find $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. $\square$ 2. ↩ Be careful, here $t\in (0,1)$ instead of $[0,1]$.

Taking supremum in ( 17.10.34 ), we find that 1B22CF257482 17.10.35  egin{equation}  \sup _{X\setminus Z} (\varphi _1-\varphi _ s)\leq (1-s)\adjustlimits \sup _{x\in X\setminus Z}\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t}\leq (1-s)C. \end{equation} When $s=0$, we deduce from corollary 5.15.21 and ( 17.10.32 ) that \[  C=\sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } \left(\varphi _1-\varphi _0ight)=\adjustlimits \sup _{x\in X\setminus Z}\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t}.  \] But this equality works equally well for the geodesic $(\varphi _{(1-s)t+s})_{t\in [0,1]}$ with the same argument. It follows that \[  \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } \left(\varphi _1-\varphi _ sight)=(1-s)\adjustlimits \sup _{x\in X\setminus Z}\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t}=(1-s)C.  \] Therefore, invoking corollary 5.15.21 again, we deduce that all inequalities in ( 17.10.35 ) are in fact equalities. In other words, 5825ABE1D62B 17.10.36  egin{equation}  \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _1-\varphi _0)= \adjustlimits \sup _{x\in X\setminus Z}\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t} =\sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } rac{\varphi _1-\varphi _ s}{1-s}. \end{equation} On the other hand, we have the trivial inequality when $s\in (0,1)$: \[  \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _1-\varphi _0)\leq s \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } rac{\varphi _ s-\varphi _0}{s}+ (1-s) \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } rac{\varphi _1-\varphi _ s}{1-s}.  \] Together with ( 17.10.36 ), we find that for $s\in (0,1)$, \[  \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _1-\varphi _0)\leq \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } rac{\varphi _ s-\varphi _0}{s}.  \] The reverse inequality follows from the convexity, and hence for $s\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } rac{\varphi _ s-\varphi _0}{s}=\sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _1-\varphi _0).  \] Using corollary 5.15.21 , we conclude ( 17.10.30 ). $\square$ 3. ↩ When dealing with convex functions, drawing a picture is the easiest way to keep track of the directions of inequalities.

text: Definition 17.10.38 . 2E335019C3A7 Let $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a family in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say $\ell $ is a geodesic ray in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\ell _0$ if for each $0\leq a\leq b$, the restriction $(\ell _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. The set of geodesic rays in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\phi $ is denoted by $\mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ has finite energy if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t>0$. The set of geodesic rays with finite energy is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ is bounded if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t\geq 0$. The set of bounded geodesic rays is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Given $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we write $\ell \leq \ell '$ if $\ell _ t\leq \ell '_ t$ for each $t\geq 0$. When $\phi =V_{\theta }$, we usually omit it from the notations and write $\mathcal{R}(X,\theta )$, $\mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta )$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$ respectively.

title: 17.10.40 The metrics on the spaces of potentials and rays
